    14052a811  7582             JNZ 0x14052a795
  Node offsets actually observed: +0x00 left pointer, +0x08 right pointer,
  +0x10 parent pointer, +0x19 byte flag, +0x20 qword compared with 0x100,
  +0x28 and +0x30 the two qwords handed to the callee. The +0x00/+0x08/+0x10
  pointer trio with a parent-based descent at 0x14052a7f8 is the MSVC
  red-black node shape; the +0x19 flag is asserted only as an observed
  offset, its exact field name is not established from this body.
  Epilogue returns the out-vector:
    14052a813  488bc6             MOV RAX,RSI
    14052a816  488b5c2450         MOV RBX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x50]
    14052a81b  488b742460         MOV RSI,qword ptr [RSP + 0x60]
    14052a820  488b7c2468         MOV RDI,qword ptr [RSP + 0x68]
    14052a825  4883c440           ADD RSP,0x40
    14052a829  415e               POP R14
    14052a82b  c3                 RET

Reading of the routine: it walks a tree held through argument 1, and for
each qualifying node appends two qwords copied from the node value into the
caller's vector. The appended payload is copied wholesale out of the tree.
The routine never writes to any object it reads from. It therefore cannot be
the producer of a +0xf4 flag on the objects it places in the vector.

Honest limits of this negative
-----------------------------
  1. The one CALL at 0x14052a7bf goes to 0x140516ab0. Its internal stores
     were NOT examined, per the scope stop. If 0x140516ab0 writes 0xf4 into
     the objects it appends, that write is invisible from inside
     FUN_14052a740. This is a substantive gap, not a formality.
  2. "No store to displacement 0xf4" is a statement about the code range
     0x14052a740..0x14052a82b only. A 0xf4 store reached indirectly, through
     a virtual dispatch or through callee 0x140516ab0, is not excluded.
  3. Flag provenance can also come from the constructor of these objects, or
     from the code that populates the tree in the first place. Neither is in
     this body, so neither is answered here.

Effect on the open question
---------------------------
  The hypothesis that FUN_14052a740 is the producer of the +0xf4 flags is
  not supported on the direct path. It relocates payloads from a tree into
  the candidate vector without touching the copied objects' fields. The only
  remaining way it could set +0xf4 is through callee 0x140516ab0.
  Exact next query if that is pursued: does 0x140516ab0 contain a store to
  displacement 0xf4, and does it dereference the pointers it receives as its
  third and fourth arguments?

===== END =====

===== Candidate append callee =====

Question: does FUN_140516ab0 write displacement 0xf4, or write through the two
pointers it is given?
Where: Vision3D.exe, copy project v3d_files_uncomp_copy/V3D_SKIP, program
/Vision3D.exe, opened read-only with update_analysis false. Mode confirmed
read_only true, active_transaction null. Nothing saved.

Context: this is the callee of FUN_14052a740, called at 0x14052a7bf.

ANSWER, two parts.
  1. Stores to displacement 0xf4: NONE. The byte 0xf4 does not occur even once
     anywhere in the 429-byte body, so there is no 0xf4 in any width, as a
     displacement or as anything else.
  2. Stores through R8 or R9: NONE. No store instruction in the body uses R8 or
     R9 as a base or index register, and neither register holds its incoming
     value at the time of any store. More strongly, the two incoming pointers are
     not object pointers at all: they are the BEGIN and END of a source range,
     and they are only ever read as range endpoints.

    Complete set of base registers across all 11 stores: RSP, RSI. Nothing else.
    Complete set of displacements across all 11 stores:
      0x00, 0x08, 0x10, 0x18, 0x20, 0x28, 0x30
    0xf4 is not among them, and R8/R9 are not among the bases.

  Calibrate step for modality 3, so the register IDs are not assumed:
    pcode_op_at 0x140516bfe shows the address expression as
    INT_ADD(register:0x30, const:0x10), and the instruction renders as
    [RSI + 0x10], so register 0x30 = RSI.
    pcode_op_at 0x140516b98 shows INT_ADD(const:0x98, register:0x20) rendering
    as [RSP + 0x98], so register 0x20 = RSP.
    pcode_op_at 0x140516ab5 shows the source COPY as register:0x80 rendering as
    R8, and 0x140516ab0 shows register:0x88 rendering as R9.
    Register ID map used throughout: 0x00 RAX, 0x08 RCX, 0x10 RDX, 0x18 RBX,
    0x20 RSP, 0x28 RBP, 0x30 RSI, 0x38 RDI, 0x80 R8, 0x88 R9, 0x90 R10,
    0x98 R11, 0xa0 R12, 0xa8 R13, 0xb0 R14, 0xb8 R15.

Part 2, the two incoming pointers
--------------------------------
Register write sets for R8 and R9 inside this body, extracted from the p-code
output varnodes of all 116 instructions:
  writes to R8: 140516b18, 140516b4c, 140516b88, 140516bab, 140516bbb,
                140516bc7, 140516be7, 140516beb, 140516bee, 140516c0f,
                140516c2a
  writes to R9: 140516ae0, 140516c42 (two outputs of that one instruction)
  reads of R8 before its first write at 140516b18: 140516ada, 140516ae0
So R8's incoming value is last consumed at 0x140516ae0 and never reloaded, and
R9's incoming value is destroyed at 0x140516ae0. From that point on neither
register holds the value it arrived with, on either control path.

The instruction that destroys both:
  140516ada  498bc0        MOV RAX,R8
  140516add  488bf1        MOV RSI,RCX
  140516ae0  4d2bc8        SUB R9,R8
  140516ae3  4d8bf1        MOV R14,R9
  140516ae6  49c1fe03      SAR R14,0x3
  140516aea  4d85f6        TEST R14,R14
  140516aed  0f845c010000  JZ 0x140516c4f
R9 minus R8, then divided by 8. That is a byte range length converted to an
element count. R8 and R9 are therefore an iterator pair, the begin and the end
of a source range, not two object pointers. This is the single most important
fact for the question: there is no object for this function to write a flag into.

Where the two values actually go, per path:
  Path A, capacity sufficient, entered at 0x140516c0f via
    140516b08  0f8301010000  JNC 0x140516c0f
    140516c0f  4d8bc1        MOV R8,R9
    140516c12  488bd0        MOV RDX,RAX
    140516c15  498bca        MOV RCX,R10
    140516c18  ff15d2528400  CALL qword ptr [0x140d5bef0]
    RAX still holds arg3 here because the write to RAX at 140516b22 lies on the
    fall-through path, which this path skips. So arg3 goes to RDX.
  Path B, reallocation, memmove at 0x140516bb1:
    140516b98  488b9c2498000000  MOV RBX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x98]
    140516ba0  488b942490000000  MOV RDX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x90]
    140516ba8  482bda           SUB RBX,RDX
    140516bab  4c8bc3           MOV R8,RBX
    140516bae  488bcf           MOV RCX,RDI
    140516bb1  ff1539538400     CALL qword ptr [0x140d5bef0]
    RDX = arg3, RCX = the new buffer plus the old byte count. arg3 is again the
    source.

Memmove argument convention on Windows x64 is dest in RCX, source in RDX, count
in R8. The target is identified from the code unit at the call site, no callee
body was entered:
  listing_code_unit_at 0x140d5bef0 -> label PTR_memmove_140d5bef0,
    bytes a8a10b0100000000, i.e. the CRT memmove import
  listing_code_unit_at 0x140d55230 -> label PTR__Xlength_error_140d55230,
    bytes 38780b0100000000, the MSVC _Xlength_error throw helper, called only on
    the vector-growth-check failure path at 0x140516b34
Therefore in every memmove of this body the incoming arg3 occupies RDX, the
source position, and never RCX, the destination position. arg3's buffer is only
ever read. arg4 is never dereferenced at all; it appears only in the two
subtractions above, as a range end.

Frame layout, and why the stack writes are not writes through the arguments
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Prologue, verbatim:
    140516ab0  4c894c2420        MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x20],R9
    140516ab5  4c89442418        MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x18],R8
    140516aba  4889542410        MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x10],RDX
    140516abf  48894c2408        MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x8],RCX
    140516ac4  53                PUSH RBX
    140516ac5  56                PUSH RSI
    140516ac6  57                PUSH RDI
    140516ac7  4154              PUSH R12
    140516ac9  4156              PUSH R14
    140516acb  4157              PUSH R15
    140516acd  4883ec48          SUB RSP,0x48
  Stack adjustment = 6 pushes of 8 plus 0x48 = 0x78.
  The four stores at the top of the body are the standard MSVC register homing
  of the four register arguments, written into the caller's shadow space before
  the frame is adjusted. After the adjustment they sit at:
    [RSP + 0x80] arg1, [RSP + 0x88] arg2, [RSP + 0x90] arg3, [RSP + 0x98] arg4
  and that is exactly what the body reads back, at 0x140516b7d reading 0x88,
  0x140516ba0 reading 0x90, 0x140516b98 reading 0x98, 0x140516bbf reading 0x88.
  The stores at 0x140516b62 and 0x140516b75 target offsets 0x20 and 0x28, which
  are callee locals, distinct from the argument homes at 0x88, 0x90 and 0x98.
  So writing the shadow slots is the prologue saving the arguments, not a store
  through R8 or R9.

What the body does, from the instruction stream
-----------------------------------------------
  Argument roles:
    arg1 RCX -> RSI at 0x140516add, the destination vector, three pointers at
    +0x00 _Myfirst, +0x08 _Mylast, +0x10 _Myend
    arg2 RDX -> [RSP + 0x88], the destination's old _Mylast
    arg3 R8  -> source range begin
    arg4 R9  -> source range end
  Early exit:
    140516ae0..140516aed, zero elements leaves immediately at 0x140516c4f
  Capacity test:
    140516af3  488b5110        MOV RDX,qword ptr [RCX + 0x10]
    140516af7  4c8b5108        MOV R10,qword ptr [RCX + 0x8]
    140516b08  0f8301010000    JNC 0x140516c0f
    Path A when capacity suffices, Path B otherwise.
  Path B, reallocation and three-way move:
    140516b18  49b8ffffffffffffff1f  MOV R8,0x1fffffffffffffff   ; max_size
    140516b34  ff15f6e68300          CALL qword ptr [0x140d55230] ; _Xlength_error
    140516b6d  e8be830900            CALL 0x1405aef30
      rel32 0x983be, next 0x140516b72, target 0x1405aef30, arithmetic checked
    140516b72  4c8bf8                MOV R15,RAX                 ; new buffer
    140516b8e  ff155c538400          CALL qword ptr [0x140d5bef0] ; memmove
    140516b94  4a8d3c3b              LEA RDI,[RBX + R15*0x1]
    140516bb1  ff1539538400          CALL qword ptr [0x140d5bef0] ; memmove
    140516bb7  488d0c3b              LEA RCX,[RBX + RDI*0x1]
    140516bca  ff1520538400          CALL qword ptr [0x140d5bef0] ; memmove
    140516bf5  e8862b0600            CALL 0x140579780
      rel32 0x62b86, next 0x140516bfa, target 0x140579780, arithmetic checked
  Commit the new header:
    140516bfa  4b8d04e7        LEA RAX,[R15 + R12*0x8]
    140516bfe  48894610        MOV qword ptr [RSI + 0x10],RAX
    140516c02  4b8d04f7        LEA RAX,[R15 + R14*0x8]
    140516c06  48894608        MOV qword ptr [RSI + 0x8],RAX
    140516c0a  4c893e          MOV qword ptr [RSI],R15
  Path B deferral, only if the ranges are not contiguous:
    140516c42  440fb6c8        MOVZX R9D,AL
    140516c46  e875a70d00      CALL 0x1405f13c0
      rel32 0xda775, next 0x140516c4b, target 0x1405f13c0, arithmetic checked
    Note R9 is reused here only as a small flag byte, R9D, after its range
    value was consumed. This write is the second and last write to R9.
  Path A commit:
    140516c4b  4c017608        ADD qword ptr [RSI + 0x8],R14
  Epilogue:
    140516c4f  4883c448        ADD RSP,0x48
    140516c5c  c3              RET

Reading of the routine: it is a range-append for a vector of 8-byte elements.
The stride is established three times independently, by SAR R14,0x3 at
0x140516ae6, by the scale of 8 in the two LEA instructions at 0x140516bfa and
0x140516c02, and by the element arithmetic in the commit. It moves qword
elements from the source range into the destination vector and rewrites the
vector's three header pointers. It does not inspect an element, does not write
into an element, and has no field-level store at all. Its only object writes are
the three header pointers of the caller's vector.

Correction to the previous section
----------------------------------
  In "Candidate vector helper flag" the call at 0x14052a7bf was described as
  handing the callee two pointers, node value +0x28 and node value +0x30, with
  the open question being whether the callee writes through them. That framing
  is now sharpened. The pair is not two independent object pointers but the
  begin and end of one source range: 0x140516ae0 subtracts them and 0x140516ae6
  divides the difference by 8. Nothing in the previous section is contradicted;
  the two registers are confirmed to carry those exact values, but their meaning
  is a range, and neither is dereferenced as an object.

Effect on the open question
---------------------------
  The +0xf4 flag is not produced anywhere on this path. The append chain from
  FUN_14052a740 is now fully closed as far as this binary allows:
    FUN_14052a740  writes only its own frame and the out-vector header
    FUN_140516ab0  writes only its own frame and the out-vector header,
                   reads the source range without writing through it
  Neither can set a field on any object. If +0xf4 is ever set on the objects that
  reach doc+0x2478, it is set before they get here, or by the constructor or by
  the code that fills the tree that FUN_14052a740 walks, none of which is in
  this body.
  Honest limits that remain:
    1. The three memmoves and the two calls to 0x1405aef30, 0x140579780 and
       0x1405f13c0 were not entered, per the scope stop. memmove is a CRT bulk
       copy and cannot write a 0xf4 field on its own, but the three internal
       callees are Vision3D code and were not examined. A 0xf4 store inside
       0x1405f13c0, the contiguous-range deferral helper, would not show up here.
    2. "No store to 0xf4" is scoped to the range 0x140516ab0..0x140516c5c.
    3. memmove is passed arg3 as its source. If the source buffer itself aliased
       a destination already holding 0xf4 values, a bulk copy could move such a
       value, but no 0xf4 field is written by any instruction in this body.

===== END =====
===== Fiducial flag bits =====

Question: which bits does VerifyAndSetFiducialSections OR into the flag dword, and
what object receives them?

Scope honored: "Stop inside VerifyAndSetFiducialSections." Every instruction quoted
below lies in 0x1405411c0..0x140541b65. No callee body was entered. (The two exceptions
where I identify an external callee are named from their IAT label, not from their code;
see "External callees named by IAT label" below.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Function identity
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Ghidra name      VerifyAndSetFiducialSections
  body             0x1405411c0 .. 0x140541b65   (0x9a5 = 2470 bytes)
  instructions     563
  convention       __thiscall
  signature        bool __thiscall VerifyAndSetFiducialSections(
                       CDataCaoTraitement * this, bool param_1,
                       CRect param_2, CRect param_3, bool param_4, ushort * param_5)

Prologue (hot-patch frame, so RBP is NOT RSP_final):

  1405411c0  488bc4             MOV RAX,RSP
  1405411c3  885010             MOV byte ptr [RAX + 0x10],DL
  1405411c6  55                 PUSH RBP
  1405411cf  4157               PUSH R15
  1405411d1  488da828feffff     LEA RBP,[RAX + -0x1d8]
  1405411d8  4881eca0020000     SUB RSP,0x2a0

So RBP = RSP_entry - 0x1d8. Two consequences used below:

  * [RBP+0x1e8] = [RSP_entry+0x10] = the home slot DL was parked in at 0x1405411c3.
    So [RBP+0x1e8] holds param_1 (the `bool`).
  * [RBP-0x80] is a genuine local (frame low is RSP_entry-0x2a0; [RBP-0x80] =
    RSP_entry-0x258, which is 0x48 bytes above the frame low).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The two OR stores, quoted
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  ADDR       BYTES            INSTRUCTION
  1405415d8  099ff4000000     OR  dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX
  140541836  099ff4000000     OR  dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX

These are the ONLY two OR-to-0xf4 stores in the function, and in fact the only two
references to a 0xf4 displacement that are stores. Confirmed by two independent
modalities over the full 563-instruction listing, which agree exactly (10 references):

  search_instructions query "0xf4", start 0x1405411c0, end 0x140541b65  -> count = 10
    140541355  8483f4000000  TEST byte ptr [RBX + 0xf4],AL
    14054139f  f683f400000001  TEST byte ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0x1
    1405413cc  83a3f4000000fe  AND  dword ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0xfffffffe
    1405413e8  f683f400000002  TEST byte ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0x2
    140541433  f683f400000002  TEST byte ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0x2
    140541460  83a3f4000000fd  AND  dword ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0xfffffffd
    1405415d8  099ff4000000  OR   dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX     <-- store 1
    140541836  099ff4000000  OR   dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX     <-- store 2
    14054199b  83a1f4000000fe  AND  dword ptr [RCX + 0xf4],0xfffffffe
    1405419ab  83a1f4000000fd  AND  dword ptr [RCX + 0xf4],0xfffffffd

  positive control: count = 10 > 0, and the two ORs are among the 10. The same set is
  reproduced by an independent pass that filters the 563 disassembled rows on the
  literal text "0xf4]" -> 10 rows, identical.

Listing completeness note: concatenating the 563 instruction byte strings gives 4922 hex
chars = 2461 bytes, against a 2470-byte span. The 9-byte difference is 9 one-byte gaps.
Each was read individually and typed; they are 0xCC (7 of them) and 0x90 (2 of them)
sitting between seven identical guard-report calls at 0x1405418bb..0x1405418e4:

  1405418bb  e8e6dd2300  CALL 0x14077f6a6
  1405418c0  cc         <-- gap (int3)
  1405418c1  e8e0dd2300  CALL 0x14077f6a6
  1405418c6  cc         <-- gap
  1405418cc  cc
  1405418d2  90         <-- gap (nop)
  1405418d3  e8cedd2300  CALL 0x14077f6a6
  1405418d8  cc
  1405418de  90
  1405418e4  cc

These seven calls are the shared failure handlers for the range guards in the function
(0x14054167f JS -> 0x1405418d3, 0x1405417f3 JS -> 0x1405418d9, 0x1405417fd JGE -> 0x1405418d9,
0x14054162e JLE -> 0x1405418df), i.e. one reporting call per guard so each guard can
report its own state. They are single inter-instruction bytes and cannot conceal a 6-byte
OR ... [reg+0xf4],reg. Conclusion unaffected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The instruction that sets RDI before each OR
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Store 1 (0x1405415d8):

  1405415af  488b38         MOV  RDI,qword ptr [RAX]

    with, immediately above it,
  1405415ab  488b4608       MOV  RAX,qword ptr [RSI + 0x8]

    and RDI is not written again between 0x1405415af and 0x1405415d8.

Store 2 (0x140541836):

  140541807  4a8b3ce8       MOV  RDI,qword ptr [RAX + R13*0x8]

    with, immediately above it,
  140541803  488b4608       MOV  RAX,qword ptr [RSI + 0x8]

    and RDI is not written again between 0x140541807 and 0x140541836.

Provenance of those RDI setters, established by p-code register write-set sweep over the
entire function (the authoritative modality for "which register was written where"):

  writes to RDI:  1405412a9 MOV EDI,R12D / 140541471 INC EDI /
                  1405415af MOV RDI,[RAX] / 140541659 MOV RDI,R12 /
                  1405417e0 INC RDI / 140541807 MOV RDI,[RAX + R13*0x8] /
                  1405418ed MOV RDI,[RBP + 0x50] / 140541b62 POP RDI

  So the last RDI definition before each OR is unambiguously the one quoted. Note the
  interleaving: the write at 0x1405417e0 (INC RDI) is the inner loop's element counter,
  and it is 0x27 bytes past store 1 and 0x58 bytes before store 2; the store-2 RDI
  reload at 0x140541807 is what discards it.

Both forms are the same shape: RDI = *( RAX + k*8 ) where RAX = [RSI+0x8]. So RDI is a
POINTER LOADED FROM AN ELEMENT of a vector whose data pointer lives at [RSI+0x8], not the
element itself. The vector at [RSI+0x8] therefore holds 8-byte POINTERS, and RDI is the
pointee.

  store 1: k = 0     -> the FIRST element
  store 2: k = R13   -> the element at index R13

R13 at store 2 is the index chosen by the inner loop. That loop is a running best-of scan
on a floating-point key:

  1405417bd  660f2ff7       COMISD XMM6,XMM7
  1405417c1  760d           JBE    0x1405417d0
  1405417c3  0f28fe         MOVAPS XMM7,XMM6
  1405417c6  4489bde0010000 MOV    dword ptr [RBP + 0x1e0],R15D
  1405417cd  4c8bef         MOV    R13,RDI
  ...
  1405417e0  48ffc7         INC    RDI
  1405417e6  483b4610       CMP    RAX,qword ptr [RSI + 0x10]
  1405417ea  0f8c80feffff   JL     0x140541670

XMM7 starts at zero (0x140541649 XORPS XMM7,XMM7) and is only overwritten when XMM6
compares strictly greater, so the scan retains the extreme of the per-element value
produced by the call at 0x14054169e, together with that element's index in R13. I am not
asserting which extreme is "better"; that is a domain question outside this binary.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The instruction that sets EBX before each OR
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Store 1 (0x1405415d8):

  1405415b7  8b1a           MOV  EBX,dword ptr [RDX]

    On pass 1, RDX is established immediately above by
  140541571  488d5580       LEA  RDX,[RBP + -0x80]

    and the next RDX write is 0x1405415c8 (MOV EDX,0x5), strictly AFTER the load.

    On pass 2 the LEA does NOT re-execute -- it sits before the loop head 0x140541593,
    and the back edge 0x1405418b6 targets 0x140541593, not 0x140541571. RDX is instead
    carried into pass 2 from the previous pass's tail. See section 4; this is why the two
    passes reach the same dword by different routes.

Store 2 (0x140541836):

  140541815  8b18           MOV  EBX,dword ptr [RAX]

    with RAX established by
  140541810  488b442450     MOV  RAX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x50]

    and [RSP+0x50] itself established by
  140541571  488d5580       LEA  RDX,[RBP + -0x80]
  140541575  4889542450     MOV  qword ptr [RSP + 0x50],RDX

So both EBX setters read the SAME 4-byte local: [RBP-0x80].

Last-definition proof (p-code write set for EBX across the function):
  140541203 MOV RBX,RCX / 1405412cd MOV EBX,R12D / 1405412f7 MOV RBX,RAX /
  140541473 MOVSXD RBX,EDI / 1405415b7 MOV EBX,[RDX] / 1405416a4 MOV RBX,RAX /
  140541815 MOV EBX,[RAX] / 1405418fe MOV RBX,R12 / 1405419b7 INC RBX /
  1405419df MOV RBX,R12 / 140541a56 INC RBX / 140541ada MOV BL,0x1 /
  140541af5 XOR BL,BL / 140541b3f MOV RBX,[R11 + 0x50]

  The next EBX write after 0x1405415b7 is 0x1405416a4; after 0x140541815 it is
  0x1405418fe. The only instruction between each EBX load and its OR is the CALL at
  0x1405415d2 / 0x140541830, and EBX is callee-saved under the Windows x64 ABI, so the
  call cannot perturb it. The loads are therefore the live values at the stores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Value of EBX at each store  -- THE ANSWER
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

EBX is NOT a constant in the instruction. It is a dword loaded from an iterating cursor.
The cursor is [RSP+0x50]; it is written in exactly two places and read in exactly three:

  140541575  4889542450  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x50],RDX    ; init  = &[RBP-0x80]
  140541602  488b542450  MOV RDX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x50]   ; read
  140541810  488b442450  MOV RAX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x50]   ; read (the EBX source for store 2)
  140541875  488b542450  MOV RDX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x50]   ; read
  140541893  4883c204    ADD RDX,0x4                    ; advance
  140541897  4889542450  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x50],RDX    ; store = advanced cursor

The cursor walks a 2-element dword array in the frame, and that array has exactly two
writes in the whole function, both constants:

  140541539  c7458001000000  MOV dword ptr [RBP + -0x80],0x1     <-- arr[0] = 1
  140541540  c7458402000000  MOV dword ptr [RBP + -0x7c],0x2     <-- arr[1] = 2

([RBP-0x7c] is arr[1] because the cursor advances by 4: 0x140541893 ADD RDX,0x4 with
RDX loaded from [RSP+0x50] at 0x140541875 turns &[RBP-0x80] into &[RBP-0x7c].)

The initializer dominates both loads. 0x140541539 is a join point reached by two
branches, and nothing branches out of the 0x140541539..0x140541547 block, and no branch
target lands anywhere in (0x140541539, 0x1405415b7):

  1405414dd  755a           JNZ 0x140541539
  1405414e3  7d54           JGE 0x140541539

The loop that drives the cursor runs 1 or 2 times, and both OR stores execute once per
pass:

  outer head / store-1 block
  140541593  4c8b740de8     MOV R14,qword ptr [RBP + RCX*0x1 + -0x18]
  14054159d  756f           JNZ 0x14054160e
  1405415a4  48837e1000     CMP qword ptr [RSI + 0x10],0x0
  1405415a9  7e63           JLE 0x14054160e
  1405415af  488b38         MOV RDI,qword ptr [RAX]        <-- store 1 receiver
  1405415b7  8b1a           MOV EBX,dword ptr [RDX]        <-- store 1 bits
  1405415d8  099ff4000000   OR  dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX <-- store 1

  cursor advance + loop tail
  140541881  440fb6ade8010000  MOVZX R13D,byte ptr [RBP + 0x1e8]
  140541889  41ffc0         INC  R8D
  14054188c  44898500020000  MOV  dword ptr [RBP + 0x200],R8D
  140541893  4883c204       ADD  RDX,0x4
  140541897  4889542450     MOV  qword ptr [RSP + 0x50],RDX
  14054189c  4883c108       ADD  RCX,0x8
  1405418a0  48894c2448     MOV  qword ptr [RSP + 0x48],RCX
  1405418a5  418bc4         MOV  EAX,R12D
  1405418a8  4180fd01       CMP  R13B,0x1
  1405418ac  0f94c0         SETZ AL
  1405418af  ffc0           INC  EAX
  1405418b1  443bc0         CMP  R8D,EAX
  1405418b4  7d2f           JGE  0x1405418e5
  1405418b6  e9d8fcffff     JMP  0x140541593          <-- back edge to outer head

  R8D is seeded at 0x14054156a (4489a500020000 MOV dword ptr [RBP+0x200],R12D) and the
  limit is R12D + (param_1 == 1) + 1. So the loop makes 1 pass when param_1 != 1 and
  2 passes when param_1 == 1. The store-2 block at 0x140541803..0x140541836 sits between
  the head and the tail, so it runs once per pass too.

Therefore:

  pass 1  (both stores):  EBX = arr[0] = 1
  pass 2  (both stores, only when param_1 == 1):  EBX = arr[1] = 2

  ==> EBX at 0x1405415d8 = 1, or 1 then 2 across the two passes.
  ==> EBX at 0x140541836 = 1, or 1 then 2 across the two passes.

The two passes reach those dwords by DIFFERENT routes, and this matters, so here is each
route verified rather than assumed.

  Pass 1, store 1 (0x1405415b7):  RDX comes from the constant LEA at 0x140541571,
    RDX = &[RBP-0x80] = &arr[0]. No CALL lies between 0x140541571 and 0x1405415b7
    (0x140541575, 57a, 57d, 582, 58a, 593, 598, 59d, 59f, 5a4, 5a9, 5ab, 5af, 5b2), so
    nothing can clobber the caller-saved RDX in between. EBX = *(arr[0]) = 1.

  Pass 1, store 2 (0x140541815):  RAX is loaded from the cursor slot at 0x140541810
    (488b442450 MOV RAX,qword ptr [RSP + 0x50]). The cursor slot was written at
    0x140541575 with &[RBP-0x80] and has not been written since (the only other write is
    0x140541897, which is later). So RAX = &arr[0] and EBX = *(arr[0]) = 1.

  Pass 2, store 2 (0x140541815):  by the time store 2 runs a second time, the cursor
    HAS advanced, so RAX = &arr[1] = &[RBP-0x7c] and EBX = *(arr[1]) = 2. This is the
    direct route: the cursor is the mechanism.

  Pass 2, store 1 (0x1405415b7):  this is the indirect route. The LEA at 0x140541571 is
    not re-executed, so RDX must be carried in. Full RDX write list over
    0x140541560..0x1405418bb (p-code register write set), in address order:

      140541571 LEA RDX,[RBP + -0x80]     1405416c5 MOV RDX,RAX
      1405415c8 MOV EDX,0x5              1405416f5 MOV EDX,[RAX + 0x20]
      1405415de XOR EDX,EDX              140541724 MOV EDX,0x2
      1405415f1 MOV RDX,[R14 + 0x10]     14054177e MOV EDX,[RAX + 0x20]
      140541602 MOV RDX,[RSP + 0x50]     1405417ad MOV EDX,0x2
      140541638 LEA RDX,[RBP + 0x80]     140541826 MOV EDX,0x5
      140541693 LEA RDX,[RBP + 0x110]    14054183c MOVSXD RDX,[RBP + 0x1e0]
      1405416ad LEA RDX,[RBP + 0x80]     140541856 MOV RDX,[R14 + 0x10]
      140541875 MOV RDX,[RSP + 0x50]     140541893 ADD RDX,0x4

    The last RDX write before the back edge is 0x140541893 ADD RDX,0x4, and 0x140541897
    then stores it back to the cursor. Between 0x140541897 and the JMP at 0x1405418b6
    there is no RDX write (0x14054189c, 8a0, 8a5, 8a8, 8ac, 8af, 8b1, 8b4, 8b6), and
    none in 0x140541593..0x1405415b7 either. So on entry to pass 2, RDX = the advanced
    cursor = &[RBP-0x7c] = &arr[1], and 0x1405415b7 loads EBX = *(arr[1]) = 2.

    I want to be explicit that this pass-2 store-1 route runs on a register the compiler
    left holding a value, not on a value the code re-derives. It is correct here because
    the RDX write set is fully enumerated above and contains nothing in between. It is
    also the one place in this answer where a different compiler schedule would have
    changed the answer, so it is flagged rather than buried.

  The cursor is advanced at 0x140541893/0x140541897, i.e. AFTER the last read on the
  final pass, so it is never read at &[RBP-0x78] or beyond. The only two values EBX can
  ever hold at either OR are 0x1 and 0x2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Which bits: bit 0 and bit 1 only -- and this is provable from the flag itself
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The same function reads and clears precisely those two bits of the same dword, which
pins the field's width:

  bit 0  == 0x1
    14054139f  f683f400000001  TEST byte ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0x1
    1405413cc  83a3f4000000fe  AND  dword ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0xfffffffe   ; clear bit 0
    14054199b  83a1f4000000fe  AND  dword ptr [RCX + 0xf4],0xfffffffe   ; clear bit 0

  bit 1  == 0x2
    1405413e8  f683f400000002  TEST byte ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0x2
    140541433  f683f400000002  TEST byte ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0x2
    140541460  83a3f4000000fd  AND  dword ptr [RBX + 0xf4],0xfffffffd   ; clear bit 1
    1405419ab  83a1f4000000fd  AND  dword ptr [RCX + 0xf4],0xfffffffd   ; clear bit 1

0xFFFFFFFE = ~0x1 and 0xFFFFFFFD = ~0x2. So the +0xf4 dword carries a two-bit mask, and
the values OR'd in (1 and 2) are exactly its two defined bits.

  ==> The function ORs in BIT 0 (pass 1) and BIT 1 (pass 2, when param_1 == 1).
  ==> No bit at or above bit 2 is ever set or cleared by this function. The mask is
      two bits wide. This is a complete statement about the field's use in this
      function, not an inference about other writers elsewhere in the binary.

The clear sites also show the same object shape, closing the loop on the receiver: at
0x14054199b/0x1405419ab the base is RCX, loaded by
  140541997  488b0cdf       MOV RCX,qword ptr [RDI + RBX*0x8]
i.e. the same "load a pointer out of a vector, write a dword at +0xf4" pattern as the two
OR stores. Set and clear of these two bits are performed on the same kind of object.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. What object receives them
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The receiver is NOT `this`. It is an object reached through a per-section vector:

  RAX = [RSI + 0x8]          ; RSI is a vector header; +0x8 is its data pointer
  RDI = [RAX + k*8]          ; a POINTER stored in the vector; RDI is the pointee
  flag dword at RDI + 0xf4

So: a `std::vector`-shaped object at a per-section slot, holding 8-byte pointers to
fiducial objects; the flag dword is at offset +0xf4 of the pointed-to fiducial object.
The vector itself is selected from a frame table indexed by RCX, which steps +8 per
outer pass (0x14054189c ADD RCX,0x8):

  store 1:  RSI = [RBP + RCX*0x1 + -0x78]   (0x14054159f, 488b740d88)
            R14 = [RBP + RCX*0x1 + -0x18]   (0x140541593, 4c8b740de8)
            k = 0   (first element)
  store 2:  RSI = same vector as the pass-1 RSI for this pass
            k = R13 (the index the inner best-of scan settled on)

The frame slots that table indexes are filled in the preamble:

  14054154b  488945e8   MOV qword ptr [RBP + -0x18],RAX   ; RAX = &[RBP + -0x40]
  140541553  488945f0   MOV qword ptr [RBP + -0x10],RAX   ; RAX = &[RBP + -0x68]
  14054155b  48894588   MOV qword ptr [RBP + -0x78],RAX   ; RAX = &[RBP + 0x20]
  140541563  48894590   MOV qword ptr [RBP + -0x70],RAX   ; RAX = &[RBP + -0x8]

The receiver's field at +0x20 is read immediately before each OR and is used as the
first %d of the log message, identifying the fiducial:

  1405415bd  448b4f20       MOV R9D,dword ptr [RDI + 0x20]
  1405415c1  4c8d0590d09000 LEA R8,[0x140e4e658]
  1405415c8  ba05000000     MOV EDX,0x5
  1405415cd  488d4c2458     LEA RCX,[RSP + 0x58]
  1405415d2  ff15801c8100   CALL qword ptr [0x140d53258]
  1405415d8  099ff4000000   OR  dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX

  14054181b  448b4f20       MOV R9D,dword ptr [RDI + 0x20]
  14054181f  4c8d0532ce9000 LEA R8,[0x140e4e658]
  140541826  ba05000000     MOV EDX,0x5
  14054182b  488d4c2458     LEA RCX,[RSP + 0x58]
  140541830  ff15221a8100   CALL qword ptr [0x140d53258]
  140541836  099ff4000000   OR  dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX

Format string at 0x140e4e658 (Ghidra data unit):
  ds "Fiducial #%d will be used for section %d\n"

Argument mapping: R9 = *(int*)(receiver + 0x20) = the fiducial number; the second %d is
the stack argument set at 0x1405415b9 / 0x140541817:

  1405415b9  895c2420  MOV dword ptr [RSP + 0x20],EBX
  140541817  895c2420  MOV dword ptr [RSP + 0x20],EBX

  ... which is the very same EBX that the next instruction ORs into +0xf4.

So the log line and the store agree: the dword OR'd at +0xf4 is the SECTION NUMBER, and
the message reads "Fiducial #<n> will be used for section <1 or 2>". The pass-2 value of
2 is the second section; the log's second %d and the OR'd mask are literally the same
value in the same register. This is the strongest available confirmation that the bits
mean "which of sections 1 and 2 this fiducial was selected for".

  ==> The receiver is a fiducial object pointed to by an element of a per-section
      vector; its +0xf4 dword is a 2-bit "used for section" mask, and this function
      sets the bit(s) for the section(s) it just selected the fiducial for.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. External callees named by IAT label (not entered)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Per the stop condition I did not enter any callee. The only one I need to name is the
call target of both 0x1405415d2 and 0x140541830, identified from the label of the
indirect operand rather than from its body:

  0x140d53258   label  PTR_Write_140d53258

The other rel32 targets quoted in this section, re-derived from the encodings rather than
copied from the rendered text:

  1405415c1  4c8d0590d09000    LEA  R8,  rel32 = 0x0090D090 -> 0x140e4e658
  14054181f  4c8d0532ce9000    LEA  R8,  rel32 = 0x009ECE32 -> 0x140e4e658
  1405415d2  ff15801c8100      CALL [rip] rel32 = 0x00811C80 -> 0x140d53258
  140541830  ff15221a8100      CALL [rip] rel32 = 0x00811A22 -> 0x140d53258
  1405415e7  e8241d1a00        CALL rel32   = 0x001A1D24 -> 0x1406e3310
  1405418b6  e9d8fcffff        JMP  rel32   = 0xFFFF FCD8 -> 0x140541593
  1405418b4  7d2f              JGE  rel8    = 0x2f       -> 0x1405418e5
  140541613  0f8570020000      JNZ  rel32   = 0x00000270 -> 0x140541889
  140541623  0f8e60020000      JLE  rel32   = 0x00000260 -> 0x140541889
  1405414dd  755a              JNZ  rel8    = 0x5a       -> 0x140541539
  1405414e3  7d54              JGE  rel8    = 0x54       -> 0x140541539

  positive control for the rel32 arithmetic: 140541206 488d15e3d29000 LEA RDX,
  rel32 = 0x0090D2E3 -> 0x140e4e4f0, matching the listing's own rendering of that LEA.

Note the 7-byte LEA encodings. 0x1405415c1 is 7 bytes, not 8:
  4C 8D 05 90 D0 90 00  = LEA r8, [rip+0x0090D090]
and the byte following it (0xba) is the first byte of 0x1405415c8's MOV EDX,0x5. I
initially mis-transcribed this as an 8-byte operand; a fresh memory_read caught it. Both
LEAs are 7 bytes and were re-verified at 7 bytes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Limits of this answer, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * Everything above is derived from instructions inside VerifyAndSetFiducialSections.
    The receiver object's class is NOT named, because nothing inside this function names
    it; the +0xf4 field and the vector-of-pointers shape are the strongest claims
    available from here. Naming the class needs the callers or the owning type's vftable.
  * The OR'd bits are proven to be within {0x1, 0x2} because [RBP-0x80] has exactly one
    write in this function and [RSP+0x50] is read at most twice. That reasoning is
    closed within the function and does not depend on any callee: the only instruction
    between each EBX load and its OR is a call that preserves EBX.
  * Whether a given run takes 1 or 2 passes depends on param_1 (== 1 -> 2 passes). I did
    not determine what callers pass, so I am reporting both cases rather than picking one.
  * The inner best-of scan's XMM6 value is produced by a call at 0x14054169e whose body I
    did not enter, so I describe it as "the value the per-element call returns" and make
    no claim about what it measures.
  * The two OR sites and the four bit-test/clear sites use different base registers
    (RDI, RBX, RCX) but identical structure; I have matched them by encoding and
    displacement, not by a dataflow proof that they are the same runtime object.

===== Fiducial object type =====

Question: what type of object receives the two OR stores? Inside
VerifyAndSetFiducialSections the first receiver is loaded at 0x1405415af from the vector
whose header address was stored at [RBP - 0x78]. Quote the call or constructor in this
function that places a pointer into that vector. Name the object's class from a symbol,
a vtable store, or a log string at that call. If the pointer is an existing object
rather than a new one, say which register it comes from.

Scope honored: "Stop inside VerifyAndSetFiducialSections." Every instruction quoted
below lies in 0x1405411c0..0x140541b65. No callee body was entered, and none was read.
External callees are identified only by their IAT label or by a decorated-name string
that already exists in the binary as a data unit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The object is a CMire.

  The pointer is NOT newly constructed in this function. It is an existing object and
  it comes from register RAX: RAX is the return value of GetLineMire at 0x1405412f1, and
  it is stashed to [RSP+0x40] at 0x1405412fa before being handed to the container.

  The call that places it into that vector is:

    14054138b  4c8d442440  LEA   R8,[RSP + 0x40]
    140541390  488b5530    MOV   RDX,qword ptr [RBP + 0x30]
    140541394  488d4d20    LEA   RCX,[RBP + 0x20]
    140541398  e8a3e6ffff  CALL  0x14053fa40

  Two notes on the naming evidence, because the question allowed three routes and only
  one of them actually exists here:

    * There is NO vtable store anywhere in this function. Proven in section 5.
    * The string at the call does not name a class; it names a role ("Fiducial").
      See section 6.
    * The class name therefore comes from the third route, a symbol: the decorated name
      of the producer call in this same function, ?GetLineMire@CDataCao@@QEAAPEAVCMire@@_J@Z.
      See section 4.

  The callee 0x14053fa40 is itself unnamed, and the constructor 0x14051d560 is unnamed.
  Neither places the object; they are named only as far as section 3 goes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Which vector: the [RBP-0x78] slot, and why it is provably that slot
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The frame table is built in a straight-line block before the pass loop:

    14054154b  488945e8    MOV  qword ptr [RBP + -0x18],RAX     ; -> &[RBP-0x40]
    14054154f  488d4598    LEA  RAX,[RBP + -0x68]
    140541553  488945f0    MOV  qword ptr [RBP + -0x10],RAX     ; -> &[RBP-0x68]
    140541557  488d4520    LEA  RAX,[RBP + 0x20]
    14054155b  48894588    MOV  qword ptr [RBP + -0x78],RAX     ; -> &[RBP+0x20]   <== the vector
    14054155f  488d45f8    LEA  RAX,[RBP + -0x8]
    140541563  48894590    MOV  qword ptr [RBP + -0x70],RAX     ; -> &[RBP-0x8]

  The slot is read with an index register:

    14054159f  488b740d88  MOV  RSI,qword ptr [RBP + RCX*0x1 + -0x78]
    1405415ab  488b4608    MOV  RAX,qword ptr [RSI + 0x8]
    1405415af  488b38      MOV  RDI,qword ptr [RAX]            ; the OR'd receiver

  Correction of a gap I left open last time: I previously recorded that the value of
  RCX at that load was not established, so it was not pinned whether the first receiver
  came from slot [RBP-0x78] or slot [RBP-0x70]. It is now closed. R12 is zeroed at
  function entry:

    14054122e  4533e4      XOR  R12D,R12D

  and the pass loop advances the index by 8 from a zero base, so the first pass indexes
  slot 0, i.e. [RBP-0x78], which is &[RBP+0x20]. The second pass indexes slot 8, i.e.
  [RBP-0x70], which is &[RBP-0x8]. [RBP+0x20] is therefore the section-1 container and
  [RBP-0x8] the section-2 container, which is consistent with the OR'd bit being 1 on
  the first pass and 2 on the second.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The five containers, and the one the question asks about
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Five locals are constructed by one unnamed function and destroyed by one other, in
  mirrored order:

    140541277  488d4d48  LEA  RCX,[RBP + 0x48]     ; 14054127b  CALL 0x14051d560  (ctor)
    140541281  488d4dc0  LEA  RCX,[RBP + -0x40]    ; 140541285  CALL 0x14051d560
    14054128b  488d4d98  LEA  RCX,[RBP + -0x68]    ; 14054128f  CALL 0x14051d560
    140541295  488d4d20  LEA  RCX,[RBP + 0x20]     ; 140541299  CALL 0x14051d560  <== ours
    14054129f  488d4df8  LEA  RCX,[RBP + -0x8]     ; 1405412a3  CALL 0x14051d560
                                                    ; 140541b05  CALL 0x14051ef30  (dtor)
    140541b01  488d4d20  LEA  RCX,[RBP + 0x20]     ;   the dtor of ours

  The constructor at 0x140541299 does NOT place an object pointer. It initialises the
  container header. The question asks for the call that places a pointer, so it is not
  the answer; it is quoted here only to show that [RBP+0x20] is a constructed local and
  not a borrowed member.

  Layout, read straight out of the use sites: +0x8 is the data array, +0x10 is the
  element count.

    1405415a4  48837e1000    CMP  qword ptr [RSI + 0x10],0x0   ; count == 0 ?
    1405415ab  488b4608      MOV  RAX,qword ptr [RSI + 0x8]    ; data
    1405415af  488b38        MOV  RDI,qword ptr [RAX]          ; element 0  (8 bytes wide)
    140541807  4a8b3ce8      MOV  RDI,qword ptr [RAX + R13*0x8] ; element k (8 bytes wide)

  Elements are 8 bytes, so this is a container of pointers, not of objects. That matters:
  the thing that receives the OR store is the pointee of a stored pointer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The insert call, and where its value comes from
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  0x14053fa40 is called six times with the shape (container, cursor, address-of-value).
  Two of those six fill [RBP+0x20]:

    container [RBP+0x48]  "all mires" list
      14054130c  e82fe7ffff  CALL 0x14053fa40    RCX=[RBP+0x48]  RDX=[RBP+0x58]  R8=[RSP+0x40]

    container [RBP-0x40]  "section 1 extra" list   (taken when the section is already full)
      140541384  e8b7e6ffff  CALL 0x14053fa40    RCX=[RBP-0x40]  RDX=[RBP-0x30]  R8=[RSP+0x40]

    container [RBP+0x20]  "section 1" list   <== THE CALL THE QUESTION ASKS FOR
      140541398  e8a3e6ffff  CALL 0x14053fa40    RCX=[RBP+0x20]  RDX=[RBP+0x30]  R8=[RSP+0x40]

  The branch that chooses between the last two is:

    14054134a  ff1568a98100  CALL  qword ptr [0x140d5bcb8]      ; PtInRect
    140541350  83f801        CMP  EAX,0x1
    140541353  754a          JNZ  0x14054139f
    ...
    140541376  ...           JGE  0x14054138b                   ; full -> extra list
    140541384  e8b7e6ffff  CALL 0x14053fa40
    140541389  eb48          JMP  0x1405413d3
    14054138b  4c8d442440    LEA  R8,[RSP + 0x40]
    140541390  488b5530      MOV  RDX,qword ptr [RBP + 0x30]
    140541394  488d4d20      LEA  RCX,[RBP + 0x20]
    140541398  e8a3e6ffff    CALL 0x14053fa40
    14054139d  eb34          JMP  0x1405413d3

  So the object lands in [RBP+0x20] exactly when it is inside the section rectangle and
  that section is not yet full; otherwise it goes to the "extra" list, which is the list
  the "Disable extra fiducial #%d" message later talks about.

  The value argument is R8 = &[RSP+0x40]. [RSP+0x40] is filled by 0x1405412fa:

    1405412f1  ff15a1bd8100  CALL  qword ptr [0x140d5d098]       ; GetLineMire  -> RAX
    1405412f7  488bd8        MOV  RBX,RAX
    1405412fa  4889442440    MOV  qword ptr [RSP + 0x40],RAX     ; stash the pointer

  ANSWER to "which register": RAX. The object is pre-existing and owned elsewhere; this
  function only borrows the pointer.

  Proof that [RSP+0x40] still holds that value at the call, not something else: the
  function contains exactly four writes to [RSP+0x40], and only the first precedes the
  call.

    1405412fa  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x40],RAX     <-- GetLineMire result
    1405415b2  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x40],RDI
    140541677  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x40],RAX
    14054180b  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x40],RDI

  0x1405412fa lies inside the collection loop, whose head and back edge are

    1405412d0  488bd3        MOV  RDX,RBX                        ; loop head
    140541482  0f8c48feffff  JL   0x1405412d0                    ; back edge

  so the stash is refreshed on every pass, and nothing overwrites it before 0x140541398.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Naming the class, from a symbol
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The call at 0x1405412f1 goes through the IAT slot at 0x140d5d098, which Ghidra labels
  PTR_GetLineMire_140d5d098. The binary also contains, as a data unit, the decorated
  name of that very function:

    1410aec8a  ds "?GetLineMire@CDataCao@@QEAAPEAVCMire@@_J@Z"

  which demangles to

    public: class CMire * __cdecl CDataCao::GetLineMire(long) const

  The return type is CMire *. Since 0x1405412f1 is the only producer of the pointer that
  the call at 0x140541398 stores, the stored pointer has type CMire * and the OR store
  writes displacement 0xf4 of a CMire.

  Independent corroboration, all from strings already present in the image:

    1410d78c8  ".?AVCMire@@"
        RTTI TypeDescriptor name for class CMire. Structure base 0x1410d78b8; its first
        dword is 0x0140ee61 (the type_info vftable RVA), then 8 bytes of zero padding,
        then the name. CMire is a real polymorphic class, not a typedef or a forward
        declaration -- it has a vftable.

    1410ade0e  "??0CMire@@QEAA@NNFFFFHHHHW4eShapDefinition@FiducialFinder@@AEBVCPolygone@@AEBVCImagesDefinitions@@HH@Z"
        the CMire constructor.

    1410adfb4  "??1CMire@@UEAA@XZ"
        the CMire destructor.

    14102cfb0  "?AddLineMire@CDataCaoTraitement@@QEAAPEAVCMire@@NNFFFFHHHHW4eShapDefinition@FiducialFinder@@AEBVCPolygone@@AEBVCImagesDefinitions@@HH@Z"
        a sibling method of this = object's own class, also returning CMire *. Add and
        get are the same pair of operations on the same collection.

    14102cbf0  "??_7CDataCaoTraitement@@6BCDataCao@@@"
    14102cc16  "??_7CDataCaoTraitement@@6BCDocument@@@"
        CDataCaoTraitement : CDataCao : CDocument. This is why a CDataCaoTraitement
        method can call a CDataCao method at all, and why GetLineMire reaches the CAD
        table through an inherited member at this+0x180.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. There is no vtable store in this function (one of the three allowed routes is absent)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Claim: no instruction in 0x1405411c0..0x140541b65 installs a vtable pointer.

  MSVC x64 emits vtable installation as LEA reg,[vftable] followed by MOV [mem],reg, not
  as a store of an immediate, so the detector has to be the LEA/MOV pair.

  Step 1, text modality: enumerate every LEA whose target lies in .rdata. There are
  exactly 16, all of them the same shape -- 2 into RDX, 14 into R8 -- and every target is
  a format string or a string literal, not a vftable:

    0x140541206 -> RDX  [0x140e4e4f0]   "VerifyAndSetFiducialSections"
    0x140541219 -> RDX  [0x140e492b8]   "CDataCaoTraitement"
    0x1405413b5 -> R8   [0x140e4e510]   "Fiducial %d removed from section 1"
    0x140541449 -> R8   [0x140e4e538]   "Fiducial %d removed from section 2"
    0x1405414a7 -> R8   [0x140e4e560]   "TST fiducial analysis: ..."
    0x1405414fa -> R8   [0x140e4e600]   "This TST cannot be used in Production ..."
    0x1405415c1 -> R8   [0x140e4e658]   "Fiducial #%d will be used for section %d"
    0x14054171d -> R8   [0x140e4e688]   "Distance between fiducials #%d and #%d ..."
    0x1405417a6 -> R8   [0x140e4e6c0]   "Distance2 between fiducials #%d and #%d ..."
    0x14054181f -> R8   [0x140e4e658]
    0x140541962 -> R8   [0x140e4e6f0]   "Fiducial %d becomes %d"
    0x140541a06 -> R8   [0x140e4e6f0]
    0x140541a3a -> R8   [0x140e4e708]   "Disable extra fiducial #%d ..."
    0x140541a99 -> R8   [0x140e4e740]
    0x140541ac3 -> R8   [0x140e4e790]   "-> this TST is OK, ..."
    0x140541ade -> R8   [0x140e4e7c8]   "-> this TST needs more fiducials."

  Step 2, temporal check, because "RDX is stored to memory somewhere" is not the same
  claim as "the LEA result is stored to memory". For each of the 16 LEAs, walk forward in
  p-code until the destination register is next written, and check whether a
  MOV [mem],<that register> occurs first. Result: 0 of 16. Every one of those registers
  is consumed as a call argument and clobbered without ever being stored to memory. So
  there is no vtable install and the class cannot be named this way.

  Step 3, p-code STORE sweep as an independent modality: 129 STORE operations in the
  function; 0 of them store a constant whose value falls in the image's .rdata range.
  Positive control: the same sweep does detect the two OR stores, so the sweep is live.

  Conclusion: the vtable route is unavailable, and the remaining two routes are the log
  string (section 6, names a role only) and the symbol (section 4, which names the class).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The log string at the call names a role, not a class
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The nearest log emission after the call is:

    1405415b7  8b1a          MOV  EBX,dword ptr [RDX]           ; the section number
    1405415b9  895c2420      MOV  dword ptr [RSP + 0x20],EBX
    1405415bd  448b4f20      MOV  R9D,dword ptr [RDI + 0x20]    ; the fiducial number
    1405415c1  4c8d0590d09000  LEA  R8,[0x140e4e658]            ; "Fiducial #%d will be used for section %d"
    1405415c8  ba05000000    MOV  EDX,0x5
    1405415cd  488d4c2458    LEA  RCX,[RSP + 0x58]
    1405415d2  ff15801c8100  CALL qword ptr [0x140d53258]       ; Write
    1405415d8  099ff4000000  OR   dword ptr [RDI + 0xf4],EBX

  RDI here is the object that was read back out of the vector, and it is the object the
  OR store then modifies. The message calls it a "Fiducial" and reads its number from
  +0x20. That is a role name in a user-facing message, consistent with CMire, but it is
  not a class name and I am not treating it as one.

  It does fix the field layout though. On a CMire:
    +0x20  int   fiducial number, used as the %d of "Fiducial #%d"
    +0xbc  dword compared against 1 elsewhere in this function
    +0xf4  dword 2-bit mask, the OR'd field

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Why the object is a mire at all: the type gate on the CAD table
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  this+0x180 is the CAD table, reached through the CDataCao base class:

    140541203  488bd9        MOV  RBX,RCX                    ; RBX = this
    1405412ac  488db380010000  LEA  RSI,[RBX + 0x180]

  The loop walks that table and selects one row kind:

    1405412d0  488bd3        MOV  RDX,RBX                    ; loop head
    1405412d3  488bce        MOV  RCX,RSI
    1405412d6  ff15a4bd8100  CALL  qword ptr [0x140d5d080]    ; GetLineCAD   -> RAX
    1405412dc  8b4808        MOV  ECX,dword ptr [RAX + 0x8]   ; entity type code
    1405412df  81f980000000  CMP  ECX,0x80                    ; 0x80 == a mire
    1405412e5  0f857e010000  JNZ  0x140541469
    1405412eb  488bd3        MOV  RDX,RBX
    1405412ee  488bce        MOV  RCX,RSI
    1405412f1  ff15a1bd8100  CALL  qword ptr [0x140d5d098]    ; GetLineMire  -> RAX

  and everything else is dropped:

    140541469  f7c109202000  TEST  ECX,0x202009               ; any bit outside the mask?
    14054146f  7717          JA    0x140541488                ; then skip entirely
    140541471  ffc7          INC   EDI
    140541473  4863df        MOVSXD RBX,EDI
    140541476  488bce        MOV  RCX,RSI
    140541479  ff15e1b88100  CALL  qword ptr [0x140d5cd60]    ; GetSizeCadTab
    14054147f  483bd8        CMP  RBX,RAX
    140541482  0f8c48feffff  JL   0x1405412d0

  So 0x80 is the CAD entity type code that selects a mire row, and GetLineMire is the
  accessor that turns such a row into a CMire. This is a second, independent reason to
  believe the stored pointer is a CMire and not just a same-shaped struct.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. The container type, stated as an inference and not as a read-off
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The five locals are almost certainly CArray<CMire*>. The RTTI name exists in the image
  and is the only vector-like instantiation naming CMire *:

    1410d7bb0  char[40] ".?AV?$CArray@PEAVCMire@@AEAPEAV1@@@"
        structure base 0x1410d7ba0, first dword 0x0140ee61, then the name.
        Exactly one occurrence program-wide.

  Why this is an inference and not a proof: FUN_14051d560, FUN_14051ef30 and
  FUN_14053fa40 carry no Ghidra names, and naming the local type properly would mean
  walking from that CArray<CMire*> TypeDescriptor to its COL and then to its vftable,
  which is outside the scope I was given. I attempted the search and it failed for an
  unrelated reason worth recording: search_bytes returned 0 hits for the TypeDescriptor
  RVAs 0x010d7ba0 and 0x010d78b8, so that tool is not searching the RTTI blob at
  0x140f00000..0x140f18000. That is a limitation of the search modality, not evidence
  that the RTTI is absent; both TypeDescriptors were confirmed instead by reading their
  bytes directly.

  The supporting shape evidence: 8-byte elements, a +0x8 data / +0x10 count header, one
  constructor used at 5 sites, one destructor used at 5 sites, one insert used at 6
  sites, and a CMire * being the only pointer that ever enters them.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Correction to the previous section
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The previous section, "Fiducial flag bits", closed with:

    "The receiver object's class is NOT named, because nothing inside this function names
     it ... Naming the class needs the callers or the owning type's vftable."

  That limit is superseded. No caller was consulted and no vftable was consulted. The
  class is named from a decorated-name string that was already in the binary and that
  describes the producer call inside this same function,
  ?GetLineMire@CDataCao@@QEAAPEAVCMire@@_J@Z. The receiver is a CMire.

  Two further refinements to that section, neither of which contradicts it:

  (a) R12 = 0, from 0x14054122e XOR R12D,R12D. This pins the frame-table indexing, so
      the first receiver provably comes from slot [RBP-0x78] = &[RBP+0x20], as the
      question assumed, and the second pass uses [RBP-0x70] = &[RBP-0x8]. The previous
      section had left that index unresolved.

  (b) That section ended by declining to claim the [RBX+0xf4] sites and the [RDI+0xf4]
      sites touch the same object: "I have matched them by encoding and displacement,
      not by a dataflow proof that they are the same runtime object." That proof now
      exists. RBX is the CMire * returned by GetLineMire from 0x1405412f7 until
      0x140541473, and every [RBX+0xf4] site at 0x140541355, 0x14054139f, 0x1405413cc,
      0x1405413e8, 0x140541433 and 0x140541460 falls inside that window. So those sites
      test and clear bits of a CMire, and RDI is a CMire * read back out of the
      container that this same CMire * was inserted into at 0x140541398. Same class,
      and for the element that was just inserted, provably the same object. RBX is `this`
      only from 0x140541203 to 0x1405412cd; it must not be read as `this` at the bit
      sites.

  * 59 distinct instruction encodings quoted in this section were extracted from this
    payload by regex, not hand-listed, and each was re-read with a fresh memory_read and
    compared byte for byte. 59 of 59 match. The 4 encoded string constants quoted in
    sections 4 and 8 were read back and matched the same way.
  * 9 call targets re-derived from the rel32 in the encoding rather than trusted from
    the disassembly text: 0x14054127b/85/8f/99/2a3 -> 0x14051d560;
    0x14054130c/384/398 -> 0x14053fa40; 0x140541b05 -> 0x14051ef30.

    0x1405413d3; 0x14054139d JMP disp=0x34 -> 0x1405413d3. The loop back edge
    0x140541482 JL -> 0x1405412d0 was derived the same way.
  * The write-set for [RSP+0x40] was enumerated over all 563 instructions, not sampled,
    because the claim "the pointer comes from RAX" rests entirely on it.
  * Negative claims in section 5 use a working detector with a positive control, after
    an earlier version of that detector was found to be silently matching nothing.

11. Limits of this answer, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I did not enter FUN_14051d560, FUN_14051ef30 or FUN_14053fa40, so I cannot say what
    the insert does with the CMire * beyond the fact that it stores it. The readback at
    0x1405415af takes 8 bytes and dereferences them, which is what makes "stores the
    pointer" the right description.
  * The container type CArray<CMire*> is an inference from shape plus the unique
    CArray<CMire*> RTTI name, not a symbol read at the call. The pointee type CMire is
    not an inference; it comes from the producer's own decorated name.
  * The evidence for the class is a decorated-name string in the image. I matched it to
    the call by the IAT label GetLineMire at 0x140d5d098, which is a name Ghidra
    derived from that import, and by the pairing with GetLineCAD and GetSizeCadTab.
    I did not decompile GetLineMire to confirm its return type, because scope forbade it.
    If the import label were wrong the CMire conclusion would fall with it, so this is
    the one link in the chain that rests on a label rather than on code.
  * 0x80 as the mire entity type code is read off the comparison at 0x1405412df. I did
    not find a table in this binary that names 0x80.
  * Whether the pointer in RAX is a CMire owned by the CAD table or a freshly built one
    owned by GetLineMire, I cannot tell from here. It is in neither case constructed
    inside VerifyAndSetFiducialSections, which is what the question turned on.

===== Fiducial setter callers =====

Question: does the panel-load path call VerifyAndSetFiducialSections before
PV_EnvoiMacros? List every direct code caller of VerifyAndSetFiducialSections
(0x1405411c0). For each, quote the call and any log string. Say whether any caller is
PrepareVecteur (0x14053bd60), FUN_14068f0f0, or PV_EnvoiMacros (0x140533c90).

Scope honored: "Stop at one caller level." I enumerate the callers of
VerifyAndSetFiducialSections and read the body of the one caller I found, because the
question asks what that caller passes. I did NOT enumerate the callers of that caller,
so I cannot place either function in a panel-load sequence. See section 5.

Read-only throughout. No callee body was decompiled and no program was saved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  There is exactly ONE direct code caller of VerifyAndSetFiducialSections:

      CheckTstWithMachineLimits   0x140526970 .. 0x140527545   655 instructions

  and it calls it from exactly TWO sites, 0x140526bea and 0x14052731a. Both are plain
  relative CALLs inside that one function.

  None of the three functions you named is a caller:

      PrepareVecteur      0x14053bd60 .. 0x14053c245    not a caller
      FUN_14068f0f0       0x14068f0f0 .. 0x14068f884    not a caller  (PrepareExecData)
      PV_EnvoiMacros      0x140533c90 .. 0x1405343ab    not a caller

  So the direct answer to "does the panel-load path call VerifyAndSetFiducialSections
  before PV_EnvoiMacros" is: NO SUCH ORDERING IS ESTABLISHED, and in fact the two
  functions are not related by a direct call in either direction. VerifyAndSetFiducial-
  Sections is reached only from CheckTstWithMachineLimits, and CheckTstWithMachineLimits
  calls none of the three functions you named either. There is no edge between
  VerifyAndSetFiducialSections and PV_EnvoiMacros for an ordering to sit on. Deciding the
  real sequence needs one more level, which the scope forbids. Section 5 states exactly
  what is missing.

  A side finding that matters more than the ordering: both call sites pass
  param_1 == 1, which settles a question earlier sections had to leave open. See
  section 4.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Enumerating the callers, three ways
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  A negative result like "exactly one caller" is only worth as much as the detector, so
  three independent modalities were used.

  Modality A - Ghidra's call graph:

    function_callers(0x1405411c0)  -> count 1
      CheckTstWithMachineLimits
      bool __thiscall CheckTstWithMachineLimits(CDataCaoTraitement * this, bool param_1,
            bool * param_2, ushort * param_3,
            CStringT<char,StrTraitMFC_DLL<char,ATL::ChTraitsCRT<char>_>_> * param_4,
            bool param_5, bool param_6, bool param_7)

  Modality B - text search over the whole program for the literal target:

    search_instructions("1405411c0")  -> count 2
      140526bea  e8d1a50100  CALL 0x1405411c0
      14052731a  e8a19e0100  CALL 0x1405411c0

    Both fall inside 0x140526970..0x140527545. There is no third call site anywhere in
    .text, so there is no second caller function.

  Modality C - p-code CALL search:

    search_pcode("1405411c0")  -> count 2
      140526bea   CALL (ram, 0x1405411c0, 8)
      14052731a   CALL (ram, 0x1405411c0, 8)

  Both call encodings were re-read with a fresh memory_read and the targets re-derived
  from the rel32 rather than trusted from the rendered text:

      140526bea  e8 d1a50100   rel32 = +107985   0x140526bef + 107985 = 0x1405411c0
      14052731a  e8 a19e0100   rel32 = +106145   0x14052731f + 106145 = 0x1405411c0

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The three non-code references are not call paths
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  reference_to(0x1405411c0) returns 6 references. Four are not code calls, and I checked
  what each one actually is rather than assuming:

    1410289cc  DATA   ibo32 1405411c0
        A 4-byte image-base-relative entry in the same ordinal dispatch table that
        earlier sections located at 0x141028624 with 4-byte entries:
        0x1410289cc - 0x141028624 = 0x3a8 = 936 bytes = ordinal 234. Earlier work
        verified entries at ordinals 199..212 and found nothing in the binary that reads
        the table. I did not re-test readability here.

    1412c3b5c  DATA   _IMAGE_RUNTIME_FUNCTION_ENTRY
        The x64 pdata unwind record. Read as three LE dwords, raw bytes
        c0115400 661b5400 601ef600:

            BeginAddress       0x1405411c0
            EndAddress         0x140541b66  (exclusive)  -> 0x140541b65 inclusive
            UnwindInfoAddress  0x140f61e60

        The EndAddress here independently corroborates the callee extent recorded by
        earlier work on this file, 0x1405411c0..0x140541b65. That is a useful
        consistency check, and it is the last structural datum in this answer.

    140f61f10  DATA   IPToStateMapEntry[27]
        NOT an independent structure. I initially recorded this as a separate IP-to-state
        map; that was wrong. 0x140f61f10 is at offset +0xb0 inside the unwind info at
        0x140f61e60 that the pdata record above points to, i.e. it is Ghidra's decoding
        of the unwind code array, reading the opcode words as map entries. So 1412c3b5c
        and 140f61f10 are one record plus its target, not two structures.

    Both are structure, not call. Neither can execute code.

    "Entry Point"  EXTERNAL
        A Ghidra analysis artifact.

  The important negative here: VerifyAndSetFiducialSections is declared VIRTUAL. The
  decorated name in the image says so:

    1410300fa  "?VerifyAndSetFiducialSections@CDataCaoTraitement@@IEAA_N_NVCRect@@10AEAG@Z"

  The IEAA access tag means virtual __thiscall. A virtual method would normally have a
  vftable slot, and that slot would be an absolute 8-byte pointer - a possible indirect
  dispatch path that a direct-call search would miss. There is none:

    reference_to(0x1405411c0) lists no .rdata vftable address.

  That absence is meaningful because the detector was validated first. reference_to on
  CCAD_Base::_csName at 0x14076d916 returns 11 DATA references, which is exactly the 11
  vftables earlier work recorded for that slot. So reference_to does surface vftable
  entries, and it surfaces none here.

  Caveat: this rests on Ghidra's reference analysis. I attempted a second, independent
  route - searching .rdata and .data for the absolute pointer c011541400000000 - and got
  0 hits, but the same search for a KNOWN vftable address (CCAD_Base's 0x140e7b9e8,
  pattern e8b9e74000000000) also returned 0 hits. That search modality is simply not
  working on this pattern shape, so it contributes nothing either way. I am not claiming
  the absence is proven; I am reporting that the one working detector finds nothing and
  that the other was broken and discarded.

3. Caller 1 of 1: CheckTstWithMachineLimits, and its two call sites
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Both call sites, with the argument slots that are actually populated. MSVC x64 puts
  arguments 1..4 in RCX/RDX/R8/R9 and 5.. on the stack, so the 5th and 6th arguments are
  at [RSP+0x20] and [RSP+0x28].

  ---- Site 1, 0x140526bea ----------------------------------------------------

  Its guard and its log string come first, because the guard is what fixes param_1:

    140526b8f  80bf4011000001  CMP  byte ptr [RDI + 0x1140],0x1

  Log string at this call, 0x140e4e210, quoted immediately before it:

      ds "This TST opened in standalone mode has only %d fiducial affected to section 1"

  Argument mapping:

      RCX  = RDI                  this, a CDataCaoTraitement
      EDX  = byte ptr [RDI+0x1140]   param_1
      R8   = &[RBP-0x30]          param_2, the CRect copied from this+0x1164
      R9   = &[RBP-0x40]          param_3, the CRect copied from this+0x1174

  Two things to note. First, this call is TERMINAL: whatever it returns in AL is thrown
  away, BL is forced to 1, and control jumps to the function's tail. Second, R12B is
  this caller's own first argument, preserved at entry:

    140526970  488bc4          MOV  RAX,RSP
    140526977  885010          MOV  byte ptr [RAX + 0x10],DL

    1405272f3  660f7f55d0      MOVDQA xmmword ptr [RBP + -0x30],XMM2
    1405272f8  660f7f4dc0      MOVDQA xmmword ptr [RBP + -0x40],XMM1
    1405272fd  4c896c2428      MOV  qword ptr [RSP + 0x28],R13
    140527302  0fb69d28020000  MOVZX EBX,byte ptr [RBP + 0x228]
    140527309  885c2420        MOV  byte ptr [RSP + 0x20],BL
    14052730d  4c8d4dd0        LEA  R9,[RBP + -0x30]

    140527317  488bcf          MOV  RCX,RDI
    14052731a  e8a19e0100      CALL 0x1405411c0
    14052731f  80fb01          CMP  BL,0x1
    140527322  0f8591000000    JNZ  0x1405273b9

  Log string: there is NO string literal between the two call sites. The nearest one
  preceding this call in the same function is at 0x140527112:

    140527112  4c8d0547739200  LEA  R8,[0x140e4e460]
    140527119  ba05000000      MOV  EDX,0x5
    14052711e  488d4d90        LEA  RCX,[RBP + -0x70]

      ds "Panel needs 2 sections (panel width = %.0lf um and machine inspectable area width = %.0lf um).\n"

  I am not claiming that string governs this call; it is 0x208 bytes earlier and belongs
  to a separate diagnostic. I record it because it is the only log string in reach, and
  the honest statement is that this call site has no log string of its own.

  Argument mapping:

      RCX  = RDI                  this
      DL   = 0x1, written immediately before     param_1
      R8   = &[RBP-0x40]
      R9   = &[RBP-0x30]
      [RSP+0x20] = BL
      [RSP+0x28] = R13

  Note the R8/R9 order is SWAPPED relative to site 1. The two CRects are passed in the
  opposite order by the two sites.

  [RBP+0x228] and [RBP+0x230] are not locals. With RBP = RSP_entry - 0x218, [RBP+0x228]
  is RSP_entry + 0x10, the home slot of DL, and [RBP+0x230] is RSP_entry + 0x18, the
  home slot of R8. So site 2 passes this caller's own first and fourth arguments through,
  by exactly the route site 1 uses via R12B and LEA RAX.

  The byte tested right after this call is BL, which is the caller's own byte from
  [RBP+0x228] - NOT the AL return value. I did not trace how the return is consumed.

4. Correction to earlier sections: both callers pass param_1 == 1
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Earlier sections of this file repeatedly declined to choose, on the grounds that the
  question of whether callers pass param_1 == 1 was not determined. That limit is now
  removed, and both sites are determinate:

    Site 1, 0x140526bea
        param_1 is loaded from byte ptr [RDI+0x1140] at 0x140526be0, and the call is
        guarded by

            140526b8f  80bf4011000001  CMP  byte ptr [RDI + 0x1140],0x1
            140526b96  7557            JNZ  0x140526bef

        which skips past the call to the MOV BL,0x1 / JMP tail. So on every path that
        reaches 0x140526bea, that byte is exactly 1, and param_1 == 1.

    Site 2, 0x14052731a
        param_1 is the literal:

            140527315  b201            MOV  DL,0x1

  Therefore BOTH call sites run VerifyAndSetFiducialSections with param_1 == 1, which is
  the condition that makes its loop take TWO passes over the section numbers {1, 2}
  rather than one. The two-pass behaviour is not a hypothetical branch any more; it is
  what every call in this binary does.

  Also worth correcting, from the same two sites: the earlier "Fiducial flag bits"
  section could not say which object the [RBX+0xf4] sites touch. It is settled that the
  callee is a CMire, and the caller confirms the flag dword is reached through
  this+0x1140 at site 1, which is the same 2-bit field the callee ORs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The ordering question, answered as far as one caller level allows
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Facts, all verified above:

    * VerifyAndSetFiducialSections is called from exactly one function,
      CheckTstWithMachineLimits, at two sites.
    * CheckTstWithMachineLimits contains 112 CALL instructions. None of them targets
      0x140533c90 (PV_EnvoiMacros), 0x14053bd60 (PrepareVecteur) or 0x14068f0f0
      (PrepareExecData).
    * None of those three functions calls VerifyAndSetFiducialSections; the only two call
      sites in the entire program are both inside CheckTstWithMachineLimits.

  Conclusion: VerifyAndSetFiducialSections and PV_EnvoiMacros are NOT connected by a
  direct call in either direction, so there is no direct-call ordering between them to
  report. Any sequencing between them is at least two levels up, through the caller of
  CheckTstWithMachineLimits on one side and the caller of PV_EnvoiMacros on the other.

  What is missing to answer the question properly: the caller set of
  CheckTstWithMachineLimits, and where PV_EnvoiMacros is called from. Both are one level
  beyond the scope I was given, so I did not collect them. I am not going to guess at a
  sequence from names - "TST", "standalone mode" and "panel needs 2 sections" in the log
  strings suggest a setup/validation step that plausibly precedes macro sending, but that
  is a reading of English text, not a call graph, and I am flagging it as such rather
  than presenting it as an answer.

  One thing that IS worth recording, because it is the kind of edge that would change the
  answer if it existed: CheckTstWithMachineLimits contains four virtual calls through
  object vtables,

    140526c18  ff9030020000      CALL  qword ptr [RAX + 0x230]
    140526c31  41ff91c8010000    CALL  qword ptr [R9 + 0x1c8]
    140526d5d  ff9030020000      CALL  qword ptr [RAX + 0x230]
    140526d6d  41ff90b8010000    CALL  qword ptr [R8 + 0x1b8]

  Slots +0x230 and +0x1b8/+0x1c8 are far beyond any CCAD_Base vtable I have mapped, so
  the owning class is not one I have identified. Whether VerifyAndSetFiducialSections is
  reached through one of them is NOT determined: reference_to finds no vftable slot
  pointing at 0x1405411c0, but I have not resolved those four vtables, so I cannot rule
  out a slot pointing at some other definition. Resolving them needs the owning class,
  which I did not chase.

6. Log strings in CheckTstWithMachineLimits, for context
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  All 18 .rdata LEAs in the caller, read as data units. The first three are the usual
  function-name / class-name pair:

    0x140e4e1d8  "CheckTstWithMachineLimits"
    0x140e492b8  "CDataCaoTraitement"

    0x140e4e358  "Section 1 (components): right=%d, left=%d, top=%d, bottom=%d,"
    0x140e4e398  "Section 2 (components): right=%d, left=%d, top=%d, bottom=%d,"

    0x140e4e460  "Panel needs 2 sections (panel width = %.0lf um and machine inspectable area width = %.0lf um).\n"

  Four more addresses appear in the same LEA list. Ghidra's listing renders them as "??"
  and I first wrote them off as untyped data, which was wrong - reading the bytes shows
  they are ordinary ASCII format strings that Ghidra simply never defined as data units,
  each sitting in the gap of a longer neighbouring string:

    0x140e4e260  "Panel length: %.0lf \xb5m, Used Panel length: %.0lf \xb5m"
    0x140e4e298  "Panel length: %.0lf \xb5m, max inspectable length:  %.0lf \xb5m"
    0x140e4e2d8  "Stop cell distance: %.0lf \xb5m"
    0x140e4e338  "Max panel length: %.0lf \xb5m"

  \xb5 is the 0xB5 micro sign in the OEM code page, so these are the micrometre ("um")
  strings. They are genuine log format strings for this function, not junk, and the
  practical lesson is that a "??" in Ghidra's data-unit rendering means "not typed", not
  "not text". I read the raw bytes for every string in this section rather than trusting
  the rendered form.

  There is one more string in the image worth attaching to this function, found by
  searching its name rather than by reading its body:

    0x140e4e808  "CheckTstWithMachineLimits() has not been called yet"

  That reads like a guard message for a "was this called" flag. I did not enter the code
  that emits it, so I am not claiming this function checks such a flag.

  The decorated name of the caller, for the record:

    14102d591  "?CheckTstWithMachineLimits@CDataCaoTraitement@@QEAA_N_NAEA_NAEAGAEAV?$CStringT@DV?$StrTraitMFC_DLL@DV?$ChTraitsCRT@D@ATL@@@@@ATL@@_N44@Z"

  demangling to a public non-virtual member of CDataCaoTraitement taking
  (bool, bool&, bool&, unsigned short&, CString&, bool, bool).

7. An unresolved discrepancy, recorded rather than smoothed over
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The call sites populate SIX argument slots: RCX, RDX, R8, R9, [RSP+0x20] and
  [RSP+0x28]. Ghidra's decompiled signature for the callee matches that:

    bool __thiscall VerifyAndSetFiducialSections(CDataCaoTraitement * this, bool param_1,
          CRect param_2, CRect param_3, bool param_4, ushort * param_5)

  But the decorated name quoted in section 2 declares only FOUR explicit parameters:

    ?VerifyAndSetFiducialSections@CDataCaoTraitement@@IEAA_N_NVCRect@@10AEAG@Z
      -> protected virtual, returning bool, taking (bool, CRect const&, CRect const&,
         unsigned short&)

  Four explicit parameters means five slots including this, not six, and its fifth
  parameter is a reference rather than the byte that the callers actually pass at
  [RSP+0x20]. The two sources therefore disagree about arity.

  I did not resolve which is right. Possibilities include a stale string, or a signature
  that changed between the declaration and the compiled body. Both call sites are
  unambiguous about what is passed - that is a direct observation and does not depend on
  either name - so the discrepancy does not affect the caller list, the caller count, or
  the param_1 == 1 conclusion. It would matter to anyone typing the interface.
