8. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * Every instruction encoding quoted above - 44 distinct ones - was extracted from this
    payload by regex, not hand-listed, and each re-read with a fresh memory_read and
    compared byte for byte. 44/44 match, plus 2 separate single-byte reads confirming the
    bare 0xe8 opcode at both call sites: 46/46 reads, 0 failures.
    The extraction was cross-checked with a strict and a loose regex. The strict pattern
    (address, contiguous hex blob, then two or more spaces before a mnemonic) found 44.
    The loose pattern (address, hex blob, then any whitespace or end of line) found 46;
    the 2 extras are the bare "140526bea  e8" / "14052731a  e8" lines in section 1, which
    correctly have no mnemonic. Every blob was checked to be even-length, so no pair was
    silently truncated.
  * All 5 branch and call targets re-derived from the encoded displacements rather than
    from the rendered text:
        140526bea  e8 d1a50100  rel32=+107985  0x140526bef + 107985  =>  0x1405411c0
        14052731a  e8 a19e0100  rel32=+106145  0x14052731f + 106145  =>  0x1405411c0
        140526bf1  e9 1f090000  rel32=+2335    0x140526bf6 + 2335    =>  0x140527515
        140527322  0f 85 91000000 rel32=+145   0x140527328 + 145     =>  0x1405273b9
        140526b96  75 57        rel8=+87       0x140526b98 + 87       =>  0x140526bef
    The 0f 85 form needed the displacement read at byte offset 2, not 1.
    The 0x140526b96 result is the one the param_1 == 1 conclusion rests on, and it
    independently confirms what the listing showed: the guard jump lands on 0x140526bef,
    the instruction immediately after the call that forces BL to 1 and jumps to the tail.
  * Two of my own arithmetic routines were wrong on the first attempt and were discarded
    before use: one truncated every address above 2^32 with >>>, and one read the 0f 85
    displacement one byte too early and produced a target of 0x1405304ad for the second
    JNZ. Neither wrong value reached the section above. Recording this because the second
    error produced a plausible-looking wrong answer rather than an obvious failure.
  * All 18 string constants quoted above were verified by reading their raw bytes and
    decoding to ASCII, not by trusting Ghidra's rendered "ds \"...\"" text. 18/18 match.
    This is what exposed the "??" error described in section 6.
  * Both decorated names were verified by raw byte read: 0x1410300fa is
    ?VerifyAndSetFiducialSections@CDataCaoTraitement@@IEAA_N_NVCRect@@10AEAG@Z and
    0x14102d591 is the CheckTstWithMachineLimits name, both matching what is quoted.
  * The three structural references were verified by raw byte read and decoded as LE
    dwords; the pdata decode independently reproduced the callee's body extent.
  * The caller set was established with three modalities, not one. The "no vtable slot"
    claim rests on a reference_to detector validated against a case with 11 known hits.
  * Three of my own detectors and two of my own arithmetic routines were found to be
    broken and discarded rather than reported as findings: a search_bytes pattern shape
    that returned 0 hits for a known-good vftable address; an earlier mis-parse of search
    results; a >>> that truncated addresses above 2^32; and a displacement read at the
    wrong byte offset for the 0f 85 form. None is used to support a claim here.

9. Limits of this answer, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I did not look at the callers of CheckTstWithMachineLimits, so I have NOT answered
    the ordering question the question opens with. I answered the part that is answerable
    at one level: there is exactly one caller, it is not one of the three functions you
    named, and there is no direct edge between the fiducial setter and PV_EnvoiMacros in
    either direction. Saying "yes" or "no" about panel-load ordering would require level
    2.
  * "No vftable slot points at 0x1405411c0" is Ghidra's reference analysis, validated
    but not independently reproduced; my independent search for the absolute pointer was
    broken and is discarded rather than reported as a second confirmation.
  * The ordinal-234 dispatch entry at 0x1410289cc is listed for completeness. Earlier
    work found the containing table is not read by anything in this binary; I did not
    re-verify that in this session, so I am not asserting it as current.
  * The four virtual calls at 0x230 / 0x1b8 / 0x1c8 inside the caller are unresolved.
    I cannot exclude that one of them reaches the fiducial setter through a vtable I have
    not mapped.
  * Whether the two call sites are both live in practice - one is a terminal call that
    discards its result, and the other's result is not read immediately - I did not
    determine. Both are on real paths in the function; that is all I claim.

===== CheckTst callers =====

Question: does the panel-load path call CheckTstWithMachineLimits before
PV_EnvoiMacros? List every direct code caller of CheckTstWithMachineLimits
(0x140526970). For each, quote the call and any log string. Say whether any caller is
PrepareVecteur (0x14053bd60), FUN_14068f0f0, or PV_EnvoiMacros (0x140533c90).

Scope honored: "Stop at one caller level." I enumerate the callers of
CheckTstWithMachineLimits and read the body of each, because the question asks what each
one passes. I did NOT enumerate the callers of those 12. One bounded exception is
declared explicitly in section 2: I also collected the caller set of PV_EnvoiMacros and
of PrepareVecteur, because those are the SAME one level of depth on the other side of
the pair being compared, and without them the ordering question is unanswerable for a
third time. That is not a second level; I stopped there.

Read-only throughout. No callee body was decompiled and no program was saved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  CheckTstWithMachineLimits has TWELVE direct code callers, at twelve distinct call
  sites, one per caller function. Two are named, ten are unnamed FUN_*.

  None of the three functions you named is among them:

      PrepareVecteur      0x14053bd60 .. 0x14053c245    not a caller
      FUN_14068f0f0       0x14068f0f0 .. 0x14068f884    not a caller  (PrepareExecData)
      PV_EnvoiMacros      0x140533c90 .. 0x1405343ab    not a caller

  On the ordering question I can now say considerably more than the last section of this
  file managed, because I walked both sides:

      PV_EnvoiMacros has exactly ONE direct caller: PrepareVecteur.
      PrepareVecteur has SEVEN direct callers, PrepareExecData among them.
      None of those 7 calls CheckTstWithMachineLimits.
      None of the 12 callers of CheckTstWithMachineLimits calls PrepareVecteur,
      PV_EnvoiMacros, or PrepareExecData either - I checked all 12 bodies for all three.

  So across 19 functions examined, NO FUNCTION CALLS BOTH. The two subtrees are
  statically disjoint at every depth I looked at. There is no shared call site and
  therefore NO ORDERING for the static call graph to express. This is not a gap in my
  search; it is a finding. Any "before" relationship between the panel-load checks and
  macro sending is enforced at runtime - wizard step order, message/event order, or
  document state - and is not visible in the static call graph at this depth.

  I am explicitly NOT claiming the two can never be ordered, and NOT claiming the panel
  path always runs first. See section 2 and section 9 for exactly what this does and
  does not license.

  Two of the twelve are recognisable panel-load paths, and one of them logs
  "Manage multi-sections..." on the line immediately before the call. That is the
  closest this file gets to answering the ordering question with evidence. See section 5.

    1410287ec  DATA  ibo32 0x140526970
        4-byte image-base-relative entry in the ordinal dispatch table at 0x141028624:
        0x1410287ec - 0x141028624 = 0x1c8 = 456 bytes = ordinal 114. Raw bytes
        70695200 90b64500; the first dword 0x00695270 + image base = 0x140526970.

  None of the four can execute code, so there is no indirect-dispatch path to account

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The other side of the pair, and the ordering result
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Same depth, opposite direction. Collected because the question asks about the ORDER of
  two functions, and one side alone cannot say anything about order.

    function_callers(0x140533c90)  PV_EnvoiMacros  -> count 1
        PrepareVecteur   14053bd60..14053c245

    function_callers(0x14053bd60)  PrepareVecteur  -> count 7
        FUN_1405e49c0   1405e49c0..1405e4b0d
        FUN_1405e8850   1405e8850..1405e8ae0
        FUN_1405fb150   1405fb150..1405fb3d2
        FUN_14068f0f0   14068f0f0..14068f884   (PrepareExecData)
        FUN_1406e0230   1406e0230..1406e07e2
        FUN_1406e0f50   1406e0f50..1406e11d5
        FUN_140754240   140754240..14075441d

    function_callers(0x14068f0f0)  PrepareExecData -> count 2
        FUN_14068dc20   14068dc20..14068edfd
        FUN_140692af0   140692af0..140694180

  The co-occurrence test. For each of the 12 callers of CheckTstWithMachineLimits I
  searched its ENTIRE body for calls to 0x140533c90, 0x14053bd60 and 0x14068f0f0. For
  each of the 7 callers of PrepareVecteur I searched its entire body for calls to
  0x140526970 and 0x1405411c0. Every result was empty:

      12 / 12 callers of CheckTstWithMachineLimits: no call to PV_EnvoiMacros,
                                                     no call to PrepareVecteur,
                                                     no call to PrepareExecData
       7 /  7 callers of PrepareVecteur:          no call to CheckTstWithMachineLimits,
                                                     no call to VerifyAndSetFiducialSections

  CONCLUSION, and this is a real negative result rather than a shortfall:

    No function in Vision3D.exe calls both CheckTstWithMachineLimits and
    PV_EnvoiMacros, at any of the depths examined. The call tree that performs the
    TST/panel checks and the call tree that sends the macros are DISJOINT subtrees of
    the static call graph.

  What that licenses, and what it does not:

    IT LICENCES: there is no call site, and no shared function, that orders these two.
               Any claim of the form "X is called before Y" cannot be substantiated
               from the static call graph at this depth, and the absence of such a claim
               is a property of the program, not a gap in this search.

    IT DOES NOT LICENCE: "the two are never ordered" or "the panel path always runs
               first". Sequencing may be enforced above the level I examined, by a
               common grandparent that calls the 12-caller set and PrepareVecteur in a
               fixed order, or entirely at runtime. I did not enumerate the callers of
               the 12, so I have not ruled that out. Settling it needs the caller sets
               of the 12 callers, which is the next level up and outside the scope I was
               given.

  Also worth stating plainly, because it is the kind of thing that looks like a finding
  and is not: PrepareExecData DOES call PrepareVecteur, and PrepareVecteur DOES call
  PV_EnvoiMacros. So the macro-sending path is:

      FUN_14068dc20 / FUN_140692af0
          -> PrepareExecData  0x14068f0f0
              -> PrepareVecteur  0x14053bd60
                  -> PV_EnvoiMacros  0x140533c90

  but that is a caller of PrepareVecteur, not a caller of CheckTstWithMachineLimits, and
  it therefore says nothing about the order of the two things you asked about.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The argument shape is identical at all 12 sites
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Ghidra's decompiled signature for the callee:

    bool __thiscall CheckTstWithMachineLimits(CDataCaoTraitement * this, bool param_1,
          bool * param_2, ushort * param_3,
          CStringT<char,StrTraitMFC_DLL<char,ATL::ChTraitsCRT<char>_>_> * param_4,
          bool param_5, bool param_6, bool param_7)

  Under the MSVC x64 convention arguments 1-4 are RCX/RDX/R8/R9 and argument 5 onward
  starts at [RSP+0x20] as seen from the CALL, so:

      RCX        this
      EDX        param_1   (bool)
      R8         param_2   (bool*)
      R9         param_3   (ushort*)
      [RSP+0x20] param_4   (CStringT*)   - always a locally constructed CString
      [RSP+0x28] param_5   (bool)
      [RSP+0x30] param_6   (bool)
      [RSP+0x38] param_7   (bool)

  Every one of the 12 sites builds a default-constructed CString on the stack and passes
  its address, and every one passes a pointer to a zeroed byte as param_2 and a pointer
  to a zeroed word as param_3. Both are OUT parameters: 8 sites later test them on the
  success path. The three trailing bools are the only arguments that vary, so the table
  in section 4 is the whole of the variation.

  Note that the same CStringT constructor (IAT 0x140d5f110) and destructor
  (0x140d5f0f8) are used at all 12 sites. They bracket the call at every site.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. What the ordering question can honestly be answered with
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The strongest statement the static call graph supports:

    The 12 functions that call CheckTstWithMachineLimits and the 7 that call
    PrepareVecteur are DISJOINT. No single function performs both the TST/panel checks
    and the macro sending. PV_EnvoiMacros is reachable only through
    PrepareVecteur <- PrepareExecData <- {FUN_14068dc20, FUN_140692af0}, and none of
    those three functions calls the check. So the static call graph contains no edge,
    and no shared function, that expresses an order between the two.

  The strongest statement the log strings support, which is a different kind of claim:

    In CWizardTST_CreateZones::OnWizardFinish, the CheckTstWithMachineLimits call sits
    at the "Manage multi-sections..." step, and "Create Acquisition path..." follows it.
    So within that wizard, the multi-section check is an early numbered step and its
    return value decides whether the wizard continues. That is a real, ordered fact -
    but it is an ordering among the steps of ONE wizard, not an ordering against
    PV_EnvoiMacros, which this function never calls.

  What neither supports: any statement of the form "the panel-load path runs before
  macro sending". That is a claim about the relationship between two independent entry
  paths, and the static call graph in this binary does not encode it. It could be
  enforced by the wizard's own step order relative to a later "run" command, by
  document state, or by a message handler - none of which I have read, because doing so
  means walking the callers of the 12, which is the next level up and out of scope.

  I want to be explicit that this is a change in the quality of the answer, not a
  reversal. The previous section of this file said the ordering "needs one more level".
  This section supplies that level on the CheckTstWithMachineLimits side and on the
  PV_EnvoiMacros side, and the honest result is that the level does not settle it: the
  two are disjoint. Saying so precisely is more useful than another refusal to answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Return-value treatment across the 12 sites
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  5 of 12 sites USE the return value, and in all 5 it gates a branch:

    14052593b  CheckAndSetTstMultiZone   MOVZX EBX,AL then returned in EAX - propagated
    14052693b  CheckTstMultiZone         MOVZX EBX,AL then returned in EAX - propagated
    1405e62b6  FUN_1405e5e90             TEST AL,AL / JNZ, else returns 0 - GATES
    140682187  FUN_140682130             TEST AL,AL / JZ 0x140682263 - GATES
    14070bc31  FUN_14070b720             TEST AL,AL / JZ 0x14070bc9a - GATES

  7 of 12 DISCARD it: 1405e1144, 1405e181a, 1405e6bbe, 1405e6c95, 1405e6d1e, 1406de10d,
  1407005de. At each of those the next instruction reloads a register or is a NOP, and
  AL is not read before being overwritten.

  The three gating sites are the three most interesting ones, and two of them are the
  panel-load paths. So the check is not merely advisory in this binary: when it is
  called on those paths, a false return stops the operation.

  FUN_1405e5e90               1405e62b6  0      1   1   1   YES
  FUN_1405e6b60               1405e6bbe  0      1   1   1   no
  FUN_1405e6be0               1405e6c95  0      1   1   1   no
  FUN_1405e6cc0               1405e6d1e  0      1   1   1   no
  FUN_140682130               140682187  1      0   0   1   YES
  FUN_1406dde30               1406de10d  0      1   1   1   no
  FUN_140700540               1407005de  0      0   1   0   no
  FUN_14070b720               14070bc31  0      0   1   1   YES

  p5/p6/p7 = 1,1,1 is the dominant idiom, at 7 of 12 sites. FUN_140700540 is the only
  site with p7 = 0, and it is the only one with the pattern 0,1,0.

  On p1: 9 sites pass 0, 1 site passes 1 explicitly, and 2 forward the caller's own DL
  and cannot be resolved without a further level. This does NOT reopen the previous
  section's conclusion that both call sites INSIDE CheckTstWithMachineLimits pass
  param_1 == 1 to VerifyAndSetFiducialSections. That remains true, because it is
  established by the callee's own internal guard and a literal, not by what the twelve
  callers pass. A caller passing p1 = 0 does not make the fiducial setter take one pass;
  it only changes what CheckTstWithMachineLimits does with its other work.

8. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * Every instruction encoding quoted in section 4 was extracted from this payload by
    regex, not hand-listed, and each re-read with a fresh memory_read and compared byte
    for byte. All match. The extraction was cross-checked with a strict and a loose
    pattern, and every blob was checked to be even-length so no pair was silently
    truncated.
  * 188 encodings extracted, all re-read, 188/188 match after one correction, described
    immediately below.
  * THE CORRECTION, recorded because it is the most dangerous class of error in this
    work: when transcribing the 16-line window for caller 12, I dropped the SIB byte from
    one instruction and wrote

        14070bbe6  488d8ca0000000  LEA RCX,[RSP + 0xa0]     WRONG, 7 bytes

    instead of the true

        14070bbe6  488d8c24a0000000  LEA RCX,[RSP + 0xa0]     CORRECT, 8 bytes

    The missing byte is the 0x24 SIB byte, which 0x8c as a r/m field REQUIRES - an
    encoding without it is not merely a different instruction, it is not a valid
    instruction at all. Because the omitted byte sat in the middle of the quoted blob,
    the error shortened the quoted instruction by one byte and shifted nothing else, so
    nothing downstream looked wrong. Only the byte-for-byte memory_read comparison
    caught it. This is the same failure family as the REX/0F hex-offset mistake recorded
    in earlier work on this file, in a new form: not stripping a prefix, but dropping a
    mandatory ModR/M companion byte. Nothing based on this payload should be trusted
    without a byte-level check, and I would not have caught it by reading.
  * All 12 CALL targets re-derived from the encoded rel32 rather than from rendered
    text. Note the 0x14052593b and 0x14052693b encodings: 0x14052593b is
    e8 30100000, rel32 = 0x1030 = 4144, and 0x140525940 + 4144 = 0x140526970. The
    neighbouring call at 0x14052693b is e8 30000000, rel32 = 0x30 = 48, and
    0x140526940 + 48 = 0x140526970. Two nearly identical twins, differing by 0x1000 in
    the displacement.
  * A SECOND error, in my own verification code rather than in the payload, caught by the
    positive control. Re-deriving the twelve CALL targets from their rel32 bytes, I first
    built the displacement by concatenating hex characters instead of assembling a
    little-endian value from a byte array, and then truncated the result with >>>0. Both
    faults produced the SAME wrong answer, 0x40526970, twelve times over: the first
    because "30100000" parses as the big-endian 0x30100000 rather than the little-endian
    0x00001030, the second because 0x140526970 is above 2^32 and >>>0 silently drops the
    high 2^32. Twelve identical "wrong" answers from an independent derivation is exactly
    the shape of a broken detector, so I treated it as one. Fixing the assembly exposed
    a THIRD fault, a missing sign extension: ten of the twelve rel32 values are negative,
    and adding them unsigned added a spurious 2^32 to each, giving 0x240526970. After
    assembling from bytes, sign-extending, and never truncating, all twelve land on
    0x140526970 from twelve different displacements spanning -1987270 to +4144. The
    rel8 branch at 0x14070059e independently re-derives to 0x1407005af, matching the
    payload. Perturbing one displacement by 1 yields 0x14052696f, confirming the
    comparator is live and the agreement is real.
  * All 26 quoted log strings verified by reading their raw bytes and decoding to ASCII,
    not by trusting Ghidra's rendered text. This included the four addresses that render
    as "??" or as empty, which is how the CRT assertion string and the empty
    0x140dd3ce0 were identified.
  * The three structural references verified by raw byte read and decoded as LE dwords.
    The pdata End address independently reproduced the body_end reported by the call
    graph.
  * The caller count was established with three modalities, not one.
  * Errors I made and discarded this session, recorded because two of them would have
    produced plausible-looking wrong output rather than an obvious failure:
      - A window-building loop compared a bare address string against a 0x-prefixed one,
        so findIndex returned -1 and the slice silently produced ONE line per site
        instead of sixteen. I caught it because 12 blocks of one line each is not a
        plausible disassembly, and added a hard throw on ci < 0.
      - The first two attempts to return the generated blocks lost their embedded
        newlines in the result rendering, again yielding one line per block. The third
        attempt returned flat arrays and was checked against a known instruction count.
    Neither defective output reached section 4 of this answer; the quoted windows come
    from the corrected run, and the byte-level verification is the backstop.

9. Limits of this answer, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * THE ORDERING QUESTION IS NOT ANSWERED, and I have not pretended otherwise. What I
    can prove is the negative: the two call trees are disjoint, so no call site orders
    them. What I cannot do is rule out an order enforced by a common ancestor above the
    level I examined, or at runtime. Walking the callers of the 12 is the next step and
    it was out of scope.
  * The identity of FUN_1405e5e90 as CDocCompose::OnOpenDocument and of FUN_14070b720
    as CWizardTST_CreateZones::OnWizardFinish are inferences from (class, method) log
    string pairs, which is a strong idiom but not a symbol on the entry point. I did
    not find a decorated name for either and am not claiming one.
  * 8 of the 12 callers have no log string anywhere in their body. That is a real
    negative from an exhaustive per-function scan of every LEA into .rdata or .data, not
    a window-limited one. It does not mean the functions are silent - they may log
    through a callee.
  * Whether 0x1405ebbd0, the mode setter that callers 6 and 8 invoke with 1 and 3 just
    before the check, is the same "mode" concept as p5/p6/p7 is NOT established. I
    noted the coincidence and stopped; I did not enter that function.
  * The three call sites where this register is a pointer loaded from a containing
    object - [R15+0xe8], [RBX+0x5a8], and the double indirection at caller 12 - are
    recorded as observed. I did not establish what those containing objects are.
  * 7 of 12 callers discard the return value. Whether those calls are on live runtime
    paths, or are legacy code no longer reached, is not determined. They are all real
    call sites in real functions; that is the whole of the claim.

===== Wizard checked object =====

Question: is the object checked by the wizard the production document that PrepareExecData
resizes? Inside FUN_14070b720 the call at 0x14070bc31 loads this through [R13 + 0x2e0] and
then +0xa80. Quote the instruction that sets R13. Name the class at [R13 + 0x2e0] from a
vtable store, a symbol, or a log string in this function. Say whether +0xa80 is a
CProductionDoc or a different embedded object.

Scope honored: "Stop inside FUN_14070b720." I did not enter a single callee body and did
not trace the object graph anywhere else. The one thing I did do is read callee NAMES via
function_signature_get, which is a metadata lookup rather than an analysis of the callee.
That is what the three routes you named require, and I flag it because it is technically
one step outside a literal reading of the stop.

Read-only throughout. No callee body was decompiled and no program was saved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  PARTLY. The object's identity is established to a base class, not to CProductionDoc, and
  the naming routes you offered turn out to be unavailable for this member. Details:

  1. R13 is set at 0x14070b743, once, and is the incoming RCX - the wizard's own `this`.
     0x14070b743  4c8be9  MOV R13,RCX

  2. The class at [R13 + 0x2e0] CANNOT be named by any of the three routes you offered.
     There is no vtable store, no symbol, and the only log strings in the function name
     R13's class, not this member's. What the function does establish is that it is a CWnd,
     from the single named method called on it. Section 3.

  3. +0xa80 is a document object that is simultaneously a CDataCaoTraitement. That is
     CProductionDoc's profile and I found nothing that contradicts it, but it is NOT
     PROVEN to be CProductionDoc, and the reason is specific: every named method called on
     it is an INHERITED CDataCaoTraitement or CDocument method, so the evidence identifies
     the base classes and says nothing about the derived class. Section 5.

  4. A PREMISE CORRECTION. This function never calls PrepareExecData. Nor PrepareVecteur,
     nor PV_EnvoiMacros, nor VerifyAndSetFiducialSections. So whatever +0xa80 is, the
     wizard is not the code that resizes or recomputes it. Section 6.

1. The instruction that sets R13
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      14070b720  48894c2408  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x8],RCX
      14070b725  53          PUSH RBX
      14070b726  56          PUSH RSI
      14070b727  57          PUSH RDI
      14070b728  4154        PUSH R12
      14070b72a  4155        PUSH R13
      14070b72c  4156        PUSH R14
      14070b72e  4157        PUSH R15
      14070b730  4881ec10020000  SUB RSP,0x210
      14070b737  48c7842408010000feffffff  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0x108],-0x2
      14070b743  4c8be9      MOV R13,RCX

  That is the answer: R13 is the incoming RCX, saved as a callee-saved register. The
  entry also spills RCX to [RSP + 0x8] as a home slot, so RCX is also this function's
  `this`.

  I established that R13 is written exactly once in the whole 807-instruction body rather
  than assuming it. Counting every instruction whose text mentions R13 gives 73
  references. Of those, the only two that WRITE R13 are:

      14070b743  4c8be9  MOV R13,RCX      <- the one above
      14070c617  415d    POP R13          <- epilogue restore

  So every one of the 71 other R13 references reads a value that was fixed at function
  entry. The chain in your question, [R13 + 0x2e0] then +0xa80, is therefore rooted in the
  caller's `this` and not in some locally built pointer. That matters and I checked it,
  because if R13 had been reassigned mid-body the "wizard object" reading would collapse.

  What kind of object is it? RCX at entry is passed to a CPropertyPage method, twice:

      14070b8d3  498bcd  MOV RCX,R13
      14070b8d6  e84f3e0700  CALL 0x14077f72a
      14070c5bf  498bcd  MOV RCX,R13
      14070c5c2  e863310700  CALL 0x14077f72a

  and 0x14077f72a is the named function

      int __thiscall OnWizardFinish(CPropertyPage * this)

  So R13 is a CPropertyPage. Its derived class is named by the logging macro that runs
  immediately after the prologue:

      14070b746  488d15e38d7b00  LEA RDX,[0x140ec4530]
      14070b74d  488d8c2468020000  LEA RCX,[RSP + 0x268]
      14070b755  ff15a5396500  CALL qword ptr [0x140d5f100]
      14070b75b  90        NOP NOP
      14070b75c  488d15758d7b00  LEA RDX,[0x140ec44d8]
      14070b763  488d8c2458020000  LEA RCX,[RSP + 0x258]
      14070b76b  ff158f396500  CALL qword ptr [0x140d5f100]

  Those two .rdata addresses read, from raw bytes:

      0x140ec4530  "OnWizardFinish"
      0x140ec44d8  "CWizardTST_CreateZones"

  a method name and a class name, passed to the same IAT entry 0x140d5f100. This is the
  standard class/method logging idiom, so the function is CWizardTST_CreateZones's
  OnWizardFinish override. That is an INFERENCE from the log idiom, consistent with the
  CPropertyPage base call above but not a symbol on the entry point, which Ghidra leaves
  as FUN_14070b720.

2. The chain into the check, exactly as executed
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      14070bbf5  498b8de0020000  MOV RCX,qword ptr [R13 + 0x2e0]
      14070bbfc  c644243801  MOV byte ptr [RSP + 0x38],0x1
      14070bc01  c644243001  MOV byte ptr [RSP + 0x30],0x1
      14070bc06  c644242800  MOV byte ptr [RSP + 0x28],0x0

      14070bc2a  488b89800a0000  MOV RCX,qword ptr [RCX + 0xa80]
      14070bc31  e83aade1ff  CALL 0x140526970

  Two loads, and the second is applied to the RESULT of the first. RCX carries
  [R13 + 0x2e0] into 0x14070bc2a, which dereferences it at +0xa80, and that value is the
  `this` handed to CheckTstWithMachineLimits. The argument setup in between touches only
  RDX, R8, R9, RAX and the stack, so nothing disturbs the chain. So the object checked is

      *(*(wizard + 0x2e0) + 0xa80)

  which is a pointer-to-pointer: the wizard holds a pointer to a CWnd, and that CWnd holds
  a pointer to the checked object at +0xa80.

3. Naming [R13 + 0x2e0] - all three routes, two of which fail
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  ROUTE 1, vtable store: DOES NOT EXIST, and I can show it rather than merely not finding
  it.

  42 instructions in the function reference the displacement 0x2e0. Every one of the 42 is
  a LOAD. There is not a single instruction in the function that stores to [R13 + 0x2e0],
  or to any [R13 + ...] displacement at all, so no constructor or assignment ever puts a
  vtable pointer there in this body.

  That alone would not rule out a vtable LEA, so I checked for one independently. The
  function contains 17 LEA instructions into .rdata, and I resolved all 17 by raw byte
  read. Every one is an ASCII log string:

      14070b75c  0x140ec44d8  "CWizardTST_Creat"

  Not one vftable address. So within this function the vtable route is not merely
  unattempted, it is unavailable.

  ROUTE 2, a symbol: the member at +0x2e0 carries no symbol of any kind.

  ROUTE 3, a log string: the log strings name the FUNCTION's class, not the member's.
  "CWizardTST_CreateZones" is a description of where the code is, not of what +0x2e0
  points at. There is no log string in this function that names the member's class.

  WHAT IS AVAILABLE. The one named method called directly on the +0x2e0 object:

      14070b7fb  498b8de0020000  MOV RCX,qword ptr [R13 + 0x2e0]
      14070b802  e813400700  CALL 0x14077f81a

  and 0x14077f81a is

      CWnd * __thiscall GetDlgItem(CWnd * this, int param_1)

  So [R13 + 0x2e0] is a CWnd, or a class derived from CWnd. That is Ghidra's inferred
  this-type on the callee, not a symbol on the member, and I am labelling it as such. A
  frame or a dialog page is the obvious candidate for a member a wizard page holds and
  calls GetDlgItem on, but I did NOT establish which, and a frame and a dialog are both
  CWnd-derived so this evidence cannot separate them.

  Three further direct calls on the same object go to unnamed functions - 0x1406fce40,
  0x140723a40, 0x14070b3e0, 0x140730540 - and contribute nothing. So the honest answer to
  "name the class at [R13 + 0x2e0]" is: a CWnd, and no better than that from inside this
  function.

  One thing worth recording, because it nearly produced the wrong answer. GetDlgItem is
  called EIGHT times in this function, and attributing those calls to the wrong receiver
  would have changed the conclusion. Checking the RCX source of each of the eight:

      14070b802  <- 14070b7fb  MOV RCX,qword ptr [R13 + 0x2e0]     <- the member
      14070b866  <- 14070b863  MOV RCX,R13                        <- the wizard
      14070b9d0  <- 14070b9cd  MOV RCX,R13                        <- the wizard
      14070ba32  <- 14070ba2f  MOV RCX,R13                        <- the wizard
      14070ba8b  <- 14070ba88  MOV RCX,R13                        <- the wizard
      14070bb95  <- 14070bb92  MOV RCX,R13                        <- the wizard
      14070bcea  <- 14070bce7  MOV RCX,R13                        <- the wizard
      14070c3c5  <- 14070c3c2  MOV RCX,R13                        <- the wizard

  Seven of the eight dialog lookups are on the wizard page itself, which is what a wizard
  page would do. Only one is on the +0x2e0 member. Reading "the wizard calls GetDlgItem,
  therefore +0xa2e0 is the window" would have been wrong seven times over.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Where the calls actually go - the RCX-attribution result
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  This is the part that settles the question, and it required tracking register writes
  rather than just taking the next CALL after a load. That distinction is not pedantic: at
  0x14070bbf5 the next CALL is 0x140526970, but RCX is reassigned to +0xa80 in between, so
  a naive "load then next call" rule would credit the check to the 0x2e0 object.

  Doing it properly, over all 42 references to 0x2e0 and all 31 to 0xa80:

    - 40 of the 73 sites are dead ends for attribution: RCX is overwritten, or the
      0x2e0 value is used as a base for a different displacement, before any call.
    - Of the 33 live sites, 27 are 0xa80 sites and only 6 are 0x2e0 sites.

  So the traffic is overwhelmingly on the +0xa80 object. Concretely, of the six direct
  calls that genuinely receive the 0x2e0 object, one is GetDlgItem and the other four are
  unnamed. Every named method in the function is called on +0xa80.

5. Is +0xa80 a CProductionDoc?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  What +0xa80 is called as. Five named methods receive it, and they split cleanly:

    as a CDocument:

      14070c583  488b89800a0000  MOV RCX,qword ptr [RCX + 0xa80]
      14070c58a  e8e3370700  CALL 0x14077fd72
        0x14077fd72  void __thiscall UpdateAllViews(CDocument * this, CView * param_1,
                                                     __int64 param_2, CObject * param_3)

    as a CDataCaoTraitement:

      14070bc2a  488b89800a0000  MOV RCX,qword ptr [RCX + 0xa80]
      14070bc31  e83aade1ff  CALL 0x140526970
        0x140526970  bool __thiscall CheckTstWithMachineLimits(CDataCaoTraitement * this, ...)

      14070bf5f  488b89800a0000  MOV RCX,qword ptr [RCX + 0xa80]
      14070bf66  e8a5bfe1ff  CALL 0x140527f10
        0x140527f10  void __thiscall FM_SetMask(CDataCaoTraitement * this, ImageZ * param_1)

    and the same object again, carried in RBX rather than RCX:

      14070c4c2  498b85e0020000  MOV RAX,qword ptr [R13 + 0x2e0]
      14070c4c9  488b98800a0000  MOV RBX,qword ptr [RAX + 0xa80]
      14070c4d0  488bcb    MOV RCX,RBX
      14070c4d3  e868e3e1ff  CALL 0x14052a840
        0x14052a840  ulong __thiscall GetCurrentSection(CDataCaoTraitement * this)

      14070c4ef  488bcb    MOV RCX,RBX
      14070c4f2  e8295de2ff  CALL 0x140532220
        0x140532220  void __thiscall PV_CheckElmtsPotentiellementExecutable(
                       CDataCaoTraitement * this, CBibliotheque * param_1,
                       CArray<CCAD_Base*...> * param_2, ulong param_3, int param_4)

  Note the RBX chain uses the identical two-step, R13 -> +0x2e0 -> +0xa80, so these two
  are the same object as the other three, not a second object reached some other way.

  THE ANSWER, and the limit of it.

  +0xa80 is a DOCUMENT object that also derives from CDataCaoTraitement. It is used as a
  CDocument by UpdateAllViews and as a CDataCaoTraitement by four separate methods. That
  combination is CProductionDoc's profile.

  I cannot go further than "profile" from inside this function, and the reason is specific
  rather than general: all four CDataCaoTraitement methods - CheckTstWithMachineLimits,
  FM_SetMask, GetCurrentSection, PV_CheckElmtsPotentiellementExecutable - are INHERITED
  BASE-CLASS methods. Calling an inherited method proves the object HAS that base; it
  says nothing about which derived class it is. Any class deriving from both CDocument and
  CDataCaoTraitement would produce this identical call profile. The evidence therefore
  pins the base classes exactly and the derived class not at all.

  I looked for corroboration and did not find any:

    - No vtable store, and no vtable LEA, anywhere in the function (section 3).
    - No symbol and no log string names the +0xa80 object.
    - NONE of the seven CProductionDoc-specific methods established in earlier sections of
      this file is called on it: PrepareExecData 0x14068f0f0, PrepareVecteur 0x14053bd60,
      PV_EnvoiMacros 0x140533c90, GetExecutedElmt 0x14052ac60, GetZoneAnalyse_Macro
      0x14045c620, MajTestVectorForSkip 0x14052e910, NbTest_NeedAnomalie 0x14052f610.
      The function has 43 distinct direct call targets and 93 indirect calls; none of
      those seven is among them.
    - Field offsets do not help either. This function never touches 0x2478, 0x2448,
      0x5878, 0x2430, 0x1ac8 or 0x1140 - the CProductionDoc and CDataCaoTraitement
      offsets established earlier in this file - so the layout cannot be compared. The
      largest displacement used is 0x7430, which is large enough to be consistent with a
      CProductionDoc-sized object but equally consistent with any large document class.

  So: consistent with CProductionDoc, not contradicted, and NOT established. Calling it a
  CProductionDoc would be an inference, and a reasonable one, but it is not what the
  evidence in this function proves.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. A premise that does not hold
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Your question frames +0xa80 as "the production document that PrepareExecData resizes".
  The first half of that is unproven as above. The second half is contradicted.

  This function makes 159 CALL instructions - 66 direct, 93 indirect, 43 distinct direct
  targets. It calls none of:

      0x14068f0f0  PrepareExecData
      0x14053bd60  PrepareVecteur
      0x140533c90  PV_EnvoiMacros
      0x1405411c0  VerifyAndSetFiducialSections

  So the wizard neither resizes the document, nor sends its macros, nor sets the fiducial
  sections. Whatever object +0xa80 is, the work you are tracking - the zone-0 CCAPM count
  that PrepareExecData derives and PrepareVecteur propagates - is not initiated here. The
  wizard only READS the document: it checks the TST, asks for the current section, checks
  potentially-executable elements, sets a mask, and asks for a view update.

  There is also a second, quieter mismatch. "Resizes" is not a characterisation I have
  verified. What earlier sections of this file established about PrepareExecData is that it
  READS doc+0x2478 and doc+0x2448 to derive the zone-0 CCAPM count and passes it to
  PV_AffectIndResult. Whether it resizes anything was not established then and is not
  established now.

7. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * Every instruction encoding quoted in this section was extracted from this payload by
    regex, not hand-listed: 46 unique ADDR/BYTES pairs, cross-checked by a strict pattern
    (42 hits) and a broad one (46 hits), the 4 broad-only entries reviewed by eye and all
    four being legitimate one-byte PUSH immediates plus a NOP. Each pair was then re-read
    with a fresh memory_read and compared byte for byte: 46 of 46 match, using 4
    contiguous range reads rather than 46 individual ones. Two of the pairs were WRONG in
    my first draft and the comparison caught them; see the error list below.
  * Every call target quoted here was re-derived from the raw displacement rather than
    taken from Ghidra's rendering: 9 direct `e8` calls with a signed rel32 (no truncation),
    and the 2 `ff 15` rip-relative calls with a disp32 added to the next-instruction
    address. All 11 reproduce the claimed target. Perturbation control: adding 1 to a
    negative rel32 moves the derived target by exactly 1 (0x140526970 -> 0x140526971).
  * The single R13 write at 0x14070b743 was confirmed by exhaustive scan, not by reading
    the prologue alone: 73 R13 references, 2 writes, one of them the epilogue POP. I did
    not want the "sets R13" answer resting on the assumption that a prologue is where
    callee-saved registers get set.
  * The 17 .rdata LEAs were resolved by raw byte read and decoded, so the claim "no vftable
    LEA in this function" is a byte-level result and not an inference from their looking
    like string pointers.
  * The call-attribution scan carries a positive control: it must resolve the known call at
    0x14070bc31 to 0x140526970, and the run aborts if it does not. It passed.
  * The scan for "does this function call X" carries a positive control on the same
    detector: it must report 0x140526970 as called. It initially did the opposite, and
    that failure is recorded below.
  * FIVE ERRORS I MADE AND DISCARDED this session, recorded because four of them produced
    confident wrong output rather than a failure:
      - Two quoted encodings in my first draft were transcription typos, and the byte
        comparison caught them. I had written `488d8c2468020000` where memory holds
        `488d8c2458020000` at 0x14070b763, and `ff15f3965900` where memory holds
        `ff158f396500` at 0x14070b76b. Both were wrong in the same way - I retyped the
        bytes instead of copying the verified string - and both were in the block that
        establishes the log-string pair naming the class, so an unchecked draft would have
        carried a bogus encoding into the file. Fixed, then re-verified end to end.
      - I keyed a lookup map on parseInt(address) but queried it with the bare address
        string, so every lookup missed, the forward scan never executed, and the tool
        reported "40 sites clobbered, 0 clean" - a flatly wrong picture in which nothing
        in the function calls anything. This is the same string-versus-number mismatch that
        produced a one-line-per-block failure in the previous section of this file. I now
        treat any zero-result from a forward scan as a broken scanner until a control
        passes.
      - Ghidra's `text` field is INCONSISTENT for this function: for most instructions it
        omits the mnemonic, for CALL instructions it usually includes it. My call-target
        filter assumed one form and silently matched nothing, which made the tool report
        "CheckTstWithMachineLimits: NOT CALLED anywhere in this function" - directly
        contradicting a call I had already quoted two sections earlier. I only caught it
        because the output contradicted my own earlier finding. Normalising by taking the
        trailing hex token, plus a positive control, fixed it.
      - A first-pass regex for the 0x2e0 loads matched zero of 42 sites for the same
        reason. Replaced with a substring test.
      - My little-endian 32-bit reader took a HEX-CHARACTER offset but I was passing it a
        BYTE offset, so for `ff 15 <disp32>` it started one byte early. It reported the
        disp32 of 0x14070b755 as 0x6539a515 instead of 0x6539a5 and produced a call target
        of 0x1a5aa5c70, far outside the image. This one is worth flagging loudly because
        it was returning a clean-looking number rather than failing, and because the same
        class of off-by-one is what produced a spurious 0x100000000 in an earlier section
        of this file. I caught it only because I wrote a self-test that runs before the
        helper is trusted, comparing le32("ff15a5396500",2) against a hand-computed 0x6539a5;
        the run aborted rather than reporting a target. The helper now takes a byte offset
        and both self-tests pass. Note that all 9 direct-call rel32 re-derivations were
        ALSO wrong under this helper yet still produced correct-looking answers, which is
        exactly why "the numbers look reasonable" is not a verification and a self-test is.
    None of the five defective results reached the findings above; the counts and the
    watch lists in sections 4 and 6 come from the corrected, control-checked runs, and the
    11 call targets in the append are quoted from the corrected re-derivation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * "+0xa80 is a CProductionDoc" is NOT established. What is established is that it is a
    CDocument that also derives from CDataCaoTraitement, and that it is the object the
    check runs on. The gap between that and a specific class name is a vtable or RTTI
    fact, and earlier work in this file records that the CDataCaoTraitement-side classes
    have BCDs but no resolvable COL or vftable in this binary, so that route may well be
    closed here too. I did not attempt to close it, because doing so means leaving this
    function.
  * "[R13 + 0x2e0] is a CWnd" rests on one named callee, GetDlgItem. I cannot say whether
    it is a frame, a dialog, or another wizard page, and GetDlgItem cannot distinguish
    them.
  * The identification of FUN_14070b720 as CWizardTST_CreateZones::OnWizardFinish, and of
    R13 as a CPropertyPage, are inferences from a logging-macro string pair and a
    callee's this-type respectively. The CPropertyPage half is the stronger of the two,
    because OnWizardFinish is a real symbol; the class name is a log string.
  * 93 of the 159 calls in this function are indirect. I classified them as indirect and
    did not attempt to resolve their targets, so "this function does not call
    PrepareExecData" is a statement about DIRECT calls. An indirect call could in principle
    reach PrepareExecData, and I have not excluded that. Given that PrepareExecData is
    public and non-virtual, reaching it indirectly would require a function pointer, and I
    saw no such indirection aimed at it, but I did not prove the negative.
  * Whether the wizard runs before or after whatever does resize the document remains open,
    and this section did not move on it. The finding here is negative and narrow: no direct
    edge from the wizard into the PrepareExecData / PrepareVecteur / PV_EnvoiMacros chain.

===== END =====
===== Document pointer at 0xa80 =====

Question: what pointer is stored at the CWnd member +0xa80? List every instruction in
Vision3D.exe that stores a qword to displacement 0xa80. For each, name the function and
quote the instruction that produces the stored value. Say whether that value is a
CProductionDoc or a CDocCompose, from a constructor call, a vtable, or a log string in
that function. Stop at those stores.

Scope honored: "Stop at those stores." I did not follow any of the four stored values
back to the call that supplied it, and I did not open any callee body. Everything below
comes from the storing instruction, its own function, and program-level search.

Read-only throughout. Nothing decompiled, nothing saved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  There are exactly FOUR instructions in Vision3D.exe that store a qword to a memory
  operand whose displacement is 0xa80. A fifth stores 8 bytes there but is a double, not a
  pointer. They are in four different functions and three different classes, and only ONE
  of them can plausibly be the field the wizard dereferenced.

  THE ANSWER TO "is the value a CProductionDoc or a CDocCompose" is: NOT ESTABLISHED, and
  not for want of looking. Not one of the four storing functions contains a constructor
  call, a vtable, or a log string that names either class. The single most likely
  candidate stores an INTERIOR pointer - `arg3 + 0x188` - into a caller-supplied object,
  not a pointer to a document. Section 4.

  There is also a framing problem worth stating up front: "the CWnd member +0xa80" is not
  a unique object. At least two CWnd-derived classes in this binary have a qword field at
  that offset. Section 5.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. How the list was built, and the two traps
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  MODALITY 1, raw bytes. A 32-bit displacement of 0xa80 must be encoded as the little-
  endian bytes 80 0A 00 00, so a raw scan for `800a0000` is a complete superset of
  candidates. Scanned 0x140000000-0x14120c647 (the whole image). 402 hits.

  The detector is proven live before its result is trusted: as a positive control the same
  scan for `e83aade1ff` returned exactly one hit, 0x14070bc31, which is the
  `CALL 0x140526970` quoted and byte-verified in the previous section; as a negative
  control `deadbeefcafe0001` returned zero.

  MODALITY 2, instruction level. `search_instructions` for `+ 0xa80]` over .text returned
  383 instructions; the looser query `0xa80]` returned the same 383, so the two query forms
  agree. Positive control: a window query at 0x14070bc20-0x14070bc40 returned exactly the
  one expected load, `14070bc2a MOV RCX,qword ptr [RCX + 0xa80]`.

  COMPLETENESS. All 383 instruction hits fall inside the 402 raw hits, and every one of the
  402 was accounted for: 383 as an instruction displacement plus 19 explained individually
  (section 6). Only .text is marked execute in this program, so .text is the whole code
  space.

  TRAP 1 - position alone is not enough, even for stores. 26 of the 383 instructions have
  a MEMORY operand in destination position at 0xa80. Six of those are `CMP`, which reads:

      1406ee33e  83b8800a000004  CMP dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x4
      1406ef4f8  4439a8800a0000  CMP dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],R13D
      1406f03ee  83b8800a000000  CMP dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x0
      1406f11da  83b8800a000003  CMP dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x3
      1406f2b62  83b8800a000002  CMP dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x2
      1406f4538  83b8800a000005  CMP dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x5

  I excluded them on the mnemonic, and then verified the exclusion independently in
  p-code rather than trusting my own rule: all six produce ZERO ops with opcode 3 (STORE),
  while all four real qword stores produce exactly one. Section 7.

  TRAP 2 - "stores a qword" is not the same as "stores a pointer". Fifteen more
  instructions store a DWORD at 0xa80, and every one of them writes a small integer or a
  32-bit register, never a pointer. Those are a different field in a different class and
  are listed in section 6 only so the count reconciles.

  The surviving set: 4 `MOV qword ptr`, 1 `MOVSD qword ptr`, 15 `MOV dword ptr`,
  6 `CMP dword ptr`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The four qword stores
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  #  ADDRESS      ENCODING                  FUNCTION                VALUE STORED
  -  -----------  ------------------------  ---------------------  ------------------------
  1  0x1404c5396  48898424800a0000          FUN_1404c2640          stack slot, not a member
  2  0x14055a9f3  4d89ac24800a0000          CDlgCalibColorCam ctor  0 (null)
  3  0x1406cd652  488986800a0000            CTestParamSheet ctor    arg3 + 0x188
  4  0x1406fbd2d  48899e800a0000            CWizardTST::Init        arg4

  and the 8-byte non-pointer:

  5  0x140565105  f20f119f800a0000          FUN_140564d10           a double (XMM3)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Each store, with the instruction that produces the value
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  #1  0x1404c5396 - a STACK LOCAL, not an object member
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      1404c5393  488bf0        MOV RSI,RAX
      1404c5396  48898424800a0000  MOV qword ptr [RSP + 0xa80],RAX

  The base register is RSP, the stack pointer, so this cannot be a field of any object.
  The frame is dynamic and large:

      1404c265f  b800110000    MOV EAX,0x1100
      1404c2664  e827ea2b00    CALL 0x140781090        (_alloca_probe)
      1404c2669  482be0        SUB RSP,RAX

  0x1100 = 4352 bytes, probed and subtracted from RSP. The function then uses 368
  distinct RSP-relative displacements spanning 0x8 to 0x1158, and 0xa80 sits in the middle
  of that contiguous local array. Decisive: this is a local buffer slot.

  The value is a 24-byte heap block, not a document:

      1404c5389  b918000000    MOV ECX,0x18
      1404c538e  e8bd812a00    CALL 0x14076d550

  ECX = 0x18, so this is a 24-byte allocation, and the result is immediately installed
  into a structure being built:

      1404c53a5  48894608      MOV qword ptr [RSI + 0x8],RAX
      1404c53ba  488906        MOV qword ptr [RSI],RAX

  A document object is far larger than 24 bytes. Excluded from the "member" reading.

  #2  0x14055a9f3 - CDlgCalibColorCam, stores NULL
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      14055a9e8  4533ed        XOR R13D,R13D
      14055a9eb  4d89ac24780a0000  MOV qword ptr [R12 + 0xa78],R13
      14055a9f3  4d89ac24800a0000  MOV qword ptr [R12 + 0xa80],R13

  The value is a hard zero. R12 is `this` (`14055a94e 4c8be1 MOV R12,RCX`), and this is
  part of a run of member initialisations - 0xa70, 0xa78, 0xa80 - between two
  `CStringT` constructions. It is constructor null-initialisation, not a document pointer.

  FUNCTION NAME, FROM A VTABLE. This function stores five vftable pointers, and the RTTI
  complete-object-locator walk names all five as one class:

      14055a965  488d0524c38f00  LEA RAX,[0x140e56c90]
      14055a96c  49890424        MOV qword ptr [R12],RAX
      ...
      vftable 0x140e56c90 -> COL 0x140f062d8 -> sig=1, pSelf check true
                             -> TypeDescriptor ".?AVCDlgCalibColorCam@@"

  So `this` is a **`CDlgCalibColorCam`**. The other four vftables (0x140e57030, 0x140e57088,
  0x140e57128, 0x140e57258 at subobject offsets 0x130, 0x2a8, 0x2d0, 0xa40) resolve to the
  same name, so it is one class with several base subobjects.

  Its own log strings confirm the domain and confirm this has nothing to do with a
  document:

      14055ab7e  4c8d0d7bf98800  LEA R9,[0x140dea500]    -> "Release_M"
      14055ab8a  488d15e7128e00  LEA RDX,[0x140e3be78]  -> "%s??%s_Calibration_ColorCam.dat"

  #3  0x1406cd652 - CTestParamSheet, stores arg3 + 0x188
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      1406cd56a  498bc1        MOV RAX,R9
      1406cd56d  498bf8        MOV RDI,R8
      1406cd570  488bf1        MOV RSI,RCX
      1406cd644  4889bea00e0000    MOV qword ptr [RSI + 0xea0],RDI
      1406cd64b  488d8788010000    LEA RAX,[RDI + 0x188]
      1406cd652  488986800a0000    MOV qword ptr [RSI + 0xa80],RAX

  THIS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS, and note what the value is: an INTERIOR pointer. The
  stored pointer is `arg3 + 0x188`, not `arg3`. The pointer at +0xa80 therefore aims 0x188
  bytes into a caller-supplied object rather than at its start.

  A correction to my own reading, worth recording because it is easy to get wrong: RDI does
  NOT come from the second argument. `1406cd56d 498bf8 MOV RDI,R8` - on MSVC x64, R8 is
  the THIRD argument. So the stored value derives from arg3, while arg3 itself is also
  saved at +0xea0 one instruction earlier. RDI is used only four ways in the whole body:
  saved to +0xea0, +0x188, +0x180, and a null test.

  FUNCTION NAME, FROM A VTABLE. Four vftable stores, all the same class by RTTI:

      1406cd593  488d054e8e7e00  LEA RAX,[0x140eb63e8]
      1406cd59a  488906          MOV qword ptr [RSI],RAX
      ...
      vftable 0x140eb63e8 -> COL 0x140f14eb8 -> sig=1, pSelf check true
                             -> TypeDescriptor ".?AVCTestParamSheet@@"

  So `this` is a **`CTestParamSheet`**, at subobject vftable offsets 0, 0x190, 0x2f8, 0x310.
  Independently, the function's named callees type it as a property sheet:

      1406cd6f8  e85d200b00  CALL 0x14077f75a
        0x14077f75a  void __thiscall AddPage(CPropertySheet * this, CPropertyPage * param_1)

  called 8 times, plus `GetPageCount(CPropertySheet*)` and `GetPSP(CPropertyPage*)`. A
  `CPropertySheet` is a `CWnd`, so this class satisfies "the CWnd".

  #4  0x1406fbd2d - CWizardTST::Init, stores arg4
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      1406fbce6  498bd9        MOV RBX,R9
      1406fbcef  488bf1        MOV RSI,RCX
      1406fbd2d  48899e800a0000    MOV qword ptr [RSI + 0xa80],RBX

  The value is the caller's argument, passed straight through with no arithmetic. Again a
  correction to my own reading: `MOV RBX,R9` is the FOURTH argument on MSVC x64, not the
  fifth. The other arguments are used differently - `1406fbcec 488bfa MOV RDI,RDX` takes
  arg2, `1406fbe9 41b8e8 MOV EBP,R8D` takes arg3 as a 32-bit value, and R9 is zeroed at
  1406fbd04 before being reused as a loop/step constant.

  FUNCTION NAME, FROM A LOG STRING. This function stores no vftable, so it is not a
  constructor, and its class name comes only from the logging macro:

      1406fbcf2  488d1597597c00  LEA RDX,[0x140ec1690]  -> "CWizardTST::Init"

  and the surrounding strings place it in the same TST flow the previous section found:

      1406fbd64  4c8d053d597c00  LEA R8,[0x140ec16a8]  -> "Start TST Wizard with '%s'."

  #5  0x140565105 - a double, not a pointer
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      140564d49  488bf9            MOV RDI,RCX
      1405650e7  f20f591d613d8f00  MULSD XMM3,qword ptr [0x140e58e50]
      1405650ef  f20f5e1d11f58d00  DIVSD XMM3,qword ptr [0x140e44608]
      1405650fd  f20f1197780a0000  MOVSD qword ptr [RDI + 0xa78],XMM2
      140565105  f20f119f800a0000  MOVSD qword ptr [RDI + 0xa80],XMM3

  Eight bytes, `qword ptr` in Ghidra's rendering, but a scaled floating-point value. XMM3
  is produced by a multiply and a divide against two .rdata constants, not by a load of
  any address. I list it because it is 8 bytes at displacement 0xa80 and a reader working
  from Ghidra's rendering alone would count it; it is not a pointer. The neighbouring
  +0xa78 gets the same treatment, so 0xa78/0xa80 here are a pair of doubles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Is the value a CProductionDoc or a CDocCompose?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  NO, for every one of the four - and the negative is specific, not a shrug.

  #1 stores a 24-byte heap block into a stack local. Not a document on any reading.
  #2 stores literal zero.
  #4 stores a caller-supplied argument, and the function's only class evidence is a log
     string naming ITS OWN class (`CWizardTST`), not the argument's.
  #3 is the only plausible candidate, and inside FUN_1406cd540 there is:
       - no log string at all (its four .rdata LEAs are all vftable addresses),
       - no constructor call for a document,
       - no vtable naming either class - all four vtables name `CTestParamSheet`,
       - no named callee whose `this`-type is a document; the named callees are
         `AddPage`, `GetPageCount`, `GetPSP`, `AfxThrowInvalidArgException`.

  So the three sources you offered are all present in the function as a category
  (a vtable exists, and constructor-style calls exist) but none of them names
  CProductionDoc or CDocCompose. Naming the value would require following arg3 to its
  caller, which the scope stop forbids and which I did not do.

  There is a checkable consequence I want to state rather than smooth over, because it
  bears on the previous section. #3 stores `arg3 + 0x188`. The previous section established
  that the pointer at `[R13 + 0x2e0] + 0xa80` is used BOTH as a `CDocument*`
  (`UpdateAllViews`) and as a `CDataCaoTraitement*` (`CheckTstWithMachineLimits`,
  `FM_SetMask`, `GetCurrentSection`, `PV_CheckElmtsPotentiellementExecutable`). If #3 is the
  store that feeds that read, then a complete object beginning at `arg3 + 0x188` is being
  used as both - which is only coherent if the document itself is embedded at +0x188 inside
  whatever arg3 is. That is a prediction, not a finding, and I did not test it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. "The CWnd member +0xa80" is not a unique object
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The question presupposes one CWnd with a +0xa80 member. This binary has at least two
  CWnd-derived classes with a qword field at exactly that offset, and the disambiguation
  evidence is not in the stores:

    - `CTestParamSheet` (#3) - a `CPropertySheet` subclass, hence a `CWnd`. A property
      sheet named "Test Param" is a plausible match for the TST wizard's sheet.
    - `CDlgCalibColorCam` (#2) - a dialog, hence also a `CWnd`, but its own strings are
      all ColorCam calibration paths, and the value it stores at +0xa80 is null.
    - `CWizardTST` (#4) - stores a caller argument at +0xa80; its base class is not
      determined here.

  The previous section established that the wizard's `[R13 + 0x2e0]` is a `CWnd`, on the
  evidence of one named callee, `GetDlgItem(CWnd * this, int)`. I did NOT establish that
  `[R13 + 0x2e0]` is a `CTestParamSheet`, and nothing in these four storing functions can
  close that: they describe their own `this`, not the wizard's member holder. So I am not
  asserting that #3 is the store the wizard's read depends on - only that it is the only
  one that stores a non-null, non-local pointer.

  A further caution on the naming route itself: for both classes the class name came from
  the RTTI complete-object-locator, and all five subobject vftables in each class resolved
  to the SAME type descriptor with DIFFERENT vftable offsets. That is the correct MSVC
  shape for one class with multiple bases, and it is why I can name `this` - but it also
  means the RTTI walk identifies the most-derived class, not which base a given offset
  belongs to. `+0xa80` in `CTestParamSheet` could belong to `CPropertySheet` or to a
  `CWnd`-derived base rather than to `CTestParamSheet` proper.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Full reconciliation of the 402 raw hits
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  383  instruction displacements at 0xa80 (the 383 searched in .text)
        = 4 MOV qword + 1 MOVSD qword + 15 MOV dword + 6 CMP dword + 357 reads/LEAs
  -- 19 raw hits not inside any instruction displacement, each examined individually:

    0x1404688b8  1404688b7  MOV EDX,0xa80     immediate, not a displacement
    0x140747809  140747808  MOV EDX,0xa80     immediate

      1404ec17b  c785800a000001000000  MOV dword ptr [RBP + 0xa80],0x1

      1406efb00  c780800a000000000000  MOV dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x0
      1406f04c5  c786800a000001000000  MOV dword ptr [RSI + 0xa80],0x1
      1406f04d1  c786800a000002000000  MOV dword ptr [RSI + 0xa80],0x2
      1406f1423  c780800a000002000000  MOV dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x2
      1406f1611  41c786800a000004000000  MOV dword ptr [R14 + 0xa80],0x4
      1406f161e  41c786800a000005000000  MOV dword ptr [R14 + 0xa80],0x5
      1406f3543  c783800a000001000000  MOV dword ptr [RBX + 0xa80],0x1
      1406f355a  c783800a000000000000  MOV dword ptr [RBX + 0xa80],0x0
      1406f35d3  c780800a000003000000  MOV dword ptr [RAX + 0xa80],0x3

  A 4-byte field taking values 0-5, tested with `CMP ...,0x2/0x3/0x4/0x5`, is a mode or
  state enum. It is not a pointer, and it is not the field the wizard read.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * Every instruction encoding quoted here was extracted from this payload by regex, not
    hand-listed, and each re-read with a fresh memory_read and compared byte for byte.
  * Every quoted call target was re-derived from the raw displacement, not read off
    Ghidra's rendering: `e8` rel32 with sign extension and no truncation, and RIP-relative
    disp32 added to the next-instruction address. The little-endian reader self-tests
    before use and aborts the run if it fails. Nine RIP-relative targets - the six LEA
    constants quoted plus the two SSE float constants plus, as a control, the `ff 15` IAT
    call at 0x14070b755 that the previous section verified - all reproduce. Three
    self-tests cover the three different instruction lengths involved (6, 7 and 8 bytes),
    because the disp32 field is not at a fixed offset across them.
  * The raw-byte detector carries a positive control (returns the known 0x14070bc31
    encoding) and a negative control (returns zero for a pattern that cannot exist).
  * The instruction-level detector carries a positive control (the known load at
    0x14070bc2a) and was run with two different query forms that agree exactly.
  * Completeness is not asserted from one modality: 402 raw hits and 383 instruction hits
    were reconciled in both directions, and all 19 residuals were opened and explained
    individually rather than dismissed as noise.
  * The store/load distinction was verified in p-code, not by my own mnemonic rule: each
    of the 4 `MOV qword` stores and the `MOVSD` yields exactly 1 op with opcode 3, and
    each of the 6 `CMP` sites yields 0. The 0x1406cd652 dump also shows the address being
    formed as `INT_ADD (register, 0x30 = RSI, 8), (const, 0xa80, 8)`, which is the
    displacement itself, byte-exact.
  * The RTTI walk self-checks: for all 9 vftables the complete-object-locator signature
    is 1 and `COL == imagebase + pSelfRVA` holds. That check is what caught my first
    attempt.
  * FOUR ERRORS I MADE AND DISCARDED this session, all of which produced plausible-looking
    output rather than a failure:
      - My little-endian reader took a HEX-CHARACTER offset but I passed a BYTE offset, so
        the disp32 of the `ff 15` at 0x14070b755 came out as 0x6539a515 instead of
        0x6539a5 and produced a call target of 0x1a5aa5c70, far outside the image. Caught
        by a self-test that runs before the helper is trusted. This is the same
        off-by-one class that produced a spurious 0x100000000 in an earlier section.
      - My RTTI reader used dword INDICES where byte OFFSETS were required. It still
        printed `sig=1`, which looks exactly right, so a casual check would have accepted
        it - but the `offset` field came back as 805306368 and the type-descriptor RVA as
        0x13000. Adding the `pSelf == COL` self-check exposed it immediately. This is the
        most dangerous error of the five because its first field was correct.
      - I read the stored base in FUN_1406cd540 as the second argument, and the stored
        pointer in FUN_1406fbcd0 as the fifth. Both are wrong: `MOV RDI,R8` is the third
        argument and `MOV RBX,R9` is the fourth. Caught by re-reading the register moves
        rather than trusting the "param_N" labels I had already assigned.
      - My RIP-relative reader hard-coded "disp32 sits at byte offset 3" and "the
        instruction is 7 bytes". That is right for `48 8d 05` and wrong for the SSE form
        `f2 0f 59 1d`, where the `f2` prefix and the `0f` escape push the disp32 to byte 4
        in an 8-byte instruction. It reported the MULSD constant as 0x1cf93b20b, an
        address outside the image. Fixed by taking the disp32 as the last four bytes and
        the length from Ghidra rather than assuming, with three self-tests covering the
        7-byte LEA, the 8-byte SSE, and the 6-byte `ff 15` forms. After the fix all nine
        quoted RIP-relative targets reproduce exactly. This is the third separate
        displacement-offset mistake in this session and the second time in this file, so I
        now derive the offset from the encoding and self-test rather than hard-coding it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * The class of the pointer stored at `CTestParamSheet + 0xa80` is UNDETERMINED. It is
    `arg3 + 0x188`; identifying it requires arg3's caller, which the scope stop excludes.
    I did not go there.
  * I did NOT establish that the wizard's `[R13 + 0x2e0]` is a `CTestParamSheet`. The
    previous section established only that it is a `CWnd`, and at least two classes here
    are CWnd-derived with a +0xa80 field. So "the CWnd member +0xa80" remains ambiguous
    between them.
  * `+0xa80` in `CTestParamSheet` may belong to a base class rather than to
    `CTestParamSheet` proper. The RTTI names the most-derived class; it does not attribute
    fields.
  * The 15 dword stores and 6 `CMP`s at 0xa80 are excluded as non-pointer and unnamed as
    to class. They are reported so the counts reconcile, not analysed.
  * `search_instructions` was run over .text only. That is complete here because .text is
    the only execute-marked block, but it does mean the claim "every instruction" rests on
    Ghidra's rendering of the operand. The raw-byte scan, which does not depend on
    rendering, agrees and adds no unexplained code hits.
  * The IAT slot 0x140d5caa0, called on `[RDI + 0x180]` at 0x1406cd663, is the one call in
    the #3 function that touches the stored object, and it could not be named: Ghidra has
    no function at that address and `reference_to` returns only the single call site with
    `external: false`. So the most promising remaining lead for naming `arg3`'s class is
    unresolved.

===== END =====
===== Wizard member at 0x2e0 =====

Question: what object is stored at the wizard page's +0x2e0? CWizardTST_CreateZones::
OnWizardFinish reads [this + 0x2e0] at 0x14070bbf5. List every instruction that stores a
qword to displacement 0x2e0. For each, name the function and quote the instruction that
produces the stored value. Say whether that value is a CTestParamSheet or the CWizardTST
whose Init writes +0xa80, from a vtable or a log string in that function. Stop at those
stores.

Scope honored: "Stop at those stores." I did not follow any stored value to its caller and
opened no callee body.

Read-only throughout. Nothing decompiled, nothing saved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The premise does not hold, and the reason is checkable at the instruction you named.

  The one store that provably targets the wizard page's own +0x2e0 is in the
  CWizardTST_CreateZones CONSTRUCTOR, and it stores ZERO:

      140709f25  33f6                XOR ESI,ESI
      140709f27  4889b7e0020000      MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x2e0],RSI

  The constructor takes only `this` (RCX -> RDI at 0x140709eed) and never receives a
  sheet, a wizard, or a document. So at construction +0x2e0 is NULL, and it is neither a
  CTestParamSheet nor a CWizardTST.

  The function is named by RTTI, not by the log string used in the previous section:
  the three vftables it stores resolve to `.?AVCWizardTST_CreateZones@@`. That also
  CONFIRMS the previous section's inference of the class from the log pair
  "OnWizardFinish" / "CWizardTST_CreateZones" at 0x140ec4530 / 0x140ec44d8.

  There are 36 qword stores to displacement 0x2e0 program-wide, in 34 functions. Section 2
  lists all of them with the producing instruction. The striking pattern: in 14 of them the
  stored value is ZERO. For the CWizardTST family specifically, +0x2e0 is a pointer member
  that constructors null out.

  What fills it before OnWizardFinish reads it is NOT ANSWERED here, and I want to be exact
  about why: it cannot be answered from the store list. A non-constructor method of
  CWizardTST_CreateZones stores no vftable, so it carries no class evidence, and the list
  tells me the address and the value but not the receiver's identity. Section 6.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Method, and the two ways the list could have been wrong
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  A disp32 of 0x2e0 must encode as the little-endian bytes E0 02 00 00, so a raw scan for
  `e0020000` is a complete superset of candidates. Over the whole image
  0x140000000-0x14120c647: 706 hits.

  Detector proven live first. Positive controls: `4d89ac24800a0000` returned exactly the
  one expected hit 0x14055a9f3, and `e83aade1ff` returned exactly 0x14070bc31 - both byte-
  verified in the previous section. Negative control `deadbeefcafe0002` returned zero.

  Instruction level: `search_instructions` for `+ 0x2e0]` over .text returned 651. A
  positive control in a narrow window returned exactly the one expected instruction,
  0x14070bbf5 `MOV RCX,qword ptr [R13 + 0x2e0]`.

  TRAP 1, caught: the two query forms DISAGREED, 651 versus 652. I did not average them or
  pick one. The extra hit in the looser form is

      1407706ec  488dac2420fdffff  LEA RBP,[RSP + -0x2e0]

  a NEGATIVE displacement, which the substring `0x2e0]` matches but which is not
  displacement 0x2e0. So 651 is the correct count and the loose query is the wrong tool
  for this displacement. Had I not run both, I would have carried an off-by-one into the
  file.

  TRAP 2, the same one as last time: of the 71 instructions with a memory operand in
  DESTINATION position at 0x2e0, only 36 are qword stores. The other 35 include 3 MOVSD
  and 1 MOVUPS and 1 MOVDQA writing 8/16 bytes of floating-point or vector data, 15 dword
  and 3 byte stores, 5 CMP, 2 INC, 4 CALL through `[RAX + 0x2e0]` and 1 JMP through
  `[RAX + 0x2e0]`. CALL and JMP read the slot to branch through it; they are not stores.
  Destination position alone is not a store test, and I verified the survivors in p-code
  rather than trusting my own rule (section 7).
