    branch into the middle of the function, which is the ordinary sense for this claim. There are
    no jump-into-the-middle targets here; all control flow is forward branches within the single
    entry at 0x1404fdfe0. I read all 114 instructions.
  * I did not follow the three callers of the splitter's virtual methods at vtable offsets 0x2e8
    and 0x2e0, which might have constrained R8's role as their trailing argument. That is past
    the pointer the question told me to stop at.
  * I did not open the writer of R8's own +0x8 field, which would name R8's class directly. Also
    past the stop boundary, and also not reachable, since R8 has no caller here.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * All 21 encodings quoted above were extracted from this payload by regex and each re-read with
    a fresh memory_read and compared byte for byte: 21/21 exact, 0 failures.
  * THE NEGATIVE IN SECTION 2 IS PROVEN LIVE. The R8-writer detector returns 8 hits for this
    function, all of them listed with addresses, and zero before 0x1404fdff8. A detector that
    finds nothing anywhere would be worthless; this one finds the eight later writes, so the
    earlier zero is a measurement rather than a broken pattern.
  * The premise that the other two stores write zero was checked, not accepted: I located the
    zeroing instruction before each store (1404fd5e1, 1406c3abd) and confirmed no intervening
    write to the register.
  * The claim in section 5 used a positive control in the same form as before: the COL range is
    0x140f00000-0x140f18000, the value found is 0x14077fca0, and the same range test finds real
    COLs at the vftables verified elsewhere in this investigation.
  * No error of my own in this section. The one premise failure I did find - the absent R8 writer -
    is in the question, not in my analysis, and it is reported in section 0 rather than papered
    over by quoting a later R8 write as though it were the one asked for.

===== END =====
===== CChild2 third argument =====

Question: what is passed as R8 into CChild2's virtual method at 0x1404fdfe0?
That method stores [R8 + 8] at [this + 0x1da0]. The only call through vtable displacement 0x350 is
the thunk at 0x140615d50, and that thunk's address is stored at 0x140e839a8. Find every
instruction that loads 0x140e839a8 or calls 0x140615d50. For each, quote the instruction that
produces R8 at the call. Name the class of that value, and the class of the pointer at [R8 + 8],
from a vtable or a log string. Say whether [R8 + 8] is a CDocCompose or a CProductionDoc. Stop
at R8.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  THERE ARE NO SUCH INSTRUCTIONS. THE SET IS EMPTY, SO THERE IS NO R8 PRODUCER TO QUOTE.

  Not one instruction in Vision3D.exe loads 0x140e839a8, and not one calls 0x140615d50. The
  thunk is a vftable entry that no code in this module invokes.

      instructions loading 0x140e839a8                       0
      instructions calling 0x140615d50                       0
      instructions dispatching through CFindComp + 0x220      0   (all four encodings scanned)
      rel32 references to the thunk's address                0
      recorded callers of the thunk                          0

  This is not a gap in my search. The premise itself points at a dead path, and I confirmed the
  reachability question from the other end too: the thunk is the ONLY thing in the program that
  dispatches through vtable displacement 0x350, so if the thunk is never called, then
  FUN_1404fdfe0 - which is the 0x350 entry of CChild2 - has no caller at all in this binary.

  And I can name nothing that the question asks to be named, because both subjects are empty:
  there is no "value" at a call to classify, since there is no call. Section 5 gives the two
  answers that ARE determined.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Both of the question's premises are correct
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  I checked both before acting on them, because the whole answer rests on them.

  PREMISE 1 - FUN_1404fdfe0 IS THE CChild2 VTABLE ENTRY AT DISPLACEMENT 0x350. Its 8-byte
  little-endian address occurs exactly once in .rdata/.data, at 0x140e45ae0. Taking
  0x140e45ae0 - 0x350 = 0x140e45790 as the vftable start, the qword at vftable[-1] = 0x140e45788
  is 0x140f027a0, a complete-object-locator. Validated:

      COL          0x140f027a0
      signature    1
      pSelfRVA     agrees with COL (COL == imagebase + pSelfRVA)
      vftOffset    0
      type name    .?AVCChild2@@

  and 0x140e45ae0 is confirmed to be that vftable's slot 0x350. The CChild2 vftable is loaded in
  exactly one place, its constructor:

      1404fd57f  488d050a829400    LEA RAX,[0x140e45790]
      1404fd586  488907              MOV qword ptr [RDI],RAX

  with the LEA target re-derived from its disp32.

  PREMISE 2 - THE THUNK AT 0x140615d50 IS THE ONLY +0x350 DISPATCH, AND ITS ADDRESS IS AT
  0x140e839a8. The thunk is five instructions and moves nothing:

      140615d50  4883ec28        SUB RSP,0x28
      140615d54  488b01            MOV RAX,qword ptr [RCX]
      140615d57  ff9050030000      CALL qword ptr [RAX + 0x350]
      140615d5d  33c0              XOR EAX,EAX
      140615d5f  4883c428        ADD RSP,0x28
      140615d63  c3                RET

  It takes RCX, reads the receiver's vtable, dispatches 0x350, and returns 0. It does not touch
  R8, so R8 arrives at FUN_1404fdfe0 exactly as it arrived at the thunk - from the thunk's
  caller, which is the thing the question asks me to find.

  The qword at 0x140e839a8 is 0x140615d50, confirmed by a fresh read.

  AND THE THRESHOLD DETECTOR IS PROVEN LIVE. I searched every instruction in the program for
  text containing "0x350"; 186 instructions mention it, and exactly ONE is a call or jump
  through a +0x350 displacement, at 0x140615d57. As an independent confirmation, the byte pattern
  ff9050030000, which encodes precisely `CALL [RAX+0x350]`, occurs exactly once in the whole
  image, at 0x140615d57. The same detector returns zero for every other form, so the "only one"
  in the question is a measurement.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The search for instructions loading 0x140e839a8 or calling 0x140615d50
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  SEARCH A - rendered instruction text, program-wide, start 0x140001000 to 0x140d50a00.

      query "0x140e839a8"     0 hits
      query "0x140615d50"     0 hits
      query "0x140e45790"     1 hit   (positive control - the CChild2 vtable LEA at 0x140fd57f)
      query "0x140e83788"     1 hit   (positive control - the CFindComp vtable LEA at 0x140615978)

  The last two are positive controls in the SAME query form as the two failing ones. The search
  form finds vtable addresses when they are present, so the two zeros are absences, not a broken
  pattern.

  SEARCH B - raw bytes, for the low 32 bits of 0x140615d50, to catch any rel32 displacement
  that points at the thunk. A rel32 call encodes the DIFFERENCE between the target and the next
  instruction, not the target's low bits, so this cannot find a call - but it can find any
  embedded absolute pointer:

      bytes 50 5d 61 40 across .text  0 hits

  SEARCH C - the thunk's actual vftable offset. 0x140e839a8 is the CFindComp vftable
  (0x140e83788) plus 0x220, NOT plus 0x350. A caller would therefore dispatch [reg + 0x220] on
  a CFindComp. I scanned all four encodings of an indirect call or jump through a +0x220
  displacement, with and without the REX.B prefix that selects R8-R15:

      ff 90 20 02 00 00        CALL [reg + 0x220]      0 hits
      41 ff 90 20 02 00 00     CALL [r8-r15 + 0x220]   0 hits
      ff a0 20 02 00 00        JMP  [reg + 0x220]      0 hits
      41 ff a0 20 02 00 00     JMP  [r8-r15 + 0x220]   0 hits

  SEARCH D - the reference database. function_callers for 0x140615d50 returns zero callers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. What that means, stated carefully
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Combining the two directions:

    * Going forward: the ONLY code in the binary that dispatches vtable displacement 0x350 is the
      thunk at 0x140615d57, and the only class whose 0x350 slot is FUN_1404fdfe0 is CChild2.
      So the thunk is the sole possible invoker of FUN_1404fdfe0.

    * Going backward: the thunk has no caller of any kind - no direct call, no IAT or vftable-
      mediated call, no [reg+0x220] dispatch, no recorded reference.

  Both cannot lead anywhere unless one of them is wrong, so the conclusion is that
  FUN_1404fdfe0 IS NOT CALLED FROM WITHIN Vision3D.exe, and the thunk that would call it is dead
  code in this image.

  I want to be exact about the limit of that claim, because it is the kind of statement that
  invites overreach. What I have shown is that no STATIC code path in this binary reaches the
  thunk. I have NOT shown the thunk is unreachable at run time. It has a vftable entry in a real
  class (CFindComp, at offset 0x220), and a vftable entry with no static caller is the signature
  of exactly two things: a method invoked only through a path this analysis cannot see, or dead
  code. Both are live possibilities. I am not choosing between them, and nothing in this section
  licenses the phrase "unreachable".

  Concretely, the R8 that would reach FUN_1404fdfe0 is supplied by the thunk's caller, which
  does not exist in this image. So the value is not merely unclassified - it is not determined
  by anything here.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The two classes the question asks for, and why I cannot supply them
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  THE CLASS OF "THAT VALUE" - NOT SUPPLIED, because there is no call site. The question says
  "for each [instruction], quote the instruction that produces R8 at the call". There are zero
  such instructions, so there is nothing to quote and no value to classify. I could have quoted
  the R8 producers inside FUN_1404fdfe0 itself, but those are scratch register values for that
  function's own callees, not the R8 the function receives, and presenting them would be
  answering a different question.

  THE CLASS OF THE POINTER AT [R8 + 8] - ALSO NOT SUPPLIED from this function, for a different
  reason. Inside FUN_1404fdfe0 the value at [R8 + 8] is loaded at 0x1404fdff8 and stored at
  0x1404fe003; it is never dereferenced, so no vtable is read through it and no string names it:

      1404fdff8  498b4008          MOV RAX,qword ptr [R8 + 0x8]
      1404fe003  488981a01d0000    MOV qword ptr [RCX + 0x1da0],RAX

  So this function cannot name it either. The value must be classified from where it is
  CONSUMED, not from where it is produced - and this is exactly the point at which the dead-code
  finding blocks the question. The consumer is FUN_1404fe610, which reads the +0x1da0 field,
  and classifying that required the chain to be live enough to reason about. It does not need to
  be called to be read, though, and the previous section classified it there by offset
  arithmetic that does not depend on any call site existing:

      value + 0xef8   = the 0x330-stride container
      value + 0xf00   = the buffer PV_EnvoiMacros reads
      both close exactly from one base, so  value = CDataCaoTraitement

  So the honest answer to the last question, reached by a route that does not require the dead
  path, is: [R8 + 8] IS A CDataCaoTraitement. It is NOT a CDocCompose and NOT a CProductionDoc.
  I flag clearly that this is INHERITED from the previous section's arithmetic about the +0x1da0
  field, and is not derived from anything in this function or from the thunk.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. A correction to a conclusion I gave in the previous section
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  In the section "Stored pointer at 0x1da0" I wrote that FUN_1404fdfe0's address in .rdata was
  "NOT a vtable entry", because the qword at 0x140e45ad8 was 0x14077fca0 - a code address, not
  a COL.

  THAT WAS WRONG, and this question is what exposed it. The reason is that I assumed a vftable
  entry is immediately preceded by its COL. That holds only for the FIRST entry, at vftable[0],
  where vftable[-1] is the COL. An entry at displacement 0x350 is preceded by 0x350 bytes of
  other function pointers - which for a derived class includes the derived vftable's own
  COL-adjacent region and whatever the linker placed there. The 0x14077fca0 I read was simply the
  previous function pointer in the table, and my "not a vtable entry" verdict came from testing
  the wrong offset.

  Running the test correctly - deriving the vftable start from the KNOWN displacement
  (0x140e45ae0 - 0x350) and reading vftable[-1] at 0x140e45788 - gives a valid COL
  (0x140f027a0, sig=1, pSelf self-consistent, vftOffset=0) and the name .?AVCChild2@@. The entry
  is a vftable entry. The question's premise is right and my previous section's was wrong.

  The same reasoning applies to the OTHER false lead I reported two sections ago, 0x1404fe610 at
  0x140e45fa8, which I dismissed for the same faulty reason. I have not re-examined that one here
  and am not claiming anything about it now; it may well be a vftable entry as well, and it
  should be re-checked with the start-derived-from-displacement method rather than the
  look-one-slot-back method. I am recording the methodological error so it is not repeated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * THE CENTRAL CLAIM IS A NEGATIVE ABOUT STATIC REACHABILITY. "No instruction in this binary
    calls the thunk" is well supported by five independent searches, three of them with positive
    controls. It is not a proof that the thunk is never executed. A vftable entry can be reached
    at run time through a computed call target, a callback into a table, or code in another
    module. I have not excluded those, and I do not use the word "unreachable".
  * The four search forms in section 2 are exhaustive for the mechanisms they cover, but they do
    not cover a call through a register loaded from a table whose contents I did not walk, or a
    call through a vftable slot reached by index arithmetic rather than a fixed displacement. A
    `CALL [reg + rcx*8]` form would not match any pattern I scanned. I did not look for computed
    vftable indexing.
  * [R8 + 8] is a CDataCaoTraitement INHERITED from offset arithmetic on a different field,
    computed in a previous section and re-derived here only as a consistency check. It is not
    read from a type descriptor, and no vtable in this function or the thunk is walked to name
    it.
  * The R8 value itself is genuinely undetermined. I have no call site, and the thunk forwards
    R8 untouched, so nothing in this image sets it.
  * I named CChild2 and CFindComp from validated COLs, not from the decompiler. The CChild2
    conclusion is solid; CFindComp was validated the same way (COL 0x140f0e1b0, sig=1,
    pSelf self-consistent) but plays no role in the answer beyond locating the thunk's slot.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  * All 10 encodings quoted above were extracted from this payload by regex and each re-read
    with a fresh memory_read and compared byte for byte: 10/10 exact, 0 failures.
  * The LEA target at 0x1404fd57f was re-derived from its disp32 and equals the claimed
    CChild2 vftable 0x140e45790.
  * The thunk's 8-byte address at 0x140e839a8 was read fresh and equals 0x140615d50.
  * BOTH COLs were validated with signature, pSelf self-consistency, and vftOffset, and both
    class names were decoded from the type descriptor's name field rather than from a search
    hit.
  * EVERY NEGATIVE IN SECTION 2 HAS A POSITIVE CONTROL IN THE SAME SEARCH FORM: the vtable
    address queries returned their one real hit, and the byte pattern for CALL [RAX+0x350]
    returned exactly the one real site. The searches for 0x140e839a8, 0x140615d50 and +0x220
    returned zero using forms proven to find things.
  * ONE ERROR OF MY OWN, CORRECTED, AND IT IS A SUBSTANTIVE ONE: the previous section's claim
    that FUN_1404fdfe0 is not a vftable entry. Section 5 explains the mistake - I read
    vftable[-1] relative to the ENTRY rather than deriving the vftable start from the known
    displacement - and gives the corrected result, .?AVCChild2@@ at slot 0x350. Recording it
    because the previous section's text now states something false, and a trace file that
    silently leaves a wrong claim in place is worse than one that carries its own correction.

===== END =====
===== Panel load and the container =====

Question: does the panel-load path call the 0x330-stride container filler?
Nothing in Vision3D.exe calls CFindComp slot 0x220, the thunk at 0x140615d50. That thunk is the
only call through displacement 0x350, so CChild2's method at 0x1404fdfe0 has no static caller.
The filler is FUN_140580b70. Search only ReloadDoc (FUN_140692af0), PrepareExecData
(FUN_14068f0f0), and PV_EnvoiMacros (FUN_140533c90). List every call from those three bodies to
0x140580b70, 0x14057eda0, 0x1404fdfe0, or 0x140615d50. If there are none, say so and stop.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  NO. NONE OF THE THREE FUNCTIONS CALLS ANY OF THE FOUR TARGETS. THERE ARE NO CALLS TO LIST.

      function                      body range              instrs   call+jmp   hits for the 4 targets
      ----------------------------  ----------------------  -------  ---------  ---------------------
      ReloadDoc     FUN_140692af0   0x140692af0..0x140694180   1143        239   0
      PrepareExecData FUN_14068f0f0 0x14068f0f0..0x14068f884    417         74   0
      PV_EnvoiMacros FUN_140533c90  0x140533c90..0x1405343ab    393         58   0

  371 call and jump instructions examined across the three bodies. Zero match any of
  0x140580b70, 0x14057eda0, 0x1404fdfe0, 0x140615d50 - directly or through any vtable
  displacement. The negative is proven live with positive controls (section 3), so this is a
  measurement and not a failed search.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Scope as given, and the functions actually examined
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  I searched exactly the three bodies named, and nothing else. All three resolved to the names
  the question gave:

      FUN_140692af0   0x140692af0..0x140694180    (named ReloadDoc by the question)
      FUN_14068f0f0   0x14068f0f0..0x14068f884    (named PrepareExecData by the question)
      FUN_140533c90   0x140533c90..0x1405343ab    PV_EnvoiMacros - carries a real symbol

  Each body was taken from its own start to its own end, so no caller or callee of these three
  is included, and no part of any of them is skipped.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The four targets, and how each could in principle be reached
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  A call to a fixed address can only arrive two ways, and I checked both for all four targets.

    target          direct E8 rel32 call    reachable via a vtable slot?
    --------------  ---------------------  --------------------------------------------
    0x140580b70     yes                    NO  - 0 vftable slots anywhere in .rdata/.data
    0x14057eda0     yes                    NO  - 0 vftable slots
    0x1404fdfe0     yes                    YES - exactly 1 slot, CChild2 + 0x350 (0x140e45ae0)
    0x140615d50     yes                    YES - exactly 1 slot, CFindComp + 0x220 (0x140e839a8)

  The first two are NOT virtual - no vftable in the entire image contains either address. For
  those two a direct-call search is therefore complete, and it found nothing.

  The second two are virtual, so a `CALL [reg + disp]` could in principle land on them. Both
  slots have a fixed displacement:

      CChild2 + 0x350  and  CFindComp + 0x220

  So I scanned all three bodies for any instruction with those displacements. None exists:

      function           indirect calls   disp 0x350   disp 0x220
      -----------------  ---------------  ----------  ----------
      ReloadDoc                    121            0            0
      PrepareExecData               31            0            0
      PV_EnvoiMacros                27            0            0
      -------------------------  ------          ----          ----
      total                       179            0            0

  179 indirect calls in the three bodies, none at either of the two relevant displacements. So
  the indirect route is closed for these targets as well. The search is complete for all four.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The negative is proven live
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  A search that returns nothing is worthless unless the same detector is shown to find things.
  I ran the identical detector - scan a body for CALL or JMP whose text contains one of the four
  addresses - over three functions KNOWN to contain such calls, established in earlier sections
  of this file:

      FUN_14057c390   ->  14057c410  CALL 0x14057eda0
      FUN_14057eda0   ->  14057edc9  CALL 0x140580b70
      FUN_1405809a0   ->  1405809ca  CALL 0x140580b70

  All three fired, each on the exact call site previously established. The detector therefore
  locates these targets when they are present, and returned zero across the three bodies the
  question named. I also re-read those three call sites from memory and re-derived their targets
  from the rel32 rather than trusting the text:

      14057c410  e88b290000  -> 0x14057eda0   OK
      14057edc9  e8a21d0000  -> 0x140580b70   OK
      1405809ca  e8a1010000  -> 0x140580b70   OK

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. What the three functions do call, so the negative is not empty
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  An empty list is only useful if it is a specific empty rather than a shrug, so here is what
  these three bodies DO call in the surrounding address range 0x140500000-0x140700000 - the

  ReloadDoc, 33 direct calls in range, including:
      0x140527b50  0x14053fc60  0x140541050  0x14058b410  0x1405b3f70  0x1405b4180

      0x140694860  0x1406975e0  0x1406b3030  0x1406b3e20

  PrepareExecData, 16 direct calls in range:
      0x14052e070  0x14052e910  0x14052f610  0x1405315a0  0x1405347b0  0x14053bd60

  Two of these are worth noting because they tie this function set to the rest of the

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. What this means for the container question
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The panel-load path does not call the filler. Combined with the previous section, the picture
  of the container's producer is now:

    * FUN_140580b70, the filler, has exactly two direct callers in the whole binary:
      0x14057edc9 in FUN_14057eda0, and 0x1405809ca in FUN_1405809a0. Both were established by
      instruction-level work in the "Stride 0x330 container" section, and both were confirmed
      again as positive controls for this search.
    * FUN_14057eda0 has exactly one caller, at 0x14057c410 in FUN_14057c390 - the macro editor
      dialog's OK handler.
    * FUN_14057c390 is a dialog handler reached through CExtResizableDialog's OnOK path.
    * CChild2's FUN_1404fdfe0, the other writer of the +0x1da0 field, has no static caller.

  So the container is populated on a dialog-interaction path, not on the document panel-load
  path, and one of its two candidate writers is dead in this image. This is consistent with
  everything else the trace has found about the +0xf00 field, and it does not by itself explain
  who owns the object PV_EnvoiMacros reads - the reading side and the writing side are simply
  connected by nothing that this binary expresses.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I searched DIRECT calls from the three bodies, which is exactly what was asked. I did NOT
    search transitively. One of these three functions could call a fourth function that calls the
    filler, and that would not appear in this result. A transitive search is a different
    question and I did not run it.
  * "No vftable slot" for 0x140580b70 and 0x14057eda0 was established by searching .rdata and
    .data for their 8-byte little-endian address encodings. I did not search the relocation or
    resource sections, on the reasoning that neither holds code pointers. That reasoning is
    sound but I did not verify it by measurement.
  * The virtual-target check covers FIXED displacements 0x350 and 0x220. A call through a
    vftable slot reached by index arithmetic - `CALL [reg + rcx*8]` - would not match, and I did
    not look for that form. If such a form existed in these three bodies it would be a
    theoretically open route to CChild2's 0x350 method, though not to CFindComp's 0x220 without
    the right index.
  * I did not open the 33, 16 and 4 listed callees to see what they in turn call. The list in
    section 4 is what these three bodies call, not a full call graph.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * THE CENTRAL NEGATIVE IS PROVEN LIVE IN TWO INDEPENDENT WAYS. First, the target-matching
    detector was run over three known-answer functions and fired on all three, at the exact call
    sites established in earlier sections. Second, the three control call sites were re-read
    from memory and their targets re-derived from the rel32, all matching.
  * The "0 vftable slots" claims for 0x140580b70 and 0x14057eda0 come from a byte search using
    an 8-byte encoder that was self-tested against 0x1404fdfe0, a value verified byte-exact in
    an earlier section. The same search returns 1 hit for each of the two targets that DO have
    slots, at the addresses already established, so the zero is a measurement.
  * The per-function instruction and call/jmp counts in section 0 come from the same
    disassemble-function listings the target scan used, so the totals and the hits describe the
    same pass over the same bytes.
  * The answer to this question is a negative, so this section quotes only three instruction
    encodings, all of them positive controls rather than findings. Those three were extracted from
    this payload and re-read from memory: 3/3 byte-exact. No `ADDR  BYTES` line appears in a
    finding anywhere in this section, because there is no finding to quote - which is the result,
    not an omission.
  * No error of my own in this section.

===== END =====

3. The negative is proven live
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The filler has exactly two callers in the whole binary, both established in earlier sections of
  this file. I ran the identical detector - scan a body for a CALL whose text contains
  0x140580b70 - over those two known-answer functions:

      FUN_14057eda0  (47 instrs)  ->  14057edc9  e8a21d0000  CALL 0x140580b70
      FUN_1405809a0  (23 instrs)  ->  1405809ca  e8a1010000  CALL 0x140580b70

  Both fired, each on the exact call site previously established and byte-verified. The same
  detector returned zero across all 77 callee bodies. So the detector locates the filler when it
  is present, and the 77 zeros are a measurement.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. What this settles, and the shape of the answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Reading the three sections together, the container filler is now bracketed from both sides.

    PRODUCERS of the +0xf00 container:
      FUN_140580b70, the filler - exactly two callers program-wide, both in the
        macro-editor dialog path: FUN_14057eda0 at 0x14057edc9 and FUN_1405809a0 at
        0x1405809ca. FUN_14057eda0 has one caller, FUN_14057c390, a CExtResizableDialog
        OK handler.
      FUN_1404fdfe0, the other writer of the +0x1da0 field that leads to the same container -
        no static caller at all; its only dispatch is a thunk that nothing in this image calls.

    CONSUMERS, and this question:
      ReloadDoc, PrepareExecData and PV_EnvoiMacros - none calls the filler, and none of
        their 77 direct callees calls it either.

  So the panel-load path reaches the container region only through the zone-0 chain. ReloadDoc
  calls PrepareExecData at 0x1406930f7, and PrepareExecData calls 0x14052e910, 0x14052f610 and
  0x14053bd60 - MajTestVectorForSkip, NbTest_NeedAnomalie and PrepareVecteur. Those are the
  functions that compute the zone-0 count, not the ones that build the container. The container is
  built on a dialog-interaction path instead.

  That is a genuine asymmetry worth stating plainly: the side of the +0xf00 field that READS it
  is on the panel-load path, and the side that WRITES it is not. Nothing in this binary
  connects them, and this question is the second independent confirmation of that gap - the
  first being that the +0x1da0 writer CChild2's method has no static caller.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I stopped at one level, as instructed. None of the 77 callees' own callees was examined, so
    a path of depth two or more from the panel-load functions to the filler is NOT excluded.
    Depth two is a real possibility and I have not ruled it out.
  * "Direct call target" means the E8 rel32 form only. The three bodies also contain 111, 25 and
    25 CALLs through an IAT slot, and 10, 6 and 2 further indirect calls through a register or
    memory operand. None of those was followed, so an indirect call to a virtual method that in
    turn calls the filler would not appear here.
  * "A CALL whose text contains 0x140580b70" is a textual test. It would match a call to a
    DIFFERENT function whose address merely contains that digit sequence, though no such
    function exists. It would not match a call that reaches the filler by a different spelling,
    such as a call through a vtable slot. FUN_140580b70 is not virtual - established in the
    previous section, zero vftable slots program-wide - so a vtable-mediated call to it cannot
    exist, and the textual test is complete for this target.
  * I did not check whether any of the 77 callees has an indirect call through a vtable slot
    that resolves to the filler. The previous section's finding that the filler is in no vftable
    makes that empty, but I relied on that finding rather than re-measuring it here.
  * The bodies were read through a listing with a 6000-instruction cap. I verified that no body
    reached the cap, so the cap is not hiding a truncated search.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * THE CENTRAL NEGATIVE HAS A POSITIVE CONTROL IN THE SAME FORM. The detector found the filler
    call in both known-answer functions, at the exact addresses established in earlier sections,
    and the call bytes re-read from memory.
  * All 77 direct targets resolved to a function; the count of unresolvable targets is zero, so
    the "77 scanned" figure in section 2 is a measured fact and not an assumption.
  * The instruction and CALL totals in section 2 are accumulated from the same listings the
    target scan used, so the totals and the zero describe one pass over one set of bytes.
  * No truncation: the largest body scanned is reported implicitly by the fact that zero bodies
    reached the listing limit.
  * This section's answer is a negative, so the only instruction encodings it quotes are the two
    positive controls. Both were re-read from memory: 2/2 byte-exact. No `ADDR  BYTES` line
    appears in any finding, because there is no finding to quote - that absence is the result.
  * TWO ERRORS OF MY OWN IN THIS SECTION, both corrected before the result was written.
    First, my first attempt to classify call forms tested `bytes[0] === "e8"`, but indexing a
    string yields ONE character, so it never matched and it reported zero direct calls from a
    function that plainly has 57. I switched to parsing the rendered operand and re-collected
    the sets. Second, the first collection pass printed a large "other" list because of that same
    bug. Reporting the first because a detector that reports zero on a body full of calls is the
    exact failure mode this investigation has been guarding against, and it happened again.

===== Dialog slot 0x310 =====

Question: does the panel-load path call CMacroEditorDlg's slot 0x310?
FUN_14057c390 is that slot, at 0x140e60f80. It is the only function outside the filler's own
cluster that calls FUN_14057eda0, and it has no direct caller. Search ReloadDoc, PrepareExecData,
PV_EnvoiMacros, and their 77 direct callees for a call or jump through displacement 0x310. List

0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  NO. THERE IS NO CALL OR JUMP THROUGH DISPLACEMENT 0x310 IN ANY OF THE 79 SEARCHED FUNCTIONS.
  THERE IS NO INSTRUCTION AND NO FUNCTION TO LIST.

      ReloadDoc      FUN_140692af0         0 instructions through 0x310
      PrepareExecData FUN_14068f0f0        0

      79 distinct function bodies, 6891 instructions examined,
      702 indirect calls seen, 0 hits, 0 bodies truncated

  And this zero is stronger than the other negatives in this investigation, because I can say

      14073dfd1  48ffa010030000  JMP qword ptr [RAX + 0x310]   in FUN_14073dd50
      140754d2c  ff9010030000    CALL qword ptr [RAX + 0x310] in FUN_1407549e0

1. The premise, verified
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  FUN_14057c390 IS THE CMacroEditorDlg VTABLE ENTRY AT DISPLACEMENT 0x310, at 0x140e60f80.

  The qword at 0x140e60f80 is 0x14057c390, read fresh. Deriving the vftable start from the known
  displacement gives 0x140e60f80 - 0x310 = 0x140e60c70, and the qword at vftable[-1] = 0x140e60c68
  is a complete-object-locator, validated:

      COL          0x140f078b0
      signature    1
      pSelfRVA     agrees with COL
      vftOffset    0
      type name    .?AVCMacroEditorDlg@@

  So the class is CMacroEditorDlg and the slot is 0x310, as the question states. I checked this
  before searching because the previous section established that testing vftable[-1] at the wrong
  offset produces a confident false negative.

      distinct function bodies searched                              79

  Every one of the 77 targets resolved to a real function body, so nothing was skipped for want
  of one. Each body was read from its own start to its own end.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The result, and how the negative was proven
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  SEARCH: within each of the 79 bodies, every instruction whose text matches a +0x310
  displacement, restricted to CALL and JMP.

      functions searched                         79
      total instructions read                 6891
      indirect CALL/JMP instructions seen       702
      bodies reaching the 6000-instruction cap    0
      matches for +0x310                         0

  PROOF THAT THE PATTERN IS REAL. A detector that finds nothing is worthless unless the same
  pattern is shown to exist elsewhere. I ran the identical +0x310 test over the whole program:

      instructions whose text mentions 0x310                    387
      of those, a CALL or JMP through a +0x310 displacement         2

      14073dfd1  48ffa010030000  JMP  qword ptr [RAX + 0x310]
      140754d2c  ff9010030000    CALL qword ptr [RAX + 0x310]

  Both encodings re-read from memory and byte-exact. So the +0x310 dispatch form exists, the
  detector recognises it, and it finds exactly two of them - in FUN_14073dd50 and
  FUN_1407549e0.

  AND NEITHER IS IN THE SEARCH SET. I resolved each site's enclosing function and tested it
  against the 79:

      14073dfd1  ->  FUN_14073dd50   0x14073dd50   in the 79 bodies?  NO
      140754d2c  ->  FUN_1407549e0   0x1407549e0   in the 79 bodies?  NO

  This closes the loop in both directions. The search set contains zero of the two known
  instances, which is exactly what the zero result predicts, and there is no third instance
  hiding anywhere in the image that I failed to see.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. What this means

  Combined with the two previous sections, the picture of the CMacroEditorDlg side is:

    * FUN_14057c390, the 0x310 entry of CMacroEditorDlg, is the sole gateway to
      FUN_14057eda0, and from there to the container filler FUN_140580b70.
    * It has no direct caller - established in the "Container at 0xd78" section and unchanged.
    * Its vtable slot has exactly two dispatch sites in the entire binary, at 0x14073dfd1 and
      0x140754d2c, and both belong to functions that neither the panel-load functions nor any of
      their 76 distinct direct callees reach.
    * The panel-load path therefore reaches the container filler neither directly, one level
      down, nor two levels down through a 0x310 dispatch.

  The asymmetry noted in the previous section is now confirmed by a third independent route. The
  reader of the +0xf00 container is on the panel-load path; the writer is on a dialog path whose
  only entry point is not called from anywhere in the searched region.

  I want to be careful not to overstate this. FUN_14073dd50 and FUN_1407549e0 are real functions
  that DO dispatch through 0x310, so the dialog path is not dead - it has callers, it just is not
  the panel-load path. What this section establishes is a negative about a defined region, and
  nothing about how the dialog is actually reached at run time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I searched the three bodies and their 76 distinct direct callee BODIES, which is what was
    asked. I did not go deeper. A path of depth two or more from the panel-load functions to a
    0x310 dispatch is not excluded - except that any such path must still land in
    FUN_14073dd50 or FUN_1407549e0, since those hold the only two 0x310 dispatches in the image,
    and neither is a depth-one callee.
  * The search covers FIXED displacement 0x310 only. A call through a vtable slot reached by
    index arithmetic - `CALL [reg + rcx*8]` - would not match, and I did not look for that form.
    This is the same gap I recorded in the previous two sections, and it is still open.
  * "Indirect CALL/JMP through a +0x310 displacement" was matched textually, against the
    rendered operand. A call reaching that slot by a different spelling would not match.
  * The 702 indirect calls counted in the search set are calls through a register or memory
    operand generally, not specifically through 0x310. They are counted so the reader can see the
    volume that was examined; I did not resolve any of them to a target.
  * I did not open FUN_14073dd50 or FUN_1407549e0 to ask what THEY are and who calls them. That
    is the natural next question, and it is outside both the scope given and the stop condition
    stated here.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * The two encodings quoted in this section were extracted from this payload and each re-read
    with a fresh memory_read: 2/2 byte-exact. No other instruction encoding is quoted, because
    the answer is a negative and the only instructions cited are the two that demonstrate the
    pattern is real.
  * THE ZERO IS PROVEN LIVE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. The +0x310 dispatch form was shown to exist
    twice program-wide, and both instances were shown to lie outside the search set. A negative
    backed by a known population of two, both accounted for, is stronger than one backed only by
    positive controls.
  * The premise was validated with a COL check - signature, pSelf self-consistency, and vftOffset
    - and the class name decoded from the type descriptor, not taken from a search hit.
  * The 77 direct call targets were collected by parsing the rendered operand. My first attempt
    at this classification, in the previous section, tested `bytes[0] === "e8"`, which can never
    match because string indexing yields one character; I did not repeat that mistake, and the
    77 figure is consistent with the 77 figure that section reported after its correction.
  * No truncation: zero bodies reached the listing limit.
  * No error of my own in this section.

===== END =====
===== Slot 0x310 receiver =====

Question: whose vftable is dispatched at the only two +0x310 sites?
FUN_14073dd50 and FUN_1407549e0 each do MOV RBX, RCX and then call or jump through [RBX + 0x310].
FUN_14073dd50 is the WM_COMMAND handler for control id 0x7EB at 0x140ed0930. FUN_1407549e0 is
the WM_COMMAND handler for control id 0xB43 at 0x140edad30. Name the class that owns each
message map, and read the qword at that class's primary vftable + 0x310. If that qword is
FUN_14057c390, say so. If it is another function, name the function and stop.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  NEITHER. THE QWORD AT PRIMARY VFTABLE + 0x310 IS NOT FUN_14057c390. IN BOTH CLASSES IT IS
  0x14076a88a, WHICH IS THE IMPORT THUNK FOR PROFUISM.DLL::CExtResizableDialog::OnOK.

      message map   entries array          class                 primary vftable   + 0x310 holds
      ------------  ---------------------  --------------------  ---------------  ------------------------
      0x140ed0910   0x140ed0910            CZoneJokerDlg         0x140ed0350       0x14076a88a
      0x140edac50   0x140edac50            CTCRExportFormView    0x140eda688       0x14076a88a

  0x14076a88a IS CExtResizableDialog::OnOK. It is a 6-byte thunk, ff2518f35e00, a
  `JMP qword ptr [0x140d59ba8]` into the PROFUISM.DLL import slot for that method.

  Per the question's instruction, naming the function and stopping.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The two message-map entries, verified
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Both entries decode as MFC AFX_MSGMAP_ENTRY records. The x64 record is 0x20 bytes with the
  function pointer at offset +0x18; the dword at +0x10 is the entry's _afxSig field, which is
  0x3a in both. My first read of the pfn used offset +0x10 and returned 0x3a, which is that sig
  field, not a pointer - the layout, not the data, was wrong on that pass.

      0x140ed0930   nMessage 0x111  nCode 0x0  nID 0x7eb  nLastID 0x7eb  sig 0x3a  pfn 0x14073dd50
      0x140edad30   nMessage 0x111  nCode 0x0  nID 0xb43  nLastID 0xb43  sig 0x3a  pfn 0x1407549e0

  0x111 is WM_COMMAND and the control ids are 0x7eb and 0xb43, matching the question. Both pfns
  match the functions named. So both premises hold.

  Both dispatch sites re-read and byte-exact:

      14073dfd1  48ffa010030000  JMP  qword ptr [RAX + 0x310]   in FUN_14073dd50
      140754d2c  ff9010030000    CALL qword ptr [RAX + 0x310]   in FUN_1407549e0

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Naming the classes that own the message maps
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Each class's message map is reached through MFC's GetThisMessageMap, which is a STATIC
  member function, not a virtual - which is why neither is in any vftable, and why searching
  .rdata for a pointer to them returns nothing. I followed the message map to its owner:

      message map 1:  AFX_MSGMAP at 0x1410c6058, pfnGetBaseMap = 0, pEntries = 0x140ed0910
                      GetThisMessageMap = FUN_14073d6e0, which returns &0x1410c6058
      message map 2:  AFX_MSGMAP at 0x1410c62f8, pfnGetBaseMap = 0, pEntries = 0x140edac50
                      GetThisMessageMap = FUN_140754560, which returns &0x1410c62f8

  From there, to the vftable: the handlers are non-virtual in the message map, but each class
  still has vftables. Searching all validated vftables for ones containing a pointer into the
  two handler regions gave three per class - the class's own primary vtable plus the vftables of
  its base subobjects, at vftOffsets 304, 680 and 720. The handler addresses appear at different
  offsets in each, as they do with multiple inheritance.

  Reading the complete-object-locator for each of those six vftables gave the class name, and in
  each case the SAME most-derived class:

      vftable     COL          vftOffset  class
      ----------  -----------  ---------  --------------------
      0x140ed0350 0x140f18aa8     0      CZoneJokerDlg          <- PRIMARY
      0x140ed06f0 0x140f18b90   304      CZoneJokerDlg
      0x140ed0748 0x140f18bb8   680      CZoneJokerDlg
      0x140ed07e8 0x140f18be0   720      CZoneJokerDlg

      vftable     COL          vftOffset  class
      ----------  -----------  ---------  --------------------
      0x140eda688 0x140f1a178     0      CTCRExportFormView     <- PRIMARY
      0x140edaa28 0x140f1a3a0   304      CTCRExportFormView
      0x140edaa80 0x140f1a3c8   680      CTCRExportFormView
      0x140edab20 0x140f1a3f0   720      CTCRExportFormView

  Every COL was validated with signature 1 and pSelf self-consistency. The two PRIMARY vftables,
  the vftOffset-0 ones, are the ones the question asks about.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Reading the qword at primary vftable + 0x310
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

      CZoneJokerDlg       primary vftable 0x140ed0350 + 0x310 = 0x140ed0660
                          qword there = 0x14076a88a

      CTCRExportFormView  primary vftable 0x140eda688 + 0x310 = 0x140eda998
                          qword there = 0x14076a88a

  BOTH ARE 0x14076a88a. NEITHER IS FUN_14057c390.

  And 0x14076a88a is a named import thunk:

      14076a88a  ff2518f35e00  JMP qword ptr [0x140d59ba8]

  whose target, 0x140d59ba8, is the IAT slot for PROFUISM.DLL::CExtResizableDialog::OnOK. The
  symbol search returns three entries for that name - the external, a body at 0x1404f2300, and
  this thunk at 0x14076a88a.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. What this means for the +0x310 question

  This overturns the natural reading of the previous section, and it is worth being explicit
  about how.

  The previous section established that exactly two +0x310 dispatches exist program-wide, at
  0x14073dfd1 and 0x140754d2c, and that both lie outside the panel-load path's 79 functions. It
  noted that CMacroEditorDlg's vftable has FUN_14057c390 at +0x310, and left open whose vftable
  the two sites actually dispatch. That open question is now answered, and the answer is NOT
  CMacroEditorDlg.

  What the two sites dispatch is CExtResizableDialog::OnOK - a base-class virtual, inherited by
  both CZoneJokerDlg and CTCRExportFormView. So:

    * [this + 0x310] in these two handlers calls OnOK, the dialog's accept-button handler. It is
      ordinary MFC, not a call into the macro-editor dialog.
    * FUN_14057c390, the CMacroEditorDlg method that leads to the container filler, is at +0x310
      of CMacroEditorDlg's OWN vftable and of no other vftable in the binary. I checked all 947
      validated vftables: exactly one holds FUN_14057c390 at offset 0x310, and it is
      CMacroEditorDlg's, 0x140e60c70.
    * So the two +0x310 dispatch sites do NOT reach the container filler. They were never
      candidates for it.

  The dialog that owns the filler path is CMacroEditorDlg. These two handlers belong to
  CZoneJokerDlg and CTCRExportFormView, which are different classes whose +0x310 slot is a
  different, unrelated method.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I read each class's PRIMARY vftable, the vftOffset-0 one, as the question specified. The
    three base-subobject vftables per class also hold slot 0x310, but for those the value at
    +0x310 is past the meaningful end of the subobject vftable and reads adjacent data - 0xe,
    0xb4300000b43, 0x0, 0x100000000. Those are not function pointers and I have not treated
    them as answers.
  * The class name comes from the RTTI complete-object-locator reached from each vftable, which
    is a validated name, not a decompiler guess. As always in this binary, RTTI names the
    most-derived class; it does not by itself establish the inheritance chain, and I did not
    walk the bases.
  * The handler-to-class association rests on the handler function appearing as an entry in that
    class's vftables, which is stronger than proximity in .text but is not a call-graph proof.
    Both handlers were confirmed as the pfn of the stated WM_COMMAND entries, and both appear in
    all three vftables of their class, so the association is solid.
  * I did not open CExtResizableDialog::OnOK at 0x1404f2300. I am naming the function from its
    import thunk, which is the authoritative name for the call target. I am not claiming what
    OnOK does.
  * I did not follow either WM_COMMAND handler past the [this + 0x310] call to see what else
    they do. The question said to stop at the vftable read.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * All 3 encodings quoted were extracted from this payload and re-read from memory: 3/3
    byte-exact - the two +0x310 dispatches and the OnOK thunk.
  * Both primary vftable +0x310 slots were re-read from memory and confirmed to hold 0x14076a88a.
  * The thunk at 0x14076a88a was re-read (ff2518f35e00) and its RIP-relative target re-derived
    as 0x140d59ba8, matching the PROFUISM.DLL::CExtResizableDialog::OnOK IAT slot.
  * All eight COLs were validated with signature and pSelf self-consistency, and both class names
    were decoded from the type descriptor's name field.
  * The "exactly one vftable holds FUN_14057c390 at 0x310" claim comes from checking all 947
    validated vftables, and the enumeration was cross-checked: the count of vftables found by
    scanning .rdata for slots holding a validated COL pointer (947) equals the count of
    validated COLs, which is the consistency condition for that enumeration.
  * TWO ERRORS OF MY OWN, both corrected before the answer was written.
    First, I read the message-map pfn at offset +0x10 instead of +0x18 and got the _afxSig value
    0x3a; the corrected offset gives the real pointers. Second, while scanning the RTTI blob for
    primary COLs I read the type-descriptor RVA at block offset 0xC instead of o+0xC, which
    returned zero matches for both classes and looked like a real negative; fixing the index
    returned the primary COLs. The second is the more serious of the two, because it produced a
    plausible empty answer to the exact question being asked.

===== END =====
===== Command id 0xB2E9 =====

Question: does the panel-load path contain control id 0xB2E9?
FUN_1404fe610 is the only direct caller of the CMacroEditorDlg constructor, and it is CChild2's
WM_COMMAND handler for 0xB2E9. Search ReloadDoc, PrepareExecData, PV_EnvoiMacros, and their 77
direct callees for the immediate 0xB2E9. List every instruction and the function that contains
it. If there are none, say so and stop.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  NO. THERE IS NO INSTRUCTION CONTAINING THE IMMEDIATE 0xB2E9 IN ANY OF THE 79 SEARCHED BODIES.
  THERE IS NO INSTRUCTION AND NO FUNCTION TO LIST.

      panel-load function      direct targets   bodies searched   instrs   hits for 0xB2E9
      ----------------------  --------------  ---------------  -------  -----------------
      ReloadDoc     FUN_140692af0              57               57         -        0
      PrepareExecData FUN_14068f0f0            20               20         -        0
      PV_EnvoiMacros FUN_140533c90              6                6         -        0
      ----------------------  --------------  ---------------  -------  -----------------
      deduped union                             77               79      6891         0

  6891 instructions across 79 function bodies, and 1293 distinct hex operands extracted from
  them. None is 0xb2e9. The negative is proven live in two independent ways (section 3), and it
  is in fact stronger than the question requires - see section 2.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The premise, verified
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  FUN_1404fe610 IS CChild2'S WM_COMMAND HANDLER FOR CONTROL ID 0xB2E9. Its 8-byte address occurs
  exactly once in .rdata/.data, at 0x140e45fa8, and that address is the pfn field of a message-map
  entry at 0x140e45f90. Decoded as an MFC AFX_MSGMAP_ENTRY (0x20 bytes on x64, pfn at +0x18,
  _afxSig at +0x10):

      140e45f90  1101000000000000 e9b20000 e9b20000 3a000000 00000000 10e64f4001000000
                 nMessage=0x111 nCode=0x0   nID=0xb2e9 nLastID=0xb2e9 sig=0x3a pfn=0x1404fe610

  0x111 is WM_COMMAND and the control id is 0xb2e9 in both nID and nLastID, exactly as the
  question states. The pfn is 0x1404fe610. So the handler identification holds.

  I also checked the two related claims for completeness, and one of them needs a small note:

    * "the only direct caller of the CMacroEditorDlg constructor" - the constructor is FUN_14057bf30
      at vftable offset 0x310 of CMacroEditorDlg. In the section "Panel load and the container"
      I established that FUN_14057eda0's only caller is FUN_14057c390, and here that the
      constructor is called from FUN_1404fe610. I did not re-derive the full caller set of the
      constructor in this pass, so I report the handler identification as verified and the
      "only direct caller" claim as inherited rather than re-measured.
    * FUN_1404fe610 and the constructor FUN_14057bf30 are NEITHER in the 79-body search set, so
      the handler that owns this control id is not itself among the functions searched.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The search, and a stronger negative than was asked for
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  I extracted every 0x-hex operand from every instruction of all 79 bodies - not only immediates
  but displacements and constants too, so the search is strictly wider than the one requested.

      deduped direct call targets in the three panel-load bodies   77
      of those, resolved to a function body                        77   (0 unresolvable)
      distinct callee BODIES                                       76
      plus the three panel-load bodies                              3
      ------------------------------------------------------------
      distinct function bodies searched                            79
      instructions read                                          6891
      bodies reaching the 6000-instruction limit                    0
      distinct hex operands extracted                             1293
      of those equal to 0xb2e9                                      0

  A stronger observation, which the question did not ask for but which bears on it. I searched
  the WHOLE PROGRAM for the immediate 0xB2E9 first, and it does not occur anywhere:

      instructions whose rendered text contains "0xb2e9"        0

  I then checked that at the byte level, where 0xB2E9 as a little-endian dword is e9 b2 00 00.
  That pattern occurs 6 times in .text - and on inspection all 6 are coincidences, not the
  immediate:

      140016ae7  e9b2000000  JMP 0x140016b9e   in FUN_140016a70
      1404b2092  e9b2000000  JMP 0x1404b2149   in FUN_1404b1f00
      14064c4d0  e9b2000000  JMP 0x14064c587   in FUN_14064c0c0
      140729183  e9b2000000  JMP 0x14072923a   in FUN_140729030
      140735774  e9b2000000  JMP 0x14073582b   in ExecuteAll_Components
      14073e4e6  e9b2000000  JMP 0x14073e59d   in FUN_14073e1a0

  In every one, the e9 is the OPCODE of a JMP rel32 and the b2 00 00 is the high end of the
  displacement. None of these is a 0xB2E9 immediate, and none of the six functions is in the
  search set either.

  So the value 0xB2E9 exists in this program only as DATA - in the message-map entry at
  0x140e45f98 - and never as a code immediate. That is the expected shape for an MFC control id:
  the framework dispatches on the message map, so the handler never compares against the id. It
  also means the answer would be "no" for any set of functions asked about, not just these 79.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The negative is proven live
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Two independent controls, in the same forms as the searches that returned zero.

  CONTROL A - the query form finds immediates. A program-wide rendered-text search for 0x1548,
  a value known to appear as an immediate from an earlier section, returns 4 hits, and a
  byte-level search for its little-endian dword returns 5, at 0x1404dbbf4, 0x1404eceab,
  0x1405976ca, 0x1405ab43b and one more. So both search forms find 4-byte values when they are
  present.

  CONTROL B - within the search set specifically, immediates are extracted in bulk. Restricting
  to genuine MOV/CMP/ADD/SUB/AND/OR/XOR/TEST/IMUL with an immediate operand, the 79 bodies yield
  612 such instructions, for example:

      140692b0e  4881ecc0050000  SUB RSP,0x5c0
      140692b57  ba10000000      MOV EDX,0x10
      140692ce0  4869c810040000  IMUL RCX,RAX,0x410
      140692df7  41b900010000    MOV R9D,0x100

  612 immediates extracted from these bodies, zero of them 0xb2e9. The extraction is working
  and the value is absent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. What this means

  The panel-load path contains no reference to control id 0xB2E9, and neither does any other
  code in the binary. The CChild2 dialog that owns that command - the one whose WM_COMMAND
  handler FUN_1404fe610 is the only direct caller of the CMacroEditorDlg constructor - is not
  reachable from the panel-load path, and does not mention the id.

  This is consistent with everything the last three sections have established, and it closes one
  more possible route. The chain of writers for the +0xf00 container now reads:

    * CMacroEditorDlg's slot 0x310 is FUN_14057c390, and exactly one vftable in the binary holds
      it at that offset - CMacroEditorDlg's own.
    * The two +0x310 dispatch sites in the program belong to CZoneJokerDlg and
      CTCRExportFormView, and dispatch CExtResizableDialog::OnOK, not the macro editor.
    * CChild2's WM_COMMAND handler for 0xB2E9 calls the CMacroEditorDlg constructor, but that
      handler is not among the panel-load functions or their 76 direct callees, and the control
      id appears nowhere in code.

  So the dialog that creates the macro editor is opened by a CChild2 command handler that the
  panel-load path never reaches, and the panel-load path contains no trace of the id that would
  trigger it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I searched 4-byte immediates. A 64-bit or 32-bit-float form of the value, or the value
    written one half at a time, would not be caught by a dword scan. I also extracted every
    rendered hex operand across the 79 bodies, so any form Ghidra renders would have been seen -
    but an arithmetic construction of 0xb2e9 from parts would not render as that literal.
  * The program-wide observation in section 2 rests on the same two forms. It is a strong
    negative, not a proof: it does not exclude a value computed at run time.
  * I did not re-measure the caller set of the CMacroEditorDlg constructor, so the "only direct
    caller" half of the premise is carried forward from earlier sections rather than confirmed
    here. The handler identification in section 1 is confirmed here.
  * I did not open FUN_1404fe610 to characterise what it does beyond confirming its message-map
    identity, which is where the question's own claim comes from.
  * The six byte-level coincidences in section 2 are each individually resolved by decoding the
    instruction at that address, so they are explained rather than merely set aside.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * All 10 encodings quoted above - the 6 JMP coincidences and the 4 control immediates - were
    extracted from this payload by regex and each re-read from memory: 10/10 byte-exact, 0
    failures. The message-map entry at 0x140e45f90 was read as 32 raw bytes and shown above in
    full, and the pfn field at 0x140e45fa8 was re-read separately and matches 0x1404fe610.
  * The program-wide rendered-text search for "0xb2e9" returns 0, and the byte search for
    e9b20000 returns 6 whose instructions were each decoded and shown - so the six are accounted
    for, not merely counted.
  * The 79-body scan, the 6891 instruction total, the 1293 distinct operands and the 612
    immediates all come from the same listing passes, so the totals and the zero describe one
    pass over one set of bytes.
  * Both controls in section 3 use the same search forms as the searches that returned zero, and
    both return non-zero, so the zeros are measurements.
  * No truncation: zero bodies reached the 6000-instruction listing limit.
  * No error of my own in this section.

===== END =====
===== Tree at 0x2448 =====

Question: what adds nodes to the tree at document+0x2448?
FUN_14052b7c0 sums (node+0x30 - node+0x28) >> 3 over the tree whose header is at
document+0x2448, skipping nodes whose +0x20 is 0x100. That sum is part of the zone-0 resize
count. The node links are +0x00 left, +0x08 parent, +0x10 right, and the nil flag is the byte
at +0x19. List every instruction that writes a qword to displacement 0x2448 or 0x2450, and name
the function that contains each one. For each function that inserts a node into this tree, say
whether ReloadDoc (FUN_140692af0) calls it directly before its call to PrepareExecData at
0x1406930f7. If ReloadDoc calls none of them, say so and stop.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
0. Short answer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  THERE IS NO SUCH INSTRUCTION. NOTHING IN Vision3D.exe WRITES A QWORD TO DISPLACEMENT 0x2448 OR
  0x2450 - NOT EVEN A STORE OF ANY WIDTH. THE LIST IS EMPTY.

      displacement   mentions in code   qword stores   stores of any width   LEAs
      ------------  -----------------  -------------  -------------------  -----
      0x2448                 112              0                     0    34
      0x2450                  59              0                     0     0

  So the first half of the question has no answer to give: there is no instruction and no
  containing function to name.

  The reason is that the field is never addressed as a displacement. The address is computed
  ONCE into a register and then written through that register at displacements +0, +0x8, +0x10
  and so on. Section 2 shows the initialisation, which is the clearest single example.

  AND RELOADDOC CALLS NONE OF THE TREE-OPERATING FUNCTIONS, BEFORE OR AFTER ITS CALL TO
  PrepareExecData. Stating that and stopping, as the question instructs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The premise, verified
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  FUN_14052b7c0 DOES SUM (node+0x30 - node+0x28) >> 3 OVER THE TREE AT document+0x2448, WITH
  THE 0x100 SKIP. Decompiled, it matches the description point for point:

      puVar4 = *(undefined8 **)*param_1;              root = *param_1
      ...
      if ((param_2 == '?0') || ((param_2 == 1) && (puVar3[4] != 0x100)))
          lVar5 = lVar5 + ((longlong)(puVar3[6] - puVar3[5]) >> 3);
      ...
      while (*(char *)((longlong)puVar3 + 0x19) != '?0')     nil flag at +0x19
      puVar4 = (undefined8 *)puVar3[2];                       right link at +0x10
      ... *puVar4 ...                                         left  link at +0x00
      ... puVar3[1] ...                                       parent link at +0x08

  puVar3[4] is node+0x20, puVar3[5] is node+0x28, puVar3[6] is node+0x30. Every field in the
  question's description is present and correct.

  And param_1 really is &document+0x2448: PV_AffectIndResult forms it at 0x14053165b
  (LEA R14,[RDI + 0x2448]) and passes it to 0x14052b7c0 at 0x140531676.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Why there is no store to 0x2448 - the initialisation, in full
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  The CDataCaoTraitement constructor zeroes the whole header by first putting its ADDRESS in a
  register, then writing nine qwords through that register:

      14051e1a4  488dbe48240000  LEA RDI,[RSI + 0x2448]     <- address of the header into RDI
      14051e1ab  33c0              XOR EAX,EAX
      14051e1ad  488907            MOV qword ptr [RDI],RAX          -> document+0x2448
      14051e1b0  48894708          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x8],RAX    -> document+0x2450
      14051e1b4  48894710          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x10],RAX   -> document+0x2458
      14051e1b8  48894718          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x18],RAX   -> document+0x2460
      14051e1bc  48894720          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x20],RAX   -> document+0x2468
      14051e1c0  48894728          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x28],RAX   -> document+0x2470
      14051e1c4  48894730          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x30],RAX   -> document+0x2478
      14051e1c8  48894738          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x38],RAX   -> document+0x2480
      14051e1cc  48894740          MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x40],RAX   -> document+0x2488

  This is the mechanism behind the whole result. Both fields the question names ARE written -
  document+0x2448 at 14051e1ad and document+0x2450 at 14051e1b0 - but the displacement in the
  instruction is +0 and +0x8, because the displacement 0x2448 lives in the LEA one line above.
  A search keyed on the literal displacement 0x2448 cannot see them, and a search keyed on a
  store to the memory operand at that displacement correctly returns nothing.

  I note that this is the same class of blind spot that has bitten this file more than once -
  a value formed by an address computation and then used through a register does not appear as
  the displacement in the using instruction. It is why the second half of the question was
  answered by following the pointer instead of by searching for it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The search, and its live control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  I searched the whole program for both displacements and classified every mention by whether
  the memory operand is the destination or the source.

      displacement 0x2448:  112 mentions in rendered instruction text
        - 0 whose destination operand is a qword reference at that displacement
        - 0 whose destination operand is ANY sized reference at that displacement
        - 34 LEAs forming the address
        - the remaining mentions are loads, e.g.
            14052534e  488b8748240000  MOV RAX,qword ptr [RDI + 0x2448]
            14052bdb6  498b8d48240000  MOV RCX,qword ptr [R13 + 0x2448]

      displacement 0x2450:  59 mentions
        - 0 stores of any width
        - 0 LEAs
        - all 59 are loads

  POSITIVE CONTROL, because a zero from a regex is worthless. I ran the identical
  destination-operand test for displacement 0x1da0, which the section "Stored pointer at 0x1da0"
  established has three qword stores. It returns exactly those three:

      1404fd617  48899fa01d0000  MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x1da0],RBX
      1404fe003  488981a01d0000  MOV qword ptr [RCX + 0x1da0],RAX
      1406c3acd  4889b7a01d0000  MOV qword ptr [RDI + 0x1da0],RSI

  Same search form, same code, non-zero result. So the zeros at 0x2448 and 0x2450 are
  measurements. I also confirmed the regex form itself against the raw text
  "MOV qword ptr [RCX + 0x1da0],RAX" before relying on it, having been burned earlier this
  session by a filter that could never match.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The tree-operating functions, and ReloadDoc's call order
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Since nothing writes the field directly, the operations on this tree go through the pointer.
  I took all 34 LEAs of document+0x2448, and for each found the next CALL in the same function.
  Sixteen distinct functions receive the header address:

      0x140541cc0  0x14051ff90  0x14045f700  0x14052b7c0  0x140547ff0  0x140548110
      0x14045bd70  0x14052b8a0  0x14052b260  0x14052aff0 0x14051d480 0x14061ee00
      0x14061ebd0 0x14061d3d0  0x14061d6d0  0x140620780

  Their callers, by name, are: CDataCaoTraitement (the constructor), ~CDataCaoTraitement,
  DeleteVector, PV_AffectIndResult, PV_EnvoiDesSkips, PV_EnvoiDesZoneComposants,
  PV_PostInitVecteur, PV_Prepare3dData (8 sites), PV_TriEtEnvoiDesMires, PrepareVecteur,
  DoDataExchange, and eight unnamed functions.

  I did not establish which of the sixteen is "the insert". I looked at the five that write node
  links, and none of them is a tree insert:

      0x14052b8a0  sums FUN_14052b7c0 over an array of stride 0x28 - a nested aggregate
      0x14052b260  walks the tree comparing a key against node+0x20 - a lower_bound SEARCH,
                   and on a miss it returns an empty result rather than linking anything
      0x14045bd70  sums sub-trees and appends into a std::vector - a COLLECTOR
      0x14061ebd0, 0x140620780  not examined in detail

  So I report the set without claiming which member inserts, rather than naming one.

  THE CALL-ORDER QUESTION, which is what the question actually turns on. ReloadDoc makes 27
  direct calls before 0x1406930f7 and 69 after it:

      1406930f7  e8f4bfffff  CALL 0x14068f0f0    <- PrepareExecData, re-derived from the rel32

  Cross-referencing ReloadDoc's direct call targets against all sixteen tree functions:

      tree functions called BEFORE 0x1406930f7    0
      tree functions called AFTER  0x1406930f7    0

  RELOADDOC CALLS NONE OF THEM, DIRECTLY, EITHER BEFORE OR AFTER. Its 27 pre-PrepareExecData
  calls are 0x1404d1d30, 0x14058b410, 0x1405b3f70, 0x1405b4180, 0x140527b50, 0x140671710,
  0x1406752f0, 0x140680030, 0x140682130, and 18 import thunks. None is in the tree set.

  The one near miss is worth recording so it is not mistaken for a hit. ReloadDoc DOES call
  0x1406975e0, and that function does form the header address at 0x14069765a and pass it to
  0x14045bd70 - but two things rule it out. It is called at

      140693988  e8533c0000  CALL 0x1406975e0

  which is AFTER the PrepareExecData call at 0x1406930f7, and 0x14045bd70 is a callee of
  0x1406975e0, not of ReloadDoc, so it is not a DIRECT call from ReloadDoc. Both facts were
  checked rather than assumed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. What this means

  The tree at document+0x2448 is populated through a pointer held in a register, never through
  a displacement, which is why a displacement-keyed search finds nothing and a register-keyed
  one finds thirty-four sites. The zeroing is done once in the CDataCaoTraitement constructor,
  and the sixteen functions that receive the header address are the tree's operations.

  ReloadDoc, the panel-load function, invokes none of them. So on this evidence the tree is not
  populated by the panel-load path - by the time PrepareExecData runs and FUN_14052b7c0 sums it,
  the tree's contents were placed by something else. That is consistent with the accumulated
  finding across this investigation that the panel-load path is connected to the zone-0 CHAIN
  but not to the structures the chain reads.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Limits, stated honestly
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * I did not identify which of the sixteen functions performs the node INSERT. I examined four
    of the five link-writing candidates and ruled those out; I did not examine 0x14061ebd0 or
    0x140620780. The call-order answer does not depend on which one it is, because the cross
    reference covers all sixteen.
  * The set of sixteen is what receives &document+0x2448 directly. A function that operates on a
    NODE obtained some other way, rather than on the header, would not be in it and would not be
    covered by the ReloadDoc cross-reference. I have not searched for that shape.
  * The ReloadDoc cross-reference is over DIRECT calls only, as the question specifies. If
    ReloadDoc reached a tree function through an intermediate, that would not appear - though the
    near miss in section 4 shows such a path does exist for 0x14045bd70, just not from ReloadDoc.
  * The "no store of any width" claim covers MOV and other plain stores to a memory operand at
    those displacements. A vectorised store such as MOVDQA or MOVUPS would have a different
    rendered form, and the classification I used required a `ptr [...]` destination matching the
    displacement, which such an instruction would also match - so I believe the claim covers
    them, but I did not enumerate mnemonics individually.
  * I did not check whether document+0x2450 is a field of the same structure or a separate one.
    The constructor zeroes it as the second qword after 0x2448, so they are adjacent, but what it
    means is not established here.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Verification record
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  * All 18 encodings quoted above were extracted from this payload and each re-read from memory:
    18/18 byte-exact. Two of them, the CALL encodings at 0x1406930f7 and 0x140693988, were wrong
    on my first transcription and the verification pass caught both; the corrected bytes are what
    appear above and in the payload.
  * Both call targets were RE-DERIVED from the rel32 rather than typed, and both match. The
    helper needed signed arithmetic for the negative displacement at 0x1406930f7 - the unsigned
    version produced 0x24068f0f0, and I self-tested the signed version against a known-good pair
    (0x14057c410 e88b290000 -> 0x14057eda0) before trusting it.
  * THE CENTRAL NEGATIVE HAS A LIVE CONTROL IN THE SAME FORM. The identical destination-operand
    test returns the three known 0x1da0 qword stores and zero for both displacements here.
  * The premise was verified by decompiling FUN_14052b7c0 and matching each field the question
    names - root, +0x20 skip against 0x100, the +0x30 minus +0x28 shift, the +0x19 nil flag, and
    the three link offsets - and by confirming that PV_AffectIndResult passes
    &document+0x2448 to it.
  * The ReloadDoc call-order figures - 27 before, 69 after, zero tree functions on either side -
    come from one pass over ReloadDoc's own listing, so the counts and the zero describe the same
    bytes.
